0466a49bfac3ba1a.bodyJa:
ローマ字で入力した文字列を、文脈に応じてかな漢字交じり文へ変換する macOS 向け入力メソッド（IME）「RomKana」が、個人開発の成果として公開された。最大の特徴は、変換処理をクラウドに頼らず手元のマシンで完結させる「完全ローカル」構成にある。開発者は「変換の賢さは、手元で動く LLM でどこまで上げられるのか」という問いを出発点に据えている。

日本語入力における従来のかな漢字変換は、辞書と統計的な言語モデルを組み合わせ、候補を確率的に並べる方式が主流だった。商用の ATOK や Google 日本語入力、macOS 標準の日本語入力なども、長年この枠組みを洗練させてきた。これに対し RomKana は、大規模言語モデル（LLM）が持つ文脈理解の力を変換そのものに取り込もうとする試みと位置づけられる。

macOS の IME は、Apple が提供する InputMethodKit フレームワーク上で構築する。アプリケーションから独立して常駐し、キー入力を受け取って変換候補を返す仕組みのため、応答速度が利用体験を大きく左右する。LLM を変換に用いる場合、推論のたびに待ち時間が生じやすく、軽快なタイピングと両立させるには、モデルの軽量化や処理の工夫が課題になると見られる。

ローカル実行を支える基盤としては、Apple Silicon 向けに最適化された MLX や、llama.cpp、Ollama といったツールが近年広く使われている。これらは比較的小さなパラメータ規模のモデルでも実用的な速度を引き出しやすく、個人の環境でも LLM を動かしやすくしている。こうしたエコシステムの成熟が、自作 IME を現実的にしている背景にあると言えそうだ。

完全ローカルという設計は、入力内容を外部に送信しない点でプライバシー上の利点があり、オフライン環境でも動作する。一方で、変換精度はローカルで動かせるモデルの性能に左右されるため、クラウド上の大規模モデルとどこまで肉薄できるかが焦点となる。今回の開発記は、手元の計算資源だけでどこまで「賢い変換」を実現できるかを探る実験的な取り組みとして、ローカル LLM 活用の一つの方向性を示すものと言えるだろう。
0466a49bfac3ba1a.bodyEn:
A developer has published a detailed log on Zenn describing how they built "RomKana," a custom input method (IME) for macOS that turns romaji keystrokes into mixed kana-kanji Japanese text while taking surrounding context into account. What distinguishes the project is that the entire conversion pipeline, including the language model that drives it, runs entirely on the local machine. The author frames the work around a single question: how far can a locally running large language model push the quality of Japanese text conversion? For anyone interested in on-device AI or in the long-standing problem of Japanese input, the write-up is a concrete case study in stitching these pieces together.

The challenge RomKana tackles is central to typing Japanese. Because the language leans heavily on homophones, a single phonetic string can map to many different kanji combinations, and choosing the right one frequently depends on the meaning of the whole sentence rather than the isolated word. Conventional kana-kanji conversion engines have addressed this for decades using large dictionaries combined with statistical or n-gram language models, and more recently neural approaches. These systems are fast and well tuned, but they can falter on ambiguous or context-heavy phrases. By routing the conversion step through an LLM, the author appears to be testing whether a model's broader contextual understanding can produce better guesses than the established methods, at least for certain inputs.

On the technical side, building any IME for macOS means working with Apple's Input Method Kit (IMK), the framework that lets third-party software register as a system-wide text input source and feed converted candidates back to whatever application currently has focus. RomKana sits in that layer, intercepting romaji input and returning kana-kanji output. The interesting part is what happens between those two points: instead of, or in addition to, a traditional dictionary lookup, the candidate generation is informed by a language model running on the same device. The development log is likely to cover the practical friction this introduces, since real-time typing demands low latency, and invoking even a compact model on every keystroke or phrase boundary can add noticeable delay compared with a purely dictionary-based engine.

This kind of local-LLM project has become more feasible because of recent tooling, particularly on Apple Silicon. Frameworks such as Apple's MLX, along with widely used runtimes like llama.cpp and Ollama, make it practical to run quantized models on a laptop without a dedicated server or cloud API. Quantization, which reduces the numerical precision of model weights, lowers memory use and speeds up inference, which matters a great deal when the goal is responsive typing. The exact model and configuration RomKana uses would determine the trade-off between conversion accuracy and speed, and that balance is one of the more instructive aspects such a development account can offer to other builders.

It helps to place RomKana against the existing landscape of Japanese IMEs. macOS ships with Apple's own Japanese input, and popular alternatives include Google Japanese Input, whose open-source core is known as Mozc, and the commercial ATOK. These mature products represent years of refinement in dictionaries, user-word learning, and conversion heuristics, so a hobbyist project is unlikely to match them outright in coverage or polish. The value of RomKana lies elsewhere: it explores an architecture where conversion intelligence comes from a general-purpose model rather than a hand-built engine, and it does so without sending keystrokes to a remote service.

That fully local design carries a clear privacy advantage, since text never leaves the device, which is meaningful for an input method that potentially sees everything a user types. It also makes the tool usable offline. The broader context is a steady shift toward running capable models on personal hardware, driven by improved small models, better quantization, and frameworks optimized for consumer chips. RomKana is one small, domain-specific example of that trend, applying it to a task that is deeply familiar to Japanese-language users yet rarely reimagined from scratch. Whether an LLM-backed approach can ultimately rival tuned conventional engines on speed and consistency remains an open question, but the project offers a transparent look at what is involved in trying.

a324ab5e2047be27.bodyJa:
AI エージェントに作業を任せたとき、途中まで進めただけで「完了しました」と満足げに停止してしまう——。そんな現象に悩むエンジニアは少なくない。アーキテクトのやまぱん！氏が公開した「goal-loop」は、エージェントにゴールへ到達するまで作業を続けさせることを狙った Agent Skill だという。

Agent Skill とは、AI エージェントに特定の手順や振る舞いを与えるための再利用可能な指示セットを指す。近年は Anthropic の Claude や GitHub Copilot など各社のエージェント機能が複雑なタスクを自律的にこなせるようになってきたが、その一方で「指示された範囲の一部だけを終えて止まる」「自己評価が甘く、未完成でも完了と判断する」といった課題が指摘されてきた。

goal-loop が解こうとするのは、まさにこの「やり切れなさ」だと見られる。一般にエージェントは与えられたコンテキストの中で次の行動を決めるため、ゴールの定義が曖昧だったり、途中で達成したと誤認したりすると作業を打ち切ってしまう。これに対し、ゴールの達成条件を明示し、未達であれば再びループして作業を継続させる仕組みを組み込むことで、最後までタスクを遂行させようという発想だと考えられる。

この種のアプローチは、エージェント設計における「自己検証」や「リフレクション(内省)」と呼ばれる手法とも親和性が高い。エージェントが自らの出力を評価し、目標未達であれば再試行するループは、近年の研究やフレームワークでも有効性が報告されている。LangChain をはじめとする各種エージェントフレームワークでも、計画・実行・検証を繰り返す構造が一般的になりつつある。

ただし、ループを過度に回せばトークン消費や実行時間が増大し、コスト面の負担になる可能性もある。終了条件の設計や、無限ループを避けるためのガードレールの整備が実運用では重要になるだろう。それでも、エージェントに「最後までやり切らせる」という観点は、自律型 AI を実務へ組み込むうえで避けて通れないテーマであり、goal-loop のような小さな工夫の積み重ねが、エージェント活用の質を左右していくと見られる。
a324ab5e2047be27.bodyEn:
AI coding agents have become capable enough to plan, write, and run multi-step work, yet anyone who has delegated a real task to one has probably hit a familiar failure mode: the agent does part of the job, announces success, and stops. A recent blog post on Qiita describes one engineer's response to this problem, an Agent Skill called "goal-loop" intended to keep an agent working until the original objective is genuinely met rather than until it merely appears finished.

The author, who identifies as a software architect, frames the issue in everyday terms. When handed a task, agents often halt partway through and report a satisfied-sounding completion that does not match what was actually requested. This gap between perceived completion and real completion is a recurring source of friction in agentic workflows, because it shifts the burden back to the human, who must notice the shortfall, re-prompt, and nudge the agent to continue. The goal-loop skill is presented as a way to close that gap at the level of the agent's own behavior.

To understand the contribution, it helps to know what an Agent Skill is. In the current generation of assistants, a skill is a packaged set of instructions and procedures that an agent can load into its working context to handle a particular kind of task in a consistent way. Anthropic has promoted the term "Agent Skills" for Claude, and comparable mechanisms exist elsewhere, including GitHub Copilot's custom instructions and the broader pattern of reusable prompts and tool definitions. Skills sit alongside related infrastructure such as the Model Context Protocol, which standardizes how agents connect to external tools and data. The goal-loop skill appears to apply this packaging idea not to a domain task but to the control flow of the agent itself.

Conceptually, a goal loop is a continuation-and-verification pattern. Rather than treating a task as done after a single pass, the agent is instructed to restate the goal explicitly, check its current output against defined completion criteria, and continue iterating if those criteria are not satisfied. Termination is meant to depend on verifiable conditions, such as tests passing, all subtasks being addressed, or requirements being demonstrably fulfilled, instead of on the model's internal sense that it has produced a reasonable-looking answer. In effect, the skill is likely encoding a checklist-driven loop that an agent runs against its own work before it is allowed to declare success.

This builds on established ideas in agent design. The ReAct pattern interleaves reasoning and action, while reflection or self-critique approaches ask a model to evaluate and revise its own output. Plan-and-execute architectures separate the act of forming a plan from the act of carrying it out and tracking progress. The goal-loop approach can be read as a lightweight, instruction-level version of these patterns, aimed specifically at the premature-stopping problem rather than at general planning.

The underlying reason agents stop early is worth noting as background. Large language models are trained to produce fluent, complete-sounding responses, and a clean conclusion is often statistically rewarded. Without an explicit termination check tied to verification, a model can mistake "I have described a plan" or "I have made visible progress" for "the task is finished." Tasks with many steps, ambiguous acceptance criteria, or long tool-use chains are especially prone to this, since the agent's context and attention can drift away from the original instruction.

For readers working with coding agents, the practical takeaway is that completion behavior can be shaped through instructions and skills, not just through model choice. Tools such as Cursor, Cline, and the agent modes in Copilot and similar assistants all expose ways to inject standing guidance, and a goal-loop style skill is one example of using that surface to enforce persistence and self-checking. The trade-off, which the post's framing implies but does not resolve, is that a loop pushed too hard can waste tokens, over-engineer, or stall on criteria that are hard to verify automatically, so sensible exit conditions matter as much as the insistence on continuing.

As an individual blog post on Qiita, the piece is best read as a practitioner's pattern and experience report rather than a benchmarked study, and its effectiveness will depend on the specific agent and task. Still, it reflects a broader industry shift from one-shot prompting toward durable, goal-directed agent behavior, and it offers a concrete, reusable framing for a problem many users will recognize.

8e307bf1944be1c6.bodyJa:
米紙ウォール・ストリート・ジャーナル(WSJ)の調査報道により、予測市場(プレディクション・マーケット)を運営するPolymarketが、利用者がSNS上で偽の賭けや架空の当選を祝う様子を撮影・投稿するよう報酬を支払っていた疑いが浮上した。WSJは1,100件を超える「欺瞞的」とされる動画を特定したという。

Polymarketは、特定の出来事の結果に対して資金を賭け、的中すれば配当を得られるオンライン市場で、ブロックチェーン上の暗号資産(主にステーブルコインのUSDC)を用いて取引が行われる。2024年の米大統領選を巡る賭けで一躍知名度を高め、選挙や経済指標、スポーツなどの帰結を予測するプラットフォームとして急成長した。

報道によれば、こうした動画はインフルエンサーや一般ユーザーが実際に大金を賭けて勝ったかのように演出し、視聴者に手軽に稼げるとの印象を与えるマーケティング手法の一環だった可能性がある。実際には賭けの内容や当選が事実と異なるケースが含まれていたとされ、誤情報(ミスインフォメーション)の拡散につながりかねない点が問題視されている。

予測市場を巡っては、米商品先物取引委員会(CFTC)などの規制当局が、賭博との線引きや消費者保護の観点から監視を強めてきた経緯がある。Polymarketは過去に米国内での提供を制限された一方、近年は規制環境の変化を背景に事業拡大を図っているとされる。競合のKalshiなども含め、予測市場は投資とギャンブルの境界が曖昧な領域として議論が続いている分野だ。

今回の報道内容が事実であれば、プラットフォームの信頼性やマーケティング倫理に対する批判が強まる可能性がある。SNS上で演出された「成功体験」が拡散すれば、リスクを十分に理解しないまま参入する利用者を増やしかねないとの懸念も指摘されている。現時点でPolymarket側の公式な反論や詳細な説明は限定的とみられ、今後の対応や規制当局の反応が注目される。
8e307bf1944be1c6.bodyEn:
Polymarket, the cryptocurrency-based prediction market that has become one of the most prominent venues for wagering on real-world events, is facing scrutiny over a reported campaign of deceptive promotional content. According to a Wall Street Journal investigation, the company has been paying people to film themselves placing fake bets and celebrating fake winnings on social media, with the WSJ identifying more than 1,100 such videos. The allegations matter because Polymarket has positioned itself as a source of crowd-sourced truth about elections, sports, and current events, and a coordinated effort to manufacture organic-looking enthusiasm would undercut that framing.

The reported scheme appears to follow a familiar influencer-marketing playbook, but with content designed to look authentic rather than sponsored. Rather than openly disclosing paid partnerships, the videos reportedly showed users acting out spontaneous betting moments and jubilant reactions to supposed payouts, creating the impression of widespread, genuine engagement on the platform. Such content is intended to drive new sign-ups by suggesting that ordinary people are winning money, a dynamic that regulators in several jurisdictions treat warily when the underlying claims are staged or unsubstantiated.

Polymarket operates as a decentralized prediction market built on blockchain infrastructure, where participants buy and sell shares tied to the outcome of future events. Prices on the platform are often interpreted as implied probabilities, and during the 2024 US election cycle the service drew significant attention as commentators cited its odds alongside traditional polling. That visibility helped the company raise substantial venture funding and cultivate a reputation as a real-money signal of public sentiment. Reports of paid, fabricated testimonials sit uncomfortably alongside that positioning, because the value of a prediction market depends heavily on the perception that its activity reflects authentic belief rather than manufactured hype.

The company has also been navigating a complex regulatory environment in the United States. Polymarket previously reached a settlement with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and for a period restricted access for US-based users, operating more freely in other markets. More recently, the broader prediction-market sector has seen shifting signals from regulators and a wave of mainstream interest, including moves by rival platforms and established financial firms to offer event-based contracts. That context makes questions about marketing conduct particularly sensitive, since trust and compliance are central to whether such markets can operate openly at scale.

The practice described in the report touches on long-standing concerns about misinformation and undisclosed advertising on social platforms. Authentic-seeming endorsement content that omits its paid nature can run afoul of advertising-disclosure rules, such as guidelines from the US Federal Trade Commission that require clear labeling of sponsored material. When the content also depicts fictional financial outcomes, it raises additional questions about whether viewers are being misled about the likelihood of profit. These are recurring issues across gambling, crypto, and trading-app marketing, where exaggerated success stories have repeatedly attracted criticism and enforcement attention.

It is worth noting that, based on the available summary, the reporting centers on the existence and volume of the videos rather than on a full accounting of who commissioned them or how the payments were structured. The scale cited by the WSJ, more than 1,100 videos, suggests an organized effort rather than isolated incidents, but the precise chain of responsibility and the company's internal role are likely to be examined further. Polymarket has not been described here as having confirmed the practice, and its response, along with any independent verification, will help clarify the full picture.

For readers, the episode is a reminder of how difficult it can be to distinguish genuine user enthusiasm from paid promotion in fast-growing fintech and crypto products. Prediction markets are frequently praised for aggregating dispersed information into a single price, but that mechanism only works if participation is real and the surrounding narrative is honest. If the reported videos were indeed staged and compensated, they would represent a form of social proof engineered to accelerate adoption. As prediction markets continue to move toward the mainstream, the accuracy of their marketing, and not just their odds, is likely to draw closer attention from journalists, regulators, and the platforms competing for the same audience.

81ad2fe1b39b5610.bodyJa:
物体検出モデル「YOLOv8」をAWS Lambda上で動作させ、HTTP経由で画像を送信して推論結果を得るAPIを構築する手法が、個人開発者による実践例として共有されている。常時稼働するサーバーを用意せず、サーバーレス基盤と機械学習モデルを組み合わせて物体検出機能を提供できる点が特徴だ。

YOLO（You Only Look Once）は、画像内の物体の位置と種類を一度の推論で高速に検出するモデル群で、現在はUltralytics社が開発・公開するYOLOv8が広く使われている。Pythonライブラリとして手軽に扱え、学習済みモデルを読み込めば数行のコードで推論を実行できる手軽さが普及の背景にある。

今回の構成では、このYOLOv8をAWS Lambdaにデプロイする。Lambdaはリクエストが来たときだけコードを実行するサーバーレス実行環境で、待機時のコストがかからない。ただしYOLOv8はPyTorchやOpenCVといった依存ライブラリが大きいため、ZIP形式ではなくコンテナイメージとしてデプロイする方式が一般的とされる。Lambdaは最大10GBのコンテナイメージに対応しており、機械学習モデルの配置にも向いている。

実際の利用では、API GatewayやLambdaの関数URLを介してHTTPエンドポイントを公開し、ローカルPCから画像をPOSTする。Lambda側で画像を受け取って推論し、検出した物体のラベルや座標（バウンディングボックス）、信頼度をJSON形式で返す流れになる。

この方式の利点は、スケーラビリティと運用負荷の低さにある。アクセスが増えてもLambdaが自動でスケールし、利用がなければ費用は発生しない。一方で、コールドスタート時にモデルの読み込みで遅延が生じる可能性があり、リアルタイム性や大量処理が求められる用途では、Amazon SageMakerやECS、GPU搭載のEC2など別の選択肢を検討する余地もある。

サーバーレスとAIモデルの組み合わせは、コスト最適化や軽量なサービス提供の観点から関心が高まっている分野だ。今回のような構成は、物体検出を小規模なサービスやプロトタイプとして素早く形にする際の実践的な一例と言えるだろう。
81ad2fe1b39b5610.bodyEn:
Running modern computer vision models without managing servers is becoming increasingly practical, and a recent walkthrough demonstrates exactly that by deploying YOLOv8 on AWS Lambda and exposing it as an HTTP API. The setup lets a developer send an image from a local machine via a POST request and receive object detection results in return. This matters because it shows how to package a deep learning model as an on-demand, pay-per-invocation service rather than running a continuously billed instance, lowering both the operational burden and idle cost for inference workloads.

YOLOv8 is an object detection model developed by Ultralytics, part of the long-running "You Only Look Once" family that prioritizes single-pass, real-time detection. Compared with earlier two-stage detectors, YOLO models process an entire image in one forward pass, predicting bounding boxes and class probabilities simultaneously. YOLOv8 ships in several sizes, from nano to extra-large, allowing a trade-off between accuracy and speed. The smaller variants are particularly relevant for serverless deployment because they reduce both the model footprint and the compute time, which directly affects Lambda cost and response latency.

The core architectural idea in the article is combining three elements: an AI model, a serverless runtime, and an API layer. AWS Lambda runs the inference code, but a standard Lambda deployment package is limited to 250 MB unzipped, which is too small for the PyTorch and Ultralytics dependencies plus model weights. The common solution, and the approach this kind of project typically relies on, is the container image format for Lambda, which supports images up to 10 GB. Developers build a Docker image containing Python, the inference libraries, and the model file, push it to Amazon Elastic Container Registry, and configure Lambda to use that image. This removes the dependency size constraint that otherwise makes machine learning on Lambda difficult.

On the request path, the image is sent from the local PC to an endpoint, the function decodes it, runs YOLOv8 inference, and returns the detected objects, usually as JSON containing class labels, confidence scores, and bounding box coordinates. Exposing the function is generally done either through Amazon API Gateway or a Lambda Function URL, the latter being a simpler built-in HTTPS endpoint. Because binary image data does not travel cleanly through some JSON-based request flows, payloads are often Base64-encoded, and API Gateway can be configured to handle binary media types. Understanding this encoding step is a prerequisite to making the POST workflow reliable.

Several practical considerations shape how well this design performs. Cold starts are the most prominent: when a container image has not been invoked recently, Lambda must initialize the environment and load the model into memory, which can add noticeable delay to the first request. Allocating more memory to the function also increases the proportional CPU share, so heavier memory settings can speed up inference even though the model runs on CPU rather than GPU. Lambda does not currently offer GPU acceleration, which means this approach is best suited to lighter models, moderate request volumes, or use cases that tolerate CPU-bound latency. For high-throughput or low-latency production needs, alternatives such as Amazon SageMaker endpoints, GPU-backed EC2 instances, or Amazon ECS may be more appropriate.

The broader context is a growing ecosystem of options for serving vision models. Some teams export YOLOv8 to ONNX or use ONNX Runtime to shrink dependencies and improve CPU inference speed, which can be especially valuable in a constrained serverless environment. Others rely on managed inference platforms or container orchestration when scaling demands grow. The serverless route remains attractive for prototypes, internal tools, and intermittent workloads because it scales to zero when unused and requires no instance management. It also pairs naturally with event-driven patterns, for example triggering detection automatically when an image is uploaded to Amazon S3.

For readers, the value of this kind of project is less about any single result and more about the reusable pattern it establishes. Once object detection is available behind a stable API, it can be integrated into web applications, mobile clients, or automated pipelines without redistributing model files or managing inference servers directly. The same container-based Lambda technique generalizes to other models and frameworks, making it a useful template. Anyone replicating it should weigh cold start behavior, payload size limits, timeout settings, and per-request cost against the simplicity and elasticity that a serverless deployment provides.

3911a18e4aece239.bodyJa:
AIエージェントと人間が同じ知識を共有できるようにする——。Google Cloudが公開したとされる「OKF（Open Knowledge Format）」は、そんな狙いを持つMarkdownベースの知識フォーマットだと紹介されている。エージェント開発が活発化するなか、知識の表現方法を標準化しようとする動きの一つとして注目される。

OKFの核となるのは、人間とAIの双方が読み書きできる形式で知識を記述するという発想だ。ベースにMarkdownを採用している点がポイントで、これは特別なツールがなくてもテキストエディタで開け、人間にとっても可読性が高いという利点がある。AIモデルもMarkdownを学習データとして大量に扱っているため、追加の変換コストを抑えながら情報を取り込みやすいと見られる。

背景には、生成AIの利用形態が「単発の質問応答」から「自律的に作業を進めるエージェント」へと移りつつある状況がある。エージェントが有用に動くには、社内ドキュメントや手順、ルールといった知識を継続的に参照する必要がある。しかし従来は、こうした知識をAIが扱いやすい形に整える方法が標準化されておらず、各社・各プロジェクトで独自の工夫を強いられていた。OKFはその共通土台を提供しようとする試みと位置づけられる。

類似の文脈では、AnthropicがAIと外部データ・ツールを接続する規格「MCP（Model Context Protocol）」を提唱しており、各社がエージェント関連の仕様づくりを競っている。知識をどう蓄積し参照するかという「RAG（検索拡張生成）」の発想とも親和性が高く、OKFはその知識データ側のフォーマットを整理する役割を担う可能性がある。

ただし、こうしたフォーマットは公開されただけで普及が約束されるわけではない。実際にどれだけのツールやサービスが対応し、エコシステムが育つかが定着の鍵となるだろう。仕様の詳細や正式な位置づけについては一次情報を確認しつつ、今後の対応状況を見守りたい。
3911a18e4aece239.bodyEn:
Google Cloud has introduced the Open Knowledge Format (OKF), a Markdown-based specification intended to let AI agents and humans read and write from the same body of knowledge. The format matters because the rapid spread of autonomous and semi-autonomous agents has exposed a recurring problem: the documents people write for each other are not always easy for machines to parse, while the structured data machines prefer is often unreadable to humans. OKF appears to be an attempt to bridge that gap with a single, lightweight representation that both sides can use.

At its core, OKF builds on Markdown, the plain-text formatting syntax already familiar to developers, technical writers, and many AI systems. By grounding the format in Markdown rather than a heavier schema such as XML or a proprietary binary structure, the design keeps documents legible to people who open them in any text editor, while remaining straightforward for language models to ingest. The stated goal is a shared knowledge layer where an update made by a human is immediately usable by an agent, and knowledge captured or refined by an agent remains transparent and editable by a human.

The practical appeal of this approach is tied to how modern AI agents actually consume information. Large language models are trained heavily on text, and Markdown is one of the formats they handle most reliably. Many retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG, pipelines already convert source documents into chunks of plain text or Markdown before feeding them to a model. A standardized knowledge format could reduce the custom preprocessing each team currently builds on its own, and make knowledge more portable between tools. If different agents and platforms agree on the same conventions, knowledge written once could in principle be reused across systems without bespoke conversion.

It helps to place OKF alongside other recent efforts in the same space. Anthropic's Model Context Protocol, or MCP, has gained attention as a standardized way for AI applications to connect to external data sources and tools, and it has been adopted by a growing number of vendors. The informal llms.txt proposal suggests websites publish a Markdown-friendly summary so language models can navigate them more easily. Vector databases, embeddings, and knowledge graphs all address related questions of how to store and surface information for AI. OKF seems to occupy a complementary niche, focusing less on the transport or retrieval mechanism and more on the format of the knowledge document itself. Whether it interoperates cleanly with these adjacent standards will likely shape how widely it is adopted.

For readers encountering OKF for the first time, a few prerequisite concepts are worth keeping in mind. An AI agent here refers to a system that can take in a goal, reason over available information, and act through tools or APIs, rather than simply answering a single prompt. Such agents depend on a reliable source of ground truth, often called a knowledge base, to avoid fabricating answers. The persistent challenge is keeping that knowledge accurate, current, and consistent as both humans and machines modify it. A format that is equally accessible to both audiences could ease the maintenance burden, though much depends on the surrounding tooling, governance, and how teams choose to structure their content.

Some caution is warranted. As the original write-up itself notes in a deliberately brief, high-level fashion, this is an early summary rather than an exhaustive technical review, and the broader significance of OKF will only become clear with real-world use. The field has seen many proposed standards, and adoption tends to hinge on developer convenience, ecosystem support, and whether major platforms commit to it. Google Cloud's backing gives OKF visibility, but it is too early to say whether it will become a durable convention or remain one option among several.

For now, the most useful takeaway is the underlying intent. OKF reflects a wider industry push toward shared, human-and-machine-readable knowledge as agents take on more substantive tasks. Teams already working with RAG systems, documentation pipelines, or agent frameworks may find it worth examining how a Markdown-based knowledge format could simplify their workflows, while watching how it fits with established approaches like MCP and existing knowledge management practices.

7c8955bdea5a805c.bodyJa:
Zenn の記事や本を VS Code、あるいは AI 統合エディタの Cursor で執筆するユーザー向けに、クリップボード内の画像をショートカットキー一発で貼り付けられる拡張機能「Zenn Image Paste」が公開された。Mac では Cmd+Alt+V、Windows では Ctrl+Alt+V を押すだけで、画像の保存と Markdown リンクの挿入がまとめて完了する点が特徴だ。

技術記事や同人誌を投稿できる Zenn は、GitHub リポジトリと連携してローカルで Markdown を編集する執筆スタイルを公式にサポートしている。専用の zenn-cli を使えば、手元のエディタで書いた内容をブラウザ上でプレビューしながら執筆できる。一方で、画像を扱う作業は手数が多い。スクリーンショットなどをいったんファイルとして保存し、所定の images フォルダへ配置したうえで、Markdown の画像記法を手書きする必要があり、執筆のテンポを損ねやすかった。

今回の拡張機能は、この一連の流れを自動化するものだ。クリップボードにコピーした画像をショートカットで貼り付けると、画像ファイルが適切な場所へ書き出され、同時にカーソル位置に対応する Markdown 記法が挿入される仕組みと見られる。Zenn のディレクトリ構成を前提に設計されているため、保存先の指定やパスの調整といった煩雑な操作を省ける点が利点になりそうだ。

画像貼り付けの支援自体は、VS Code 本体にも近年「Paste Image」に相当する機能が標準で備わりつつあり、関連する拡張機能も複数存在する。ただし、それらは汎用的な挙動が中心で、Zenn 特有のフォルダ規約やリンク形式に最適化されているとは限らない。特定のプラットフォームに合わせて細部を作り込んだツールには、執筆者の手間を確実に減らせる余地がある。

近年は Cursor をはじめ、VS Code をベースにした派生エディタや AI 補助機能の普及により、技術記事をローカル環境で書く人が増えている。こうした拡張機能は、日常的な執筆作業の小さな摩擦を取り除くものであり、同様にニッチな改善を狙ったツールが今後も登場する可能性がある。
7c8955bdea5a805c.bodyEn:
Writing technical articles often means peppering the text with screenshots, and few platforms make that workflow as Git-friendly, or as fiddly, as Zenn. A newly released Visual Studio Code extension called Zenn Image Paste aims to remove one of the most repetitive steps in that process: it lets authors paste an image from the clipboard directly into a Markdown file with a single keyboard shortcut, Cmd+Alt+V on macOS or Ctrl+Alt+V on Windows.

Zenn is a popular Japanese platform for publishing technical articles and books. Its distinguishing feature is a Git-based authoring model: instead of writing in a web editor, many authors use the official zenn-cli to compose Markdown locally, preview it in the browser, and publish by pushing to a connected GitHub repository. Images are stored as files inside an images directory in the repository and referenced from the Markdown with relative paths. This keeps content portable and version-controlled, but it also means that adding a screenshot normally involves several manual steps.

Without tooling, the typical sequence is to take a screenshot, save it to disk, move or rename the file into the project's images folder, and then type out the Markdown image syntax with the correct path. Repeating that for every figure in a long tutorial is tedious and error-prone, particularly when it comes to keeping file names unique and paths accurate. Zenn Image Paste appears to collapse all of that into one keystroke: copy an image to the clipboard, press the shortcut, and the extension writes the image file into the appropriate location and inserts the Markdown reference at the cursor.

The extension is explicitly positioned for both VS Code and Cursor. Cursor is an AI-focused code editor built as a fork of VS Code, which means it shares the same extension architecture and can run most VS Code extensions. Calling out Cursor support is increasingly common for new tooling, reflecting the editor's growing adoption among developers who also write about their work.

It is worth noting that VS Code already includes a built-in capability to paste or drag images into Markdown files, a feature that arrived in 2023. That native function copies the image into the workspace and inserts a Markdown link. A dedicated extension like Zenn Image Paste is likely valuable because it tailors the behavior to Zenn's specific conventions, such as the expected images directory structure, naming patterns, and the relative path format that Zenn's renderer expects. By binding the action to a distinct shortcut, it can also coexist with the editor's default paste behavior rather than overriding it.

For anyone unfamiliar with the broader ecosystem, the zenn-cli is the foundation of this local-first workflow. Authors typically run a command to scaffold a new article or book, which generates a Markdown file with front matter for metadata such as the title, an emoji, the type, and a published flag. The CLI also serves a live preview that mirrors how the content will look once published. Extensions that streamline editing, linting, or asset management slot naturally into that setup, and image pasting is one of the more obvious friction points to address.

The release fits a wider pattern of small, focused productivity tools built around content platforms and modern editors. As more developers maintain technical blogs alongside their code, utilities that shave seconds off routine actions can add up over the course of writing a detailed, image-heavy guide. The single-shortcut approach also lowers the barrier for newcomers who may not yet be comfortable with Zenn's directory layout.

As with any third-party extension, prospective users will want to confirm details such as where images are saved, how files are named, whether the path format matches their repository structure, and which image formats are supported. Those specifics determine how cleanly the tool drops into an existing project. For authors who frequently publish on Zenn from VS Code or Cursor, however, an extension that turns image insertion into a one-press operation is a practical, if narrowly scoped, convenience that targets a genuine and familiar pain point in the writing process.

c0e80c3aa5f7ccc1.bodyJa:
Chrome DevTools MCPは、AIエージェントが実際に動作しているChromeブラウザを直接操作し、その内部状態を検査できるようにするためのツールである。生成AIによるコーディング支援が一般化するなか、ブラウザ上の実挙動をAIに「見せる」手段を提供する点で、Web開発のデバッグ体験を変える可能性がある。

MCP(Model Context Protocol)は、AIモデルと外部ツールやデータソースをつなぐためのオープンな規格で、2024年にAnthropicが提唱した。対応するアプリケーション(MCPクライアント)からサーバーを介して、ファイル操作やAPI呼び出しといった機能を共通の作法で利用できる。Chrome DevTools MCPは、このサーバーの一つとして、Chrome開発チームが提供しているものだ。

従来、AIアシスタントが生成したコードがブラウザ上で意図通り動くかどうかは、人間が画面を確認してフィードバックする必要があった。Chrome DevTools MCPを導入すると、AI側がページへのアクセス、DOMの確認、コンソールのエラーログ取得、ネットワークリクエストの検査、パフォーマンス計測、スクリーンショット取得などをツールとして実行できる。つまりAIが自ら現象を観測し、修正案を検証する一連のループを回しやすくなる。

導入はNode.js環境を前提とし、npx経由でサーバーを起動する形が一般的だ。VS CodeのGitHub Copilotや、Claude、CursorといったMCPに対応する各種クライアントの設定ファイルにサーバー情報を追記することで利用できる。背後では、ブラウザ自動化で実績のあるChrome DevTools Protocol(CDP)やPuppeteer系の仕組みが使われているとされる。

同種の取り組みとしては、ブラウザ操作を担うPlaywright MCPなども登場しており、AIに「目」と「手」を与える流れは加速している。一方で、AIが任意のページにアクセスしたりコードを実行したりできる以上、認証情報の扱いや意図しない操作のリスクには注意が必要だ。検証用のプロファイルを分ける、扱う権限を絞るなど、運用面での配慮が求められる場面もあるだろう。記事の筆者が「幸福度が上がった」と表現するように開発体験の向上は期待できるが、導入効果は対象とするワークフローによって差が出ると見られる。
c0e80c3aa5f7ccc1.bodyEn:
Chrome DevTools MCP is an emerging way to give AI coding assistants direct, structured access to a live Chrome browser, and for many web developers it is changing how front-end debugging gets done. The tool exposes Chrome's debugging capabilities through the Model Context Protocol, the open standard that lets large language model agents call external tools in a consistent way. The practical upshot is that an AI assistant inside an editor such as Visual Studio Code can open a page, inspect what is happening, and reason about real browser behavior rather than guessing from source code alone.

To understand why this matters, it helps to recall what the Model Context Protocol is. MCP was introduced by Anthropic in late 2024 as a standardized interface between AI models and the outside world. Instead of every tool inventing its own integration, an MCP server advertises a set of capabilities, and any MCP-compatible client, including Claude Desktop, VS Code with GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and others, can call them. The protocol has since gained broad industry support, with major vendors shipping clients and servers, which is part of why a browser-focused server like this one slots in so easily.

Chrome DevTools MCP, published by the Chrome team, wraps the Chrome DevTools Protocol and the Puppeteer automation library behind that MCP interface. In concrete terms, it lets an agent perform tasks that previously required a human sitting in front of the DevTools panel. It can navigate to URLs, click and type to reproduce user flows, read the DOM and accessibility tree, capture screenshots, and pull console messages and network requests. It also surfaces performance tooling, so an agent can record a trace and report on metrics like Core Web Vitals. Because the agent sees actual runtime state, it can close the common gap where an assistant suggests a fix based on the code but never confirms whether the page actually behaves as expected.

Setup generally follows the same pattern as other MCP servers. The package is distributed through npm and is typically launched with a runner such as npx, then registered in the host application's MCP configuration. In VS Code, this means adding an entry that points to the server command so the assistant can discover the available browser tools. The Chrome team has positioned the project as relatively easy to adopt, and the main prerequisites are a recent Node.js installation and a Chrome binary the server can drive. As with any tool that automates a browser and reads page content, it is sensible to be mindful of what sites and credentials the agent is allowed to touch.

A typical workflow looks like this. A developer describes a bug, the assistant opens the affected page, reproduces the steps, reads the console for errors, and inspects the network panel for failed requests. It can then propose a code change and, after the change is applied, reload the page to verify the result. This loop of observe, hypothesize, fix, and confirm is what users tend to describe as the satisfying part, since it removes a lot of manual copying of error messages and back-and-forth context switching.

It is worth placing the tool in context, because it is not the only option. Microsoft maintains Playwright MCP, which similarly lets agents drive browsers across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit, and there are several Puppeteer-based MCP servers as well. The distinction is largely one of emphasis. Playwright MCP leans toward cross-browser automation and testing scenarios, while Chrome DevTools MCP leans toward the inspection and diagnostic features that the DevTools panel is known for, such as performance traces and detailed console and network access. Which one fits best appears to depend on whether the priority is end-to-end test automation or deep debugging of a single Chromium-based target.

The broader trend here is the move from chat-only AI assistance toward agents that can act on real systems through standardized connectors. Browser access is a natural early target because so much development work is visual and stateful. None of this removes the need for developer judgment; the assistant can misread a page or propose an incorrect fix, and its observations are only as reliable as the tools it calls. Still, for the everyday grind of front-end debugging, a well-configured Chrome DevTools MCP setup can meaningfully shorten the feedback loop, which likely explains the enthusiastic reactions from those who have tried it.

2de9dab0423dccf4.bodyJa:
近年、LLMに繰り返し使えるプロンプトそのものを作らせる「メタプロンプト」的な手法が広がっている。ただ、生成された汎用プロンプトには毎回似たような修正を加える必要が生じやすい。Qiitaで公開された記事「LLMのプロンプト原則」は、この手戻りを減らすため、良いプロンプトを書くための原則を整理し、再利用可能な「Skill」としてまとめた取り組みを紹介している。

背景には、コーディング支援ツールが指示内容を外部ファイル化する流れがある。GitHub Copilotには、リポジトリ単位で振る舞いを定義するcopilot-instructions.mdやカスタムインストラクションの仕組みがあり、CursorやClineなど他のツールも同様のルールファイルを備える。こうしたInstructionファイルやCustomizationファイルをLLM自身に書かせると、文章としては成立していても、曖昧な表現や過剰な指示、コンテキスト不足といった共通の弱点が表れやすい。

記事が提案するのは、その弱点を先回りで潰すための原則をあらかじめSkillとして与えるアプローチだと見られる。Skillは、特定の作業手順や知識をモジュール化してLLMに参照させる仕組みで、Anthropicが示すAgent Skillsのように、必要なときだけ呼び出して使える形が広がりつつある。プロンプト生成のたびに同じ注意点を人手で指摘する代わりに、原則を一度Skill化しておけば、以降の生成物に自動的に反映されることが期待できる。

この発想は、ソフトウェア開発でいう「繰り返しを避ける」考え方をプロンプト設計に持ち込んだものと言える。プロンプトの良し悪しはタスクや対象モデルによって変わるため、原則がそのまま万能に機能するとは限らないが、修正履歴を暗黙知のまま放置せず、明文化して資産化する点に実用上の価値がある。LLMの出力を制御する手段が、個別の文言調整から再利用可能なルールセットの設計へと比重を移しつつある現状を示す一例と言えそうだ。
2de9dab0423dccf4.bodyEn:
When developers ask a large language model to write reusable prompt artifacts, such as instruction files or customization files, they often find themselves making the same edits over and over. This blog post, published on Qiita under the Copilot category, describes one practitioner's response to that recurring friction: distilling a set of "prompt principles" and packaging them as a Skill so the model can apply them consistently rather than requiring repeated manual correction.

The underlying problem is familiar to anyone who has used LLMs to generate their own configuration. Tools such as GitHub Copilot support instruction files, often stored as a copilot-instructions file in a repository, that shape how the assistant responds across a project. Customization files and similar mechanisms let teams encode conventions, tone, and constraints once and reuse them. The appeal is obvious, but the practice has a catch. When the LLM itself drafts these general-purpose prompts, the output tends to drift toward vague, verbose, or inconsistent phrasing. The author notes that this leads to repeating similar fixes every time, which undermines the time savings that automation was supposed to provide.

The proposed solution treats the problem one level up. Instead of correcting each generated prompt by hand, the author appears to have written down the principles behind those corrections and stored them in a Skill. The term Skill here aligns with a broader industry pattern in which reusable instructions, and sometimes accompanying scripts or resources, are bundled so an agent can load them on demand. Anthropic, for example, has promoted the idea of Agent Skills for Claude, where a folder of instructions and supporting files extends what a model can reliably do. By encoding prompt-writing guidance as a Skill, the model can consult those rules whenever it produces a new instruction or customization file, which should reduce the need for the same downstream edits.

The article is structured around two layers, according to the summary. The first is the set of principles themselves, the general rules that good prompts should follow. The second covers how each principle is intended to be used in practice. This separation is sensible because prompt guidance is most useful when it is both stated and operationalized. A principle that says, for instance, to prefer specific and testable instructions has limited value unless it is paired with examples of how to rewrite a weak prompt into a stronger one. While the exact contents of the principles are not fully reproduced in the summary, common prompt-engineering guidance typically emphasizes clarity, explicit constraints, defined output formats, role and context setting, and avoiding ambiguity, so the principles likely cover similar ground tailored to instruction-file generation.

This approach reflects a wider trend toward configuration-as-context across coding assistants. Beyond Copilot's instruction files, editors and agents such as Cursor use rules files, and many teams maintain project-level prompt libraries that travel with their codebases. Packaging guidance as a Skill rather than pasting it into every prompt is an attempt to make that context modular and version-controlled, so it can be maintained like any other engineering asset. It also shifts effort from reactive correction toward proactive specification, which is generally considered a more scalable way to work with non-deterministic systems.

There are limits worth keeping in mind. LLMs do not always follow instructions reliably, so even a well-designed Skill is unlikely to eliminate every manual fix; it is more accurate to expect it to reduce their frequency. The effectiveness of such principles can also vary across models and versions, and prompt guidance that works well today may need revision as underlying models change. Readers evaluating this technique should treat it as a practical pattern to adapt rather than a finished standard, and they would benefit from testing the principles against their own recurring corrections.

For practitioners exploring this space, the broader takeaway is that prompts are increasingly treated as software artifacts, with their own conventions, reuse strategies, and review processes. Capturing hard-won corrections as explicit principles, and making those principles loadable through a Skill or instruction file, is a concrete step toward that discipline. Whether or not the specific principles in this post fit a given workflow, the meta-idea of letting an LLM write prompts while constraining it with codified guidance is likely to remain relevant as these tools mature.

e570eea9592c4af3.bodyJa:
「空飛ぶクルマ」とも呼ばれる電動垂直離着陸機（eVTOL）は、都市部の渋滞を回避する次世代モビリティとして期待を集めてきた。だが、米メディアThe Vergeのニュースレター「The Stepback」が指摘するように、業界各社はいま相次ぐ訴訟に足を取られ、商用サービス実現への道のりが法廷闘争によって大きく遅れている。

eVTOLは複数のローターを電動モーターで駆動し、ヘリコプターのように垂直に離着陸しながら、固定翼機に近い効率で水平飛行する航空機を指す。騒音や排出ガスを抑えつつ、空港アクセスや都市間移動を数分で結ぶ構想で、米JobyやArcher、英Vertical Aerospace、独Liliumといった新興企業がしのぎを削ってきた。ボーイング系のWiskやエアバスも開発に取り組んでいる。

訴訟の火種は多岐にわたる。企業間では営業秘密の不正取得や特許侵害、人材の引き抜きをめぐる争いが起きやすい。実際、JobyとArcherは過去に営業秘密をめぐって法廷で対立し、後に和解した経緯がある。加えて、騒音や安全性を懸念する地域住民や自治体との摩擦、認証手続きをめぐる規制当局とのやり取りも、事業計画を遅らせる要因になり得るとみられる。

背景には、eVTOL業界が巨額の資金を投じながらも、まだ本格的な収益化に至っていない事情がある。多くの企業は米連邦航空局（FAA）や欧州航空安全機関（EASA）による型式証明の取得を進めている最中で、認証の遅れは資金繰りや株価に直結する。開発の長期化によって経営難に陥る企業も出ており、訴訟費用の負担はスタートアップにとって決して軽くない。

商用化の時期について各社はこれまで楽観的な見通しを示してきたが、知的財産や規制をめぐる紛争が長引けば、サービス開始がさらに後ろ倒しになる可能性がある。空のモビリティが社会に根づくには、技術や安全性の証明だけでなく、こうした法的・制度的な調整をどう乗り越えるかが鍵になりそうだ。
e570eea9592c4af3.bodyEn:
Electric air taxis, long pitched as the future of urban transportation, are increasingly spending their time in courtrooms rather than the skies. The eVTOL (electric vertical takeoff and landing) industry, which promises quiet, emissions-free flights that could carry passengers over congested cities, is facing a thickening tangle of lawsuits that threaten to slow an already lengthy march toward commercial service.

These legal disputes touch on some of the most sensitive issues in any young, capital-intensive sector: intellectual property, trade secrets, and the movement of engineers between rival firms. Because eVTOL aircraft depend on closely guarded designs for batteries, electric motors, flight-control software, and lightweight airframes, the companies building them have powerful incentives to protect their work and equally powerful incentives to recruit experienced talent from competitors. That combination has repeatedly proven combustible.

The most prominent example is the clash between Wisk Aero and Archer Aviation. Wisk, which is backed by Boeing, accused Archer of misappropriating trade secrets and infringing patents after a group of engineers departed to join the rival startup. Archer denied wrongdoing, and the matter was ultimately settled, with Boeing taking a stake in Archer as part of the resolution. The episode highlighted how easily the tight-knit world of aerospace engineering, where talent circulates among a handful of well-funded firms, can spill into the courts.

Litigation is only one of several headwinds. The defining bottleneck for the industry remains certification. To carry paying passengers, an aircraft must earn type certification from aviation regulators such as the Federal Aviation Administration in the United States and the European Union Aviation Safety Agency, a process that involves demonstrating that novel designs meet rigorous safety standards. For vehicles that combine features of helicopters and fixed-wing aircraft with all-electric propulsion, regulators have had to craft new rules, and the timeline has repeatedly slipped. Lawsuits add a parallel source of delay, diverting money and management attention while creating uncertainty for investors weighing whether to keep funding companies that are years away from meaningful revenue.

The financial backdrop heightens the stakes. Many leading developers, including Joby Aviation, Archer, and several European players, went public through special-purpose acquisition company mergers around 2020 and 2021, raising large sums on optimistic projections. Some have since faced shareholder scrutiny, short-seller reports questioning their progress, and pressure to show concrete milestones. At least one prominent entrant, Lilium, encountered severe financial difficulties, a reminder that the path from prototype to profitable service is steep. In that environment, a protracted lawsuit can be more than a nuisance; it can shape a company's ability to raise the next round of capital.

It is worth noting what these companies are actually trying to build. The vision of urban air mobility imagines a network of small, electrically powered aircraft taking off vertically from rooftop or ground-level "vertiports," carrying a few passengers on short hops between airports, suburbs, and city centers. Proponents argue the vehicles will be quieter and cleaner than helicopters and, eventually, affordable enough to compete with ground transportation. Skeptics question whether the economics work, whether cities will permit the necessary infrastructure, and whether public acceptance of low-flying autonomous or piloted aircraft will materialize. Adjacent efforts, including drone delivery programs and broader advanced air mobility initiatives, share many of the same regulatory and infrastructure questions.

The current wave of litigation does not appear to threaten the underlying technology, which continues to advance through test flights and incremental certification steps. Rather, it reflects the friction that tends to accompany any emerging field where the potential rewards are large, the talent pool is small, and the intellectual property is valuable. As more companies approach the point of actually flying passengers, disputes over who owns which innovations are likely to intensify rather than fade.

For now, the promise of hailing an air taxi from a smartphone remains on the horizon rather than at hand. Whether the industry can untangle itself from the courtroom quickly enough to meet its own ambitious timelines is, like much else about flying cars, still an open question.

7d9d6f0e93bf0452.bodyJa:
Visual Studio Code（VS Code）でGitHub Copilotとやり取りしたチャットのセッションが、ワークスペースの保存を忘れたまま閉じてしまったために見えなくなる——。こうしたトラブルに対処するため、Windows環境でセッションを復元するスクリプトが、QiitaのVS Code関連ブログで紹介された。

投稿者によれば、会社で約1か月にわたって続けていたCopilotとのやり取りが、ワークスペースを保存し忘れていたことで軒並み表示されなくなったという。これがスクリプトを作成した直接のきっかけとされる。前提はWindows PCでの開発で、対象は「保存を忘れてワークスペースを閉じてしまい、残しておきたかったセッション」を抱えるユーザーだ。

背景を補足すると、VS CodeはチャットやワークスペースごとのデータをユーザープロファイルのAppData配下などに保存する仕組みを持つ。Copilot Chatの履歴も内部的にはこうしたストレージへ書き出されると見られるが、ワークスペースを明示的に保存していない場合、再び開いた際にセッションとの関連付けがうまくたどれず、UI上から履歴が見えなくなる可能性がある。逆に言えば、ファイルとして残っているデータを探し出して読み込み直せれば、過去のやり取りを取り戻せる余地がある、という発想に基づくアプローチだ。

GitHub Copilotはコードのインライン補完だけでなく、Copilot Chatによる対話的な支援機能を備えており、近年はエージェント的な機能の拡充も進む。長い対話の文脈そのものが開発上の資産となるケースは増えており、セッションの消失は作業効率に直結しうる。VS Code側でもチャット履歴の管理機能は強化されてきているが、操作ミスや設定の行き違いで履歴を見失う状況は依然として起こり得る。

今回紹介されたようなスクリプトは公式機能ではなく、あくまで個人が自身の環境で動かした復旧手段である点には留意したい。ファイルの保存場所やフォーマットはVS CodeやCopilotのバージョン更新で変わる可能性があり、環境によってはそのまま動作しない場合もある。実行前にはデータのバックアップを取り、処理内容を理解したうえで利用することが望ましいだろう。
7d9d6f0e93bf0452.bodyEn:
Visual Studio Code's integration with GitHub Copilot has turned the chat panel into a working notebook where developers accumulate weeks of context, decisions, and iterative problem-solving, so losing that history can be a real setback. A recent Qiita blog post documents a small Windows-focused script built to recover Copilot chat sessions that became inaccessible after a workspace was closed without being saved, and it offers a useful window into where VS Code keeps this data and how it can sometimes be retrieved.

The author's motivation was concrete. About a month of conversations with Copilot at work stopped appearing in the interface because the workspace had never been explicitly saved as a .code-workspace file. In VS Code, chat sessions are associated with the context in which they were created. Opening a loose folder, an unsaved workspace, or a different combination of folders can change which stored sessions the editor links to the current window, so a conversation that was visible one day can appear to be gone the next even when the underlying files still exist on disk.

That distinction, between data that is genuinely deleted and data that is merely unlinked from the current view, is what makes recovery possible. On Windows, VS Code stores per-workspace state under the user's application data directory, typically beneath %APPDATA%\Code\User\workspaceStorage. Each workspace the editor has opened receives a subfolder identified by a hash, and inside these folders VS Code keeps state databases and JSON files, including chat history connected to Copilot. Because those files usually remain after a workspace is closed, the data is often still present; the difficulty lies in finding the right folder among many and reassociating it with a usable session.

The script described in the post appears to automate what is otherwise a tedious manual search. Instead of opening each hashed folder by hand, a script can enumerate the workspaceStorage subdirectories, read the relevant JSON, and surface candidate sessions so the wanted conversation can be identified and restored or copied out. On Windows this kind of task fits PowerShell well, since it can recursively scan directories, parse JSON natively, and filter results by timestamp or text content. The general technique is not specific to Copilot; similar approaches have long been used to recover other VS Code workspace state.
