The change, announced in the GitHub changelog, is aimed at giving organizations more control over how they compose and maintain the pipelines that produce the virtual machine images on which their continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) jobs run.

Custom images for GitHub-hosted runners let teams pre-install software, tools, dependencies, and configuration into a runner image so that workflows start faster and execute in a consistent, controlled environment. Until now, each custom image was typically generated from a standard base image that GitHub maintains. With the new capability, an existing custom image can itself serve as the starting point for a subsequent image build, effectively enabling a layered or chained approach to image creation.

The practical effect is that organizations can separate their image-building process into reusable stages. A platform or infrastructure team might, for example, maintain a hardened base layer that includes security agents, certificates, and baseline tooling, while individual teams extend that shared image with language runtimes, SDKs, or project-specific dependencies. This reduces duplication, because common setup steps no longer need to be repeated in every image definition, and it can shorten build times since the shared groundwork is already in place.

This model resembles patterns that are already familiar from container images, where a Dockerfile frequently begins with a FROM instruction that references another image. Applying a similar inheritance concept to full runner images appears intended to bring comparable modularity to virtual machine image generation, where rebuilding everything from scratch can be time-consuming and resource-intensive.

GitHub-hosted runners are the managed compute environments that execute Actions workflows without requiring users to provision and maintain their own machines. Over the past few years GitHub has broadened this offering with larger runners that provide more CPU and memory, support for different operating systems and architectures including arm64, and additional networking and security controls. Custom images fit into this broader effort to give larger organizations the kind of governance and standardization they expect, while retaining the convenience of a fully managed runner fleet.

The ability to build images from other custom images also has implications for governance and supply-chain management. By centralizing a trusted base image and requiring downstream images to build on top of it, security and platform teams can enforce a consistent foundation across many projects. Changes to the base image can then propagate to dependent images through subsequent rebuilds, which may simplify patching and policy updates compared with managing many independent image definitions.

Teams that build runner images often rely on tooling such as HashiCorp Packer or scripts derived from the open-source runner-images repository that GitHub uses to produce its standard images. Self-hosted runner users have long composed their own environments using virtual machine templates or container images, and the custom image feature brings a more managed version of that flexibility to the hosted offering. Organizations evaluating the feature will likely want to consider how image versioning, naming, and lifecycle management work in practice, since chained images introduce dependencies between build artifacts that need to be tracked.

As with other runner features, the specifics of availability, pricing, and any limits on how deeply images can be layered are governed by GitHub's documentation and may depend on a plan or enrollment in particular runner programs. Readers should consult the official GitHub Actions documentation for the exact configuration steps and supported scenarios, as details can change as the feature matures.

Overall, the addition is an incremental but practical enhancement rather than a fundamental change to how Actions works. For organizations that maintain a fleet of custom runner images, the option to build one custom image from another offers a more modular workflow that mirrors established practices elsewhere in the software supply chain. It is likely to be most valuable to platform teams seeking to standardize environments across many repositories, while smaller projects that rely on a single image may see more modest benefits. As the wider Actions ecosystem continues to emphasize speed, reproducibility, and security, capabilities like layered image builds reflect a steady move toward treating runner environments as managed, versioned artifacts.

f81e86d7cc0337d9.bodyJa:
Anthropic が提供する CLI ベースのコーディング支援ツール「Claude Code」の最新版 v2.1.181 が公開された。マイナーバージョンながら、日常的な開発作業に影響する複数の重大バグ修正を含む点が特徴とされ、既存ユーザーには早めの更新が有用なリリースと位置づけられている。

Claude Code は、ターミナル上で動作し、自然言語の指示からコードの生成・編集やファイル操作、テスト実行までを比較的自律的に進めるエージェント型ツールである。GitHub Copilot や Cursor、OpenAI の Codex CLI、Google の Gemini CLI などと並び、近年急速に広がる「AI コーディングエージェント」の一角を占める。短い間隔でのリリースを重ね、細かな改善や修正を継続的に積み上げているのも特徴だ。

今回のリリースで注目されているのが、設定操作に用いる /config コマンドの構文に関する変更だ。Claude Code では、モデルの選択や各種挙動の調整、権限まわりの設定を、スラッシュコマンドや設定ファイルで管理する仕組みを採用している。/config の扱いが見直されることで、設定の指定方法がより明確になる可能性がある一方、利用しているスクリプトや手順によっては従来の書き方を見直す必要が生じる場合もあり、変更点の確認が望ましい。

加えて本バージョンでは、プロンプト処理など中核的な動作に関わる不具合の修正が含まれるとされる。エージェント型ツールでは、指示の解釈やセッションの状態管理に関わる不具合が作業全体の信頼性に直結するため、こうした修正は地味ながら影響が大きいと考えられる。

Claude Code のようなツールは更新頻度が高く、リリースごとに挙動が変わることも少なくない。チームで利用する場合は、バージョンを固定したうえで変更履歴(チェンジログ)を追い、影響範囲を見極めてから更新する運用が無難だろう。具体的な修正内容については公式のリリースノートを確認し、自身の環境で動作を検証することが推奨される。
f81e86d7cc0337d9.bodyEn:
Claude Code v2.1.181 is the latest point release of Anthropic's terminal-based coding assistant, and the source describes it as more consequential than its incremental version number suggests. According to the original write-up, the update is not a routine maintenance build but a release that resolves several bugs affecting everyday development workflows, alongside a refresh of the /config command syntax. For teams that have embedded Claude Code into their daily routines, these changes appear to matter more in practice than the small jump in version number implies.

The headline change is the revised /config syntax. In Claude Code, slash commands are the primary way to control the tool from inside an interactive session, and /config governs how preferences and project-level settings are read and applied. Adjusting the syntax of such a command is significant because it touches muscle memory and any scripts or documented procedures that reference the old form. Users who maintain shared onboarding notes or internal wikis will likely need to confirm whether existing examples still work as written, since even minor syntax adjustments can break copied-and-pasted commands. The source frames this as one of the three most notable items in the release, though the full enumeration of those points is truncated in the available summary.

The second emphasis is on bug fixes that are described as serious rather than cosmetic. The original article singles out problems tied to prompt handling, suggesting that earlier builds exhibited behavior that could disrupt the core loop of sending instructions and receiving results. When a coding agent mishandles prompt input, the downstream effects can range from wasted iterations to incorrect file edits, so corrections in this area tend to have an outsized impact on reliability. Without the complete change list it is difficult to quantify the severity precisely, but the framing implies these were defects encountered frequently enough to warrant prioritized attention.

For readers unfamiliar with the tool, Claude Code is an agentic command-line interface that lets a Claude model read a codebase, run commands, edit files, and execute multi-step tasks from the terminal. It typically relies on a project context file, often named CLAUDE.md, to capture conventions and instructions that persist across sessions, and it supports the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, which standardizes how external tools and data sources connect to the assistant. Configuration therefore sits at the center of the experience: settings determine which model is used, how permissions for file and shell access are granted, and how the agent behaves during longer tasks. That centrality is part of why a /config syntax change is worth flagging even when the underlying capability is unchanged.

The broader context is a crowded and fast-moving market for AI coding assistants. Claude Code competes with editor-integrated tools such as GitHub Copilot and Cursor, as well as other terminal-first agents like Aider and the various command-line offerings from rival model providers. In this segment, vendors ship frequent updates, and version histories often show a steady cadence of small releases that fold in fixes and refinements rather than large feature drops. A release like v2.1.181 fits that pattern: the value is concentrated in stability and quality-of-life improvements rather than headline-grabbing new functionality. For professional users, that cadence is generally welcome, because reliability in an agent that can modify source code directly is arguably as important as raw capability.

Practical guidance for anyone adopting this build is straightforward. Updating to the current version is advisable if the earlier prompt-related bugs were affecting work, since the fixes appear aimed at the common path most users follow. At the same time, it is worth reviewing any local automation, shell aliases, or documentation that invokes /config to ensure they align with the updated syntax before relying on them in a shared environment. Because the available summary is partial, readers seeking the authoritative and complete list of changes should consult the official release notes or changelog rather than depending solely on third-party recaps.

In sum, Claude Code v2.1.181 is presented as a stability-focused update whose importance lies in correcting real workflow problems and tidying configuration ergonomics. The exact scope of every fix is not fully detailed in the source, so some specifics remain to be confirmed, but the overall direction is consistent with a tool maturing through incremental, reliability-oriented releases.

83afd76f71f7ed3b.bodyJa:
GitHubは、GitHub Actionsのワークフロー実行を保護する新機能をパブリックプレビューとして公開した。Enterprise、Organization、リポジトリの各レベルで、管理者がワークフローをトリガーできるユーザーやアクターをアローリストで制限できるようになる。CI/CDパイプラインの乱用やサプライチェーン攻撃のリスクが意識されるなか、実行の入口そのものを管理する仕組みとして注目される。

新機能の中核は「ワークフロー実行保護(workflow execution protections)」と呼ばれる制御だ。従来、ワークフローはプッシュやプルリクエスト、手動実行(workflow_dispatch)など多様なイベントで起動するが、誰がどのアクターとしてそれを起こせるかを横断的に制御する手段は限られていた。今回のアローリスト方式では、許可された対象のみがワークフローを開始でき、それ以外のトリガーは抑止される。Enterprise単位で方針を定め、配下のOrganizationやリポジトリへ一貫して適用できる点が、大規模組織にとって利点となる可能性がある。

背景には、Actionsを起点とした権限昇格やシークレット流出への懸念がある。GitHubはこれまでも、フォークからのプルリクエストに対する承認要求、再利用可能ワークフローの参照制限、OpenID Connectによる短命トークンの発行、Environmentごとの保護ルールなど、段階的にガードレールを整えてきた。今回の機能はこうした取り組みを補完し、「実行を許可する主体」を管理する新たな層を加えるものと位置づけられる。

エンタープライズ領域では、サプライチェーンセキュリティを巡る取り組みが各社で進む。GitLabやJenkinsといった他のCI/CD基盤も承認フローや権限分離の強化を図っており、ソフトウェア部品表(SBOM)やSLSAといったフレームワークへの対応も業界的な潮流となっている。アローリストによるトリガー制御は、こうした文脈で「最小権限」の原則を実装に落とし込む手段の一つと見られる。

パブリックプレビュー段階のため、仕様や対象範囲は今後変更される可能性がある。導入を検討する組織は、既存のワークフローが意図せずブロックされないよう、適用範囲を限定して検証することが望ましい。正式提供の時期や、監査ログとの連携など運用面の詳細は、今後のアナウンスで明らかになるとみられる。
83afd76f71f7ed3b.bodyEn:
GitHub has introduced workflow execution protections for GitHub Actions, now available in public preview, that let administrators define allow lists controlling which users and actors can trigger workflow runs. The capability spans the enterprise, organization, and repository levels, and it addresses a long-standing concern for teams that rely on Actions for automation: limiting who can set automated processes in motion. For organizations managing sensitive pipelines, this offers a more granular layer of access control than was previously available out of the box.

GitHub Actions is the platform's built-in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) service, allowing developers to automate building, testing, and deploying code through workflows defined in YAML files stored in a repository. Workflows can be triggered by a wide range of events, including pushes, pull requests, scheduled timers, manual dispatches, and calls from other workflows or external systems. Because these workflows often have access to secrets, deployment credentials, and production environments, the question of who can initiate a run carries real security weight.

According to the changelog entry, the new protections give administrators the ability to specify allow lists that restrict workflow triggers to approved users and actors. In practice, this means an enterprise or organization owner can constrain execution so that only designated identities are permitted to start a workflow, rather than allowing any contributor or automated actor with repository access to do so. The feature appears designed to reduce the attack surface associated with unauthorized or unexpected workflow execution, which has been a vector in software supply chain incidents.

The distinction between "who" and "what" is notable. Workflows can be triggered not only by human contributors but also by automated actors such as bots, GitHub Apps, and integrations. By extending allow lists to cover both categories, the protections aim to give administrators control over the full range of entities capable of initiating runs. This is particularly relevant in larger enterprises where numerous apps and service accounts may have standing permissions across many repositories.

This release fits within a broader set of Actions security controls that GitHub has built up over time. Environment protection rules already allow teams to require manual approvals before deployments proceed to sensitive targets, and required reviewers can gate jobs that touch production. GitHub also supports controls over workflows triggered by pull requests from forks, which historically posed risks because external contributors could potentially expose secrets or run untrusted code. The new trigger allow lists appear to complement these existing mechanisms rather than replace them, adding control at the point where a workflow is initiated rather than only at later stages.

The timing reflects an industry-wide emphasis on securing the software supply chain. High-profile incidents in recent years have drawn attention to CI/CD systems as targets, since they sit at the intersection of source code, build infrastructure, and deployment credentials. Frameworks such as SLSA (Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts) and guidance from bodies like NIST have encouraged organizations to harden their build and automation pipelines. Features that constrain workflow execution align with the principle of least privilege, a foundational concept in access control that holds that identities should have only the permissions necessary to perform their tasks.

As a public preview, the feature is available for testing and feedback but should be approached with the expectation that behavior, configuration options, or scope may change before general availability. Organizations evaluating it will likely want to test allow list configurations in non-critical repositories first, to confirm that legitimate automation and contributor workflows are not inadvertently blocked. Administrators should also consider how the controls interact with existing branch protections, environment rules, and any third-party integrations that depend on triggering workflows programmatically.

For enterprises with strict compliance or governance requirements, centralized control at the enterprise level may be especially useful, since it can establish a baseline policy that propagates across constituent organizations and repositories. As with many GitHub Enterprise capabilities, the precise availability and management interface may differ between GitHub Enterprise Cloud and self-hosted configurations, so teams should consult the official documentation for details specific to their deployment. Interested administrators can enable the preview through their GitHub settings and provide feedback to GitHub as the feature matures toward broader release.

10e9c69378bef94c.bodyJa:
GitHubは、GitHub Actionsのチェックアウト処理において、pull_request_targetトリガーに対する安全なデフォルト設定を導入したと発表した。誤用の多いこのイベントに起因するワークフローの脆弱性リスクを軽減する狙いがある。

pull_request_targetは、プルリクエストを契機にワークフローを起動するイベントの一つだが、通常のpull_requestイベントとは挙動が大きく異なる。pull_requestがフォーク側の限定された権限で実行されるのに対し、pull_request_targetはベースリポジトリ側のコンテキストで動作する。そのため、リポジトリのシークレットや書き込み権限を持つトークンにアクセスできる点が特徴だ。

問題となりやすいのは、開発者がこのイベントを使いつつ、actions/checkoutでプルリクエストのヘッド(フォーク側のコード)を明示的にチェックアウトしてしまうケースである。本来は信頼できないコードを、シークレットや高い権限を持つ環境で実行することになり、悪意ある投稿者によるトークンの窃取やコード実行(いわゆる「pwn request」)につながる可能性がある。この組み合わせは、GitHub Actionsで最も頻繁に悪用されるパターンの一つとして長く知られてきた。

今回の変更では、チェックアウトアクションがpull_request_targetで起動された際に、より安全な参照先をデフォルトとして扱うようになる。これにより、設定を強く意識せずに記述されたワークフローでも、危険な構成に陥りにくくなると見られる。

背景には、ソフトウェアサプライチェーンのセキュリティへの関心の高まりがある。GitHubはこれまでにも、デフォルトのGITHUB_TOKEN権限を読み取り専用に変更したり、Dependabotやコードスキャン、OpenSSF Scorecardといった仕組みを通じてワークフローの安全性向上を進めてきた。今回の措置も、設定ミスが起きることを前提に「安全側へ倒す」という設計思想の延長線上に位置づけられる。

ただし、デフォルトが安全になっても、意図的にヘッド参照をチェックアウトする構成自体は引き続き可能と見られる。利用者は、自身のワークフローが信頼できないコードをどの権限のもとで扱っているのかを、改めて確認しておくことが望ましいだろう。
10e9c69378bef94c.bodyEn:
The pull_request_target event has long been one of the most commonly misused triggers in GitHub Actions, and a recent change to the checkout action aims to reduce the risk by establishing safer default behavior. Because this trigger touches both untrusted contributor code and privileged repository context, errors in its configuration have historically been a leading cause of workflow security incidents, making any tightening of defaults relevant to maintainers across the ecosystem.

To understand the significance, it helps to recall how pull_request_target differs from the more familiar pull_request event. A workflow triggered by pull_request runs with a restricted GITHUB_TOKEN and, for pull requests from forks, no access to repository secrets. By contrast, pull_request_target runs in the context of the base repository rather than the fork. That means it executes with a token that can carry write permissions and with access to secrets defined in the repository. The trigger exists so that maintainers can run automation that legitimately needs elevated privileges, such as labeling pull requests, posting comments, or updating status, even when the contribution originates from an external fork.

The danger arises when a workflow combines those elevated privileges with the untrusted code contained in the pull request. By default, the checkout action operating under pull_request_target checks out the base branch of the repository, which is code the maintainers control. Problems occur when a workflow explicitly overrides this and checks out the pull request's head reference, for example by setting the ref input to the incoming commit SHA, and then executes that code through a build step, test runner, install script, or similar mechanism. At that point an attacker can submit a pull request whose code runs with the privileges of the base repository, potentially exfiltrating secrets or pushing malicious changes. Security researchers commonly refer to this class of vulnerability as a "pwn request."

According to the changelog entry, the checkout action now applies a safe default configuration when invoked under the pull_request_target trigger, reducing the likelihood that a misconfiguration silently exposes a repository. The stated goal is to lower the chance that workflows accidentally check out and run untrusted code with privileged access. The practical effect appears to be that maintainers who do not deliberately opt into the riskier behavior are steered toward the secure path, while those with a genuine need to inspect contributor code can still do so by configuring it explicitly and combining it with appropriate safeguards.

This change fits within a broader, ongoing effort by GitHub to make Actions safer by default rather than relying solely on documentation and user diligence. Related measures in recent years have included the ability to set default permissions for the GITHUB_TOKEN to read-only at the repository or organization level, controls requiring approval before workflows run on pull requests from first-time contributors, and the option to pin actions to full commit SHAs to defend against supply-chain tampering. The platform has also expanded reusable workflow controls and the allow-list mechanisms that restrict which third-party actions can run.

For maintainers, the safer pattern remains well established regardless of this update. A common recommendation is to split responsibilities into two workflows: one triggered by pull_request that builds and tests the untrusted code without access to secrets, and a separate pull_request_target workflow that performs only the privileged, trusted operations and never checks out or executes contributor code. When inspecting fork code under elevated context is genuinely necessary, the guidance is to treat all incoming content as untrusted, avoid executing it, and scope the token permissions as narrowly as possible.

It is worth noting that a default change of this kind does not retroactively fix workflows that intentionally check out and run untrusted code, since those represent deliberate configuration choices rather than defaults. The update is likely to be most beneficial for the large number of repositories that adopted pull_request_target without fully understanding its implications. Teams relying on existing automation should review their workflow files to confirm the new defaults do not alter expected behavior, and to verify that any privileged steps are isolated from untrusted input. As with many security-oriented platform changes, the benefit comes from reducing the gap between what is convenient and what is safe.

cd69a5250c2f2c7d.bodyJa:
「便利だから入れる」——VSCodeやCursorの拡張機能を、ほとんど無条件にインストールしてきた開発者は多いだろう。だが拡張は導入した瞬間から、開いているワークスペースのコード全文を読み取る権限を事実上得る。これは脆弱性ではなく、拡張機構そのものの設計に由来する点を、いま一度確認しておきたい。

背景にあるのは、VSCode系エディタの拡張実行モデルだ。拡張は「Extension Host」と呼ばれるNode.jsプロセス上で動作し、ファイルシステムやネットワークへ広くアクセスできる。ブラウザ拡張のように「この権限を許可しますか」と逐一同意を求めるマニフェスト型の仕組みは基本的になく、ユーザーが個別操作を承認する場面は限られる。つまり、コードの読み取りや外部への通信は、原理的には拡張側の裁量に委ねられている。

CursorはVSCodeをベースとするため、この実行モデルをそのまま受け継いでいる。AIエディタという性質上、補完やチャットでソースを外部のモデルへ送る処理も多く、何がどこへ渡るのかは一段と見えにくくなりがちだ。利便性と引き換えに、機密性の高いコードや認証情報が意図せず外部へ流れる可能性は否定できない。

もっとも、エコシステム側の対策が皆無というわけではない。VSCodeには信頼できないフォルダを開いた際に機能を制限する「Workspace Trust(制限モード)」があり、未知のプロジェクトへの初期防御として働く。また入手元によってもリスクは変わり、純正マーケットプレースとOpen VSXなどでは審査やなりすまし対策の度合いが異なると指摘されてきた。過去には人気拡張になりすました悪意あるパッケージが配布された事例も報告されている。

実務的にできることは地味だが有効だ。提供元と公開実績を確認する、レビューやダウンロード数だけを信用しない、不要になった拡張は削除する、機密リポジトリでは有効化する拡張を絞る、といった運用が考えられる。拡張の「権限」を読み解く文化はまだ成熟しているとは言いがたい。導入の手軽さに見合うだけの注意を、利用者側が意識的に補っていく必要があると言えるだろう。
cd69a5250c2f2c7d.bodyEn:
Every time you install an extension in Cursor or Visual Studio Code with a single click, that extension gains the ability to read every file in your open workspace. There is no permission prompt, no consent dialog, and no fine-grained control over what it can and cannot touch. This is not a bug or an oversight. It is how the editor's extension architecture was designed, and it is the starting point for any honest audit of the popular extensions developers install without a second thought.

The reason this matters has grown more acute. Modern projects routinely sit alongside proprietary source code, API keys, .env files, cloud credentials, and customer data. Cursor, an AI-focused editor built as a fork of Visual Studio Code, inherits the same extension system. When you add a linter, a formatter, a theme, a Git helper, or an AI assistant, that third-party code generally runs inside the editor with broad access to your machine and your project.

The technical detail is straightforward. Extensions run in a Node.js process known as the extension host. Through the editor's API and Node's standard libraries, an extension can read and write files across the workspace, spawn child processes, make outbound network requests, and read environment variables. The editor does not sandbox these abilities on a per-extension basis. There is no manifest in which an extension must declare "I need filesystem access" or "I will contact this domain," and there is no runtime gate that the user must approve.

This stands in contrast to adjacent ecosystems. Web browsers require extensions to list permissions such as host access or tab reading, and they surface those requests at install time. Mobile operating systems prompt for camera, location, or contacts access. The VSCode and Cursor model offers nothing comparable for the most common capabilities, so trust is effectively all-or-nothing once an extension is installed.

The practical risk is twofold. First, a well-meaning extension can transmit more than you expect. Telemetry, crash reporting, and AI features may send file contents, snippets, or metadata to remote servers, often governed only by a privacy policy that few users read. Second, the supply chain itself can be compromised. An extension that was safe yesterday can ship a malicious update today, or an attacker can publish a typosquatted package with a name close to a popular tool. Because updates can install automatically, a single compromised release can reach many machines quickly.

These concerns are not hypothetical. Security researchers have repeatedly demonstrated malicious or data-exfiltrating extensions on the Visual Studio Marketplace and on Open VSX, the open registry that Cursor and other VSCode forks rely on because they cannot use Microsoft's marketplace directly. Reported issues have included credential theft, cryptocurrency miners, and packages that quietly read workspace files. The distribution differences between registries also mean that the version you receive in Cursor may not be identical to the one vetted elsewhere.

Auditing what an extension actually does is possible but tedious. Extensions are distributed as .vsix archives, which are essentially zip files containing JavaScript. You can inspect the package.json to see declared activation events and dependencies, search the bundled code for network calls or filesystem access, and watch outbound traffic at the network level. Some teams go further by pinning specific versions, disabling auto-updates, and maintaining an allowlist of approved extensions.

Until a stricter permission model arrives, the reasonable response is awareness rather than alarm. It appears unlikely that the underlying architecture will change soon, so the burden of due diligence is likely to remain with users and organizations. Installing fewer extensions, preferring well-maintained and widely reviewed projects, scrutinizing what an AI feature transmits, and treating each install as a trust decision are all sensible precautions. The convenience of one-click installation is real, but so is the access it grants, and the two are worth weighing together before the next extension lands in your editor.

f8d5a9db010c2af4.bodyJa:
世界最大級の広告・クリエイティブの祭典「Cannes Lions(カンヌライオンズ)2026」で、NVIDIAとパートナー各社が生成AIや自律型AIを活用した広告・マーケティングの新たな運用手法を披露した。NVIDIAは、デジタル時代が業界に「スピード」をもたらしたとすれば、AI時代がもたらすのは「自律的なオペレーション(autonomous operations)」だと位置づけており、人手を介した制作・配信のワークフローが大きく変わる転換点を示すものと見られる。

背景にあるのは、生成AIから「エージェント型AI(agentic AI)」へと関心が移りつつある潮流だ。エージェント型AIとは、与えられた目標に対して計画を立て、複数の処理を自律的に実行するAIを指す。広告領域では、キャンペーンの企画立案からクリエイティブの大量生成、ターゲット別の出し分け、効果測定に基づく最適化までを一連の流れとして自動化する用途が想定される。これにより、従来は人手で繰り返していた制作やA/Bテストの工程を、より高速かつ大規模に回せる可能性がある。

技術的な土台としては、NVIDIAが提供するGPU基盤に加え、対話・推論モデルを構築するためのソフトウェア群や、企業データと連携して回答精度を高める仕組みなどが活用されているとみられる。広告・マーケティング分野では、AdobeやSalesforce、WPPといった企業がすでに生成AIを制作・運用ツールへ組み込む動きを進めており、NVIDIAはそうしたパートナーに計算基盤やモデル開発の枠組みを供給する立場にある。今回のカンヌでの発表も、こうしたエコシステム全体の連携を示す一例と位置づけられる。

一方で、ブランドが扱う広告領域でAIの自律性を高めることには、生成物の品質管理や著作権、ブランドの安全性(ブランドセーフティ)、消費者データの取り扱いといった課題も伴う。自律的に動くAIが意図しない表現や不適切な配信を行わないよう、人間による監督やガードレールの設計が引き続き重要になるとみられる。

広告は新技術の実験場となりやすい分野であり、AIによる自動化が浸透すれば、クリエイターやマーケターの役割は「制作の実行」から「目標設定とAIの監督」へと比重を移していく可能性がある。カンヌでの一連の展示は、その変化の方向性を業界に対して可視化する場になったといえる。
f8d5a9db010c2af4.bodyEn:
The advertising and marketing industry is entering a new phase of automation, and NVIDIA used this year's Cannes Lions festival to outline how that shift is taking shape. Speaking alongside a roster of technology and agency partners, the company framed the change in simple terms: where the digital era gave marketers speed and reach, the emerging AI era is increasingly about autonomous operations, in which software agents plan, generate, and optimize campaign work with reduced human intervention. For an industry built on creative output and tight production deadlines, that framing matters because it touches both how content is made and how media is managed.

At the center of the discussion is the move from generative AI as a standalone tool toward what the industry calls agentic systems. Generative models can already produce images, copy, and video variations, but agentic workflows chain those capabilities together with planning and decision-making logic, allowing a system to take a brief, draft assets, test variations against performance data, and adjust spending or targeting. NVIDIA appears to be positioning its platform as the underlying infrastructure for these workflows rather than as a consumer-facing creative app, supplying the accelerated computing, model-serving software, and simulation tools that partners build on.

Several of NVIDIA's existing building blocks are relevant here. NVIDIA NIM microservices package optimized models so they can be deployed across cloud and on-premises environments, while the broader NVIDIA AI Enterprise software stack handles the operational side of running models in production. For visual and three-dimensional content, the company's Omniverse platform supports the creation of digital twins of products and scenes, which can be used to generate large volumes of on-brand imagery without staging physical photo shoots. Taken together, these pieces are intended to let agencies and brands assemble custom pipelines, and the Cannes presentations seem designed to show partners doing exactly that.

The partner angle is significant because NVIDIA rarely sells directly to marketers. WPP, one of the world's largest advertising holding companies, has previously built a content engine on Omniverse and NVIDIA AI, using it to produce product imagery and personalized variations at scale. Consulting and services firms such as Accenture, along with creative software vendors and cloud providers, form the wider ecosystem through which these capabilities reach brands. This mirrors a broader pattern across the marketing technology landscape, where Adobe, Salesforce, Google, and other vendors have been embedding generative and agentic features into the platforms that marketers already use, from creative suites to customer data and campaign management tools.

The pitch around autonomous operations is also tied to the economics of personalization. Brands increasingly want to tailor messaging to many audience segments across many channels and formats, a volume of output that is difficult to produce manually. Automated generation and optimization promise to make that practical, though the gains depend heavily on the quality of underlying data, brand guidelines, and the guardrails placed around what systems are allowed to do. Companies presenting at events like Cannes tend to highlight efficiency and creative scale, and those claims are best treated as directional until independent results are available.

Context from the wider industry suggests the same caution. Generative AI in advertising has raised ongoing questions about copyright and the provenance of training data, brand safety when content is produced automatically, and the risk of generic or off-brand output. Regulators in several markets are also examining how AI-generated media and automated decision-making should be disclosed. These factors are likely to shape how quickly fully autonomous workflows are adopted, and many organizations are expected to keep humans in the loop for approval and oversight even as more of the production work is automated.

Cannes Lions, long known as a showcase for creative work, has become a venue where the technology underpinning that work is increasingly on display, reflecting how central data and computing have become to the business. NVIDIA's message at the event is consistent with its strategy in other verticals: provide the accelerated computing foundation and software, and let an ecosystem of partners turn it into industry-specific applications. Whether autonomous operations become standard practice will depend on how those partners deliver measurable results, and on how brands balance speed and scale against creative control and accountability.

1c5a197566b8ba4b.bodyJa:
NVIDIAは、クラウドゲーミングサービス「GeForce NOW」において、主要なゲームストアで購入したタイトルのライブラリを連携し、複数のデバイス間でプレイ状況を同期しながらストリーミングできる機能を強化したと発表した。所有するゲームを場所や端末を選ばず途切れなく遊べる点が特徴で、クラウドゲーミングの利便性をさらに高める取り組みといえる。

GeForce NOWは、定額制の遊び放題サービスとは異なり、ユーザーが自分で購入済みのゲームをNVIDIAのデータセンター上にある高性能GPUで実行し、その映像を手元の端末へ配信する仕組みを採る。今回の対応では、SteamやEpic Games Storeといった普及したストアのライブラリを接続し、対応タイトルを認識できるようにする。セーブデータの進行状況もクラウド経由で引き継がれるため、PCで中断したセッションをスマートフォンやタブレット、対応テレビなどで再開しやすくなると見られる。

クラウドゲーミング市場では、Microsoftの「Xbox Cloud Gaming」やAmazonの「Luna」などが競合し、各社がデバイス横断のシームレスな体験を競っている。多くのサービスがサブスクリプション型のゲーム見放題を中核に据えるなか、GeForce NOWは既存の購入済みライブラリをそのまま活用できる点を差別化要素としてきた。今回の機能拡張は、その強みをさらに押し出すものと位置づけられる。

利用にあたっては、安定したネットワーク環境や、サービス側が定める対応ストア・対応タイトルの範囲といった前提条件が伴う点には留意が必要だ。プレイ可能なタイトルやセーブ同期の挙動はゲームごとに異なる可能性があり、実際の体験は各タイトルの対応状況に左右されると考えられる。それでも、所有資産を生かしつつ端末を意識せずに遊べるという方向性は、ハードウェア性能に縛られないゲーム体験を求めるユーザーにとって魅力的な選択肢となりそうだ。
1c5a197566b8ba4b.bodyEn:
NVIDIA's GeForce NOW is expanding how members access their existing game collections, with the cloud gaming service connecting libraries from major storefronts and synchronizing save progress so players can move between devices without losing their place. The update matters because it addresses one of cloud gaming's persistent friction points: the gap between the games people already own and the hardware they happen to be using at any given moment.

At its core, GeForce NOW differs from subscription catalogs such as Xbox Game Pass in that it does not hand members a fixed library of titles. Instead, it streams games that users already own through linked accounts on stores like Steam, Epic Games Store, Ubisoft Connect, GOG and Microsoft's PC storefront. The latest changes deepen that model by pulling together entitlements across those storefronts and keeping save data synchronized, so a session started on a desktop can be resumed on a laptop, phone, tablet, smart TV or handheld device. According to NVIDIA, the goal is to let players jump back into a game seamlessly on virtually any supported device.

The technical foundation is server-side rendering. Rather than running a game locally, GeForce NOW executes it on data center GPUs and streams the resulting video to the user's screen while sending back input commands. This means demanding titles can run on hardware that would otherwise be incapable of playing them, provided the connection has enough bandwidth and low enough latency. Save synchronization in this context typically relies on the underlying storefront's cloud save system, with GeForce NOW acting as the layer that ties a member's various accounts together and ensures progress is current before a session begins.

Cross-device continuity has become an increasingly important selling point across the wider gaming industry, and GeForce NOW's approach overlaps with several adjacent trends. The rise of handheld PCs such as Valve's Steam Deck and various Windows-based portables has accustomed players to carrying their libraries between form factors, and cloud streaming extends that flexibility to devices without powerful internal graphics. NVIDIA has historically positioned GeForce NOW as a complement to local hardware rather than a replacement, an approach that appears intended to reassure players who want to keep ownership of their purchases rather than rent access on a month-to-month basis.

The competitive context is also worth noting. Cloud gaming has had a turbulent history: Google shut down its Stadia service in early 2023, and other entrants have scaled back ambitions, while Microsoft has folded cloud streaming into Game Pass Ultimate. Against that backdrop, GeForce NOW's bring-your-own-library model has proven comparatively durable, in part because it lowers the risk that a closing service erases access to games a player paid for. By emphasizing synchronization and broad device support, NVIDIA is likely trying to strengthen that differentiation and make the service more attractive to players who own large multi-store collections.

There are practical considerations that prospective users should weigh. GeForce NOW is offered through tiered memberships, with higher tiers providing access to more powerful virtual hardware, longer session lengths and features such as higher frame rates and resolutions. Performance depends heavily on network quality, and streaming inherently introduces some latency compared with local play, which can matter for fast-paced competitive titles. Game availability is another caveat: not every title in a member's library is necessarily supported, because publishers must opt in for their games to run on the platform, and some have chosen not to participate.

For NVIDIA, the broader strategy ties into its dominant position in graphics hardware and accelerated computing. GeForce NOW serves as both a consumer-facing showcase for its GPU technology and a way to extend the GeForce brand to people who may not buy a high-end gaming PC. The emphasis on unifying storefronts and keeping progress in sync reflects a maturing of cloud gaming from a novelty into a more practical part of how some players manage their libraries. Whether the feature meaningfully shifts user behavior will depend on how reliably the synchronization works in everyday use and how many of the games people actually own are supported, but it represents a clear step toward treating a player's collection as device-agnostic.

e2afd199ed574b53.bodyJa:
Webアプリケーションのデバッグや性能改善は、これまで開発者がブラウザの開発者ツールを手動で操作しながら進めるのが一般的だった。こうした作業をAIエージェントに委ねる動きが、MCP（Model Context Protocol）の普及とともに広がりつつある。今回取り上げる「Chrome DevTools for Agents（chrome-devtools-mcp）」は、AnthropicのコーディングエージェントであるClaude CodeをChromeの開発者ツールにMCPサーバー経由で接続するための実装だ。

MCPは、AIモデルと外部ツールやデータソースを標準化された方法でつなぐためのプロトコルで、Anthropicが2024年に公開した。対応するMCPサーバーを用意すれば、Claude Codeのようなクライアントから一貫したインターフェースで多様な機能を呼び出せる。chrome-devtools-mcpはその一つとして、ブラウザの内部機能をエージェントから操作可能にする位置づけといえる。

具体的には、Lighthouseによるパフォーマンスやアクセシビリティの監査、スマートフォンなどを想定したデバイスエミュレーション、メモリリークの検出といった操作をClaude Codeから指示できるとされる。エージェントが実際にページを読み込み、計測結果を取得して改善案を提示するワークフローが想定され、人間がDevToolsの各タブを行き来する手間を減らせる可能性がある。

導入にあたっては、Node.js環境やChromeの実行環境を整え、Claude Code側の設定ファイルにMCPサーバーを登録するのが一般的な手順となる。MCPサーバーはローカルで動作するものが多く、対象ブラウザを制御する都合上、ヘッドレスモードや専用のデバッグポートを利用する構成が採られることが多い。

同種の取り組みとしては、Microsoftが主導するPlaywrightのMCP対応や、ブラウザ操作を自動化する各種エージェント向けツールが登場しており、ブラウザとAIをつなぐ周辺エコシステムは急速に拡大している。一方で、エージェントにブラウザ操作を任せる際は、認証情報や閲覧データの扱いに注意が必要との指摘もある。実際の運用では、対象環境を限定しつつ挙動を確認しながら段階的に導入することが現実的と見られる。
e2afd199ed574b53.bodyEn:
Chrome DevTools for Agents, distributed as the chrome-devtools-mcp package, has reached its v1 release and gives agentic coding tools like Claude Code direct access to a real Chrome instance through the Model Context Protocol (MCP). For developers who already rely on Claude Code for editing and refactoring, this integration matters because it closes a long-standing gap: the assistant can observe how a page actually behaves in a browser rather than reasoning only about static source code.

At a high level, MCP is an open protocol introduced by Anthropic that standardizes how language-model clients talk to external tools and data sources. An MCP server exposes a set of callable tools, and a client such as Claude Code discovers those tools and lets the model invoke them. The chrome-devtools-mcp server fills that role, translating model requests into commands for the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), the same low-level interface that powers the DevTools panel and automation libraries such as Puppeteer and Playwright.

Once connected, the agent gains a set of browser-grade capabilities. It can run Lighthouse audits to measure performance, accessibility, SEO, and best-practice scores, then use the structured results to suggest concrete fixes. It can apply device emulation to reproduce mobile viewports and throttled network conditions, which is useful for diagnosing layout or loading issues that only appear on constrained devices. It can also capture heap snapshots and performance traces, supporting workflows such as memory-leak detection where the agent compares allocations over time. Other typical tools include navigating to URLs, reading console output, inspecting network requests, evaluating JavaScript, and taking screenshots.

Setup follows the standard MCP pattern. Because the server is published to npm, it is commonly launched with npx, so a working Node.js installation is the main prerequisite alongside a local Chrome or Chromium binary. In practice you register the server with Claude Code, either through the claude mcp add command or by editing the client's JSON configuration, pointing it at the chrome-devtools-mcp executable. After Claude Code restarts and discovers the tools, you can prompt it in natural language, for example asking it to audit a running development server or to profile a page that feels slow. The server can drive an existing browser session or start its own, and depending on configuration it may run headless or with a visible window.

The practical workflow tends to be iterative. A developer might ask Claude Code to load a local build, run an audit, and report the largest performance regressions. The agent then reads the results, proposes edits to the codebase, applies them, and re-runs the audit to confirm the change. This loop of observe, change, and verify is where browser-connected agents appear to add the most value, because the model can ground its recommendations in measured data instead of assumptions.

It helps to place this release in a broader context. Browser automation for AI is a crowded and fast-moving area: Playwright ships its own MCP server, and projects such as browser-use and various computer-use agents pursue similar goals of letting models drive a browser. Chrome DevTools for Agents is notable mainly because it surfaces DevTools-specific diagnostics such as Lighthouse, tracing, and heap profiling, rather than focusing only on clicking and typing. That positioning makes it complementary to end-to-end testing tools rather than a direct replacement.

A few caveats are worth keeping in mind. Granting an agent control of a browser means it can navigate to arbitrary pages and execute scripts, so it is prudent to run it against trusted local environments and to review actions before pointing it at sensitive sites or authenticated sessions. Audit results and traces can be large, which may consume significant context tokens if returned verbatim, so well-designed tools typically summarize or paginate output. As with most MCP servers in this period, the project is evolving quickly, so exact tool names, flags, and defaults are likely to shift between versions, and consulting the project's current documentation remains the safest approach.

For teams already standardized on Claude Code, the integration offers a low-friction way to bring real browser feedback into an existing agentic workflow, turning front-end performance and quality checks into something the assistant can run, interpret, and act on directly.

b7b32cc2ccdd2274.bodyJa:
AIコーディング支援ツールが日常的な開発環境に定着するなか、「どう使うか」よりも「誰が主導権を握るか」を問い直す視点が注目されている。Zennに公開された個人開発者による振り返り記事「『AIを使ったか』ではなく『人が主体か』」は、AI協業開発で実プロダクトを完成させた経験をもとに、その境界線を論じている。

この記事は「音読速度計測アプリ 開発記」シリーズの最終回(サテライト第4回)にあたる。筆者にとって同アプリは、AIとの協業を明確な開発モードとして初めて採用した題材だったという。単発のコード補完にとどまらず、設計から実装までの一連の流れにAIを組み込んだうえで、最終的な意思決定や品質の責任を人間側が担う体制を志向した点が特徴とされる。

背景には、AI統合型エディタの急速な普及がある。本記事のカテゴリでもあるCursorは、コードベース全体を文脈として読み込み、対話的に修正や生成を進められるツールとして利用者を増やしている。同種の製品にはGitHub CopilotやAnthropicのClaude Code、Windsurfなどがあり、各社が補完中心から「エージェント的」な自律実行へと機能を広げている。こうした流れのなかで、生成されたコードをそのまま受け入れる進め方への懸念も指摘されてきた。

筆者が提起するのは、評価の軸を「AIを使ったかどうか」から「人が主体であり続けているか」へ移すという考え方だ。AIの利用自体は是非を問う対象ではなく、要件の定義や設計判断、出力の検証といった核心部分を人間が握っているかが重要だ、という整理と見られる。これは、AIに大きく委ねる「バイブコーディング」と呼ばれるスタイルとの対比でも理解しやすい論点だろう。

実プロダクトを通じた振り返りであるため、主張は抽象論にとどまらず具体的な開発体験に根ざしている可能性がある。AI協業をどのワークフローに組み込み、どこで人間が判断を差し挟むか——この問いは、ツールの性能が上がるほど各開発者が向き合うことになるテーマであり、本記事はその一つの実践記録として参照価値がありそうだ。
b7b32cc2ccdd2274.bodyEn:
A developer has published the final installment of a four-part retrospective series documenting the creation of a real product, a reading-aloud speed measurement app, built through what the author calls "AI collaborative development." The piece is notable less for the app itself than for the framing it proposes: the meaningful question in modern software work is not "did you use AI" but "was a human the principal agent" driving the project. As AI coding assistants become standard equipment, that distinction matters for how teams evaluate quality, accountability, and authorship.

The article positions itself as a satellite piece accompanying a main write-up that covers the application's full architecture. According to the summary, the reading-aloud speed measurement app was the author's first project to adopt AI collaboration as a deliberate, explicitly named mode of working rather than as occasional autocomplete assistance. That intentionality is the crux of the argument. The author appears to suggest that simply invoking an AI tool does not define a workflow; what defines it is whether the human retains ownership of decisions, intent, and final judgment.

This reframing speaks to a tension that has grown alongside tools like Cursor, the AI-native code editor referenced in the article's category. Cursor, built as a fork of Visual Studio Code, integrates large language models directly into the editing loop, offering inline edits, multi-file changes through an agent mode, and chat-based reasoning over a codebase. Competing and complementary products include GitHub Copilot, which popularized inline code completion, as well as newer entrants such as Windsurf, Claude Code, and various agentic command-line tools. Across all of them, the common trajectory is toward greater autonomy, where the assistant can plan, write, and revise larger spans of code with less line-by-line human input.

That trajectory is exactly what makes the author's "is the human the principal" framing timely. When an AI agent can scaffold a feature end to end, the boundary between using a tool and delegating the work becomes blurry. The retrospective implies that maintaining human agency is a practical discipline rather than a default outcome. In practice, this typically means the developer continues to define requirements, review generated code critically, understand the reasoning behind structural choices, and reject output that does not fit the product's intent. The risk on the other side is well documented in the broader industry: code that is accepted without comprehension can introduce subtle bugs, security gaps, or maintenance burdens that surface only later.

For readers unfamiliar with the surrounding context, a few prerequisite concepts help. "AI collaborative development" describes a workflow where the human and the model iterate together, with the model proposing and the human steering, rather than the human dictating every line or the model operating unsupervised. This sits between traditional manual coding and fully autonomous "vibe coding," a term that has circulated to describe building software by repeatedly prompting an AI and accepting results with minimal review. The author's thesis appears to stake out the middle ground, arguing that the value of the collaboration depends on who holds the initiative.

The choice to publish on Zenn, a Japanese platform popular among engineers for technical articles and book-style series, also situates the work within a growing body of practitioner reflections on AI-assisted development. Such firsthand retrospectives are useful precisely because they document lived process rather than vendor claims. They tend to surface concrete friction points, how to scope tasks for an agent, when to intervene, and how to keep architectural coherence, that marketing material rarely addresses.

It is worth treating the piece as one developer's experience rather than a generalized conclusion. The retrospective is anchored to a single, relatively small application and reflects personal working preferences, so its lessons may not transfer cleanly to large teams or complex systems. Still, the underlying question it raises is broadly relevant. As AI tools absorb more of the mechanical labor of programming, the differentiator for quality is likely to shift toward human judgment, clarity of intent, and the willingness to remain accountable for what ships. By insisting that the human stay the principal agent, the article offers a usable heuristic for navigating that shift, one that reframes AI not as a replacement for the developer but as a capability the developer is responsible for directing.

3f4f0513ba3d1b5c.bodyJa:
AnthropicのCLI型コーディング支援ツール「Claude Code」で、エージェント連携機能とみられる「TeamCreate」が廃止され、「Plan Mode」の挙動も変更された。これらは日々の開発フローに直結するため、既存の手順や自作スキルの定義を見直す必要が生じている。

TeamCreateは、バージョン2.1.178で姿を消したと報告されている。この機能は名称から、複数のサブエージェントをチームとして編成し、役割分担しながらタスクを進めるための仕組みだったと見られる。近年のAIコーディングツールは、単一エージェントが逐次的に作業するモデルから、複数エージェントが並行・協調して動く「マルチエージェント」志向へと広がりつつあり、TeamCreateもその流れに沿った機能だった可能性がある。廃止の背景は公式に詳細が示されていないが、機能の整理や、より汎用的なサブエージェント機構への統合が進んだ結果とも考えられる。

一方のPlan Modeは、Claude Codeがコードを変更する前に調査と計画立案を行い、ユーザーの承認を得てから実装へ移るためのモードだ。今回の変更で振る舞いが調整されたことにより、計画の提示方法や承認のタイミングが従来と異なる場合がある。Plan Modeの挙動を前提に組み立てていたプロンプトやワークフローは、想定どおり動作しなくなる恐れがあり、実際の出力を確認しながら手順を更新する作業が求められる。

こうした頻繁な仕様変更は、活発に開発が続くエージェント型ツールに共通する課題でもある。GitHub CopilotやCursor、OpenAIのCodex系ツールなど競合も短い周期で機能を入れ替えており、利用者としては特定の機能名や挙動に依存しすぎない設計を意識することが、変更への耐性を高めるうえで有効と見られる。アップデート時にはリリースノートを確認し、定型プロンプトやスキルを定期的に検証して動作を確かめる運用が、当面は現実的な対応策となりそうだ。
3f4f0513ba3d1b5c.bodyEn:
Anthropic's Claude Code, the command-line coding agent that has become a fixture in many developers' terminals, continues to evolve at a pace that can outstrip the documentation and the habits built around it. A recent round of updates changed two pieces that workflow authors had come to rely on: the behavior of Plan Mode shifted, and the TeamCreate capability was removed entirely as of version 2.1.178. For anyone who had encoded these features into reusable skills or scripted procedures, the changes are significant enough to warrant revisiting how those workflows are structured.

The removal of TeamCreate is the more disruptive of the two. TeamCreate had served as a mechanism for spinning up coordinated groups of subagents to tackle parallel or decomposed tasks, allowing a single invocation to fan out work across multiple agent instances. With its deprecation in v2.1.178, any skill or automation that called TeamCreate will simply fail or no longer behave as intended, so the practical first step is to audit existing definitions for references to it. The broader pattern of delegating to subagents has not disappeared from Claude Code, but the specific entry point appears to have been retired in favor of other orchestration approaches, which means the migration is less about abandoning parallelism and more about re-expressing it through whatever primitives remain supported.

Plan Mode's change is subtler but still consequential for how procedures are written. Plan Mode is the feature that lets Claude Code analyze a task and propose a course of action before it begins making edits, giving the user a checkpoint to review and approve the intended steps. When the semantics or invocation of such a gate change, instructions that assumed a particular sequence, prompt structure, or output format may no longer line up. The safest response is to treat any hard-coded assumptions about Plan Mode's flow as suspect and to re-test the workflow end to end rather than trusting that the old steps still map cleanly onto the new behavior.

This kind of churn is not unique to Claude Code; it is characteristic of the entire category of agentic coding tools, which includes OpenAI's Codex CLI, Google's Gemini CLI, and open-source efforts like Aider and Cline. These tools are shipping rapidly, often on weekly or even more frequent release cadences, and features that feel foundational one month can be reworked or removed the next. The trade-off for users is clear: capabilities improve quickly, but the surface area you build automation against is unstable. That instability is the underlying reason why a single feature removal can cascade into a workflow review rather than a quick patch.

A useful concept to keep in mind here is the distinction between Claude Code's underlying capabilities and the higher-level abstractions—skills, slash commands, custom agents, and configuration files such as CLAUDE.md—that teams layer on top. The more tightly a workflow couples to a specific named feature, the more fragile it becomes when that feature is renamed or retired. Designing procedures around stable, documented interfaces, and keeping the orchestration logic modular, makes these periodic migrations far less painful. Where TeamCreate once provided a turnkey way to coordinate agents, it may be worth re-architecting around explicit task breakdowns and sequential or independently invoked subagents that do not depend on a single bespoke command.

Practically, the recommended approach is incremental. Pin or note the Claude Code version you are running, since behavior differs across releases and v2.1.178 marks the boundary for TeamCreate's removal. Re-run representative tasks under the new Plan Mode to observe how the approval and planning steps actually behave now, then update skill definitions to match. It is also worth checking the official changelog and release notes, as Anthropic typically documents removals and behavioral shifts there, even if community-authored guides lag behind.

None of this signals that Claude Code is becoming less capable; if anything, feature consolidation often reflects an attempt to simplify or unify how agents are coordinated. But it does reinforce a habit that anyone investing heavily in agentic tooling is likely to need: treating workflows as living artifacts that require periodic maintenance, building in regular checkpoints to test against new releases, and avoiding over-reliance on any single feature that the vendor could change without much notice.

a94c0ca7df7462f1.bodyJa:
Googleは、同社の広告配信プラットフォーム「Google Ad Manager」向けに、生成AI「Gemini」を基盤とするAIエージェント「Ask Ad Manager」を発表した。パブリッシャー(媒体運営者)が収益やパフォーマンスに関するより深いインサイトを得て、迅速かつ的確に意思決定できるよう支援することを狙いとしている。

Google Ad Managerは、ニュースサイトやアプリなどの運営者が広告枠を管理・販売し、収益化(マネタイズ)を行うための基盤ツールである。広告の配信状況や売上、入札の動向といった膨大なデータを扱う一方で、これらを分析してレポートを作成し、改善策を導き出す作業には専門知識と手間がかかる。Ask Ad Managerは、こうした分析業務を自然言語による対話で行えるようにすることで、運用の負担軽減を目指していると見られる。

特徴は、従来の検索やレポート機能を超えて、自律的にタスクを進める「AIエージェント」として設計されている点にある。利用者が質問を投げかけると、関連データを横断的に参照し、パフォーマンスの傾向や要因を要約して提示する。さらに、単なる情報提供にとどまらず、状況に応じた次のアクションの示唆まで踏み込む可能性がある。基盤にはGoogleの大規模言語モデルであるGeminiが採用されており、文脈理解や要約の精度を支える役割を担っているとみられる。

こうした動きは、広告・分析分野における生成AI活用の潮流に沿ったものだ。Googleはこれまでも、広告主向けの「Performance Max」やキャンペーン制作を支援する生成AI機能を順次拡充してきた。今回はパブリッシャー、すなわち広告を掲載して収益を得る側の体験向上に焦点を当てた点が特徴と言える。媒体運営者にとって、データ分析の専門人材が限られる中で、対話型ツールが意思決定の速度と質を高める効果は小さくないだろう。

一方で、AIが生成する分析結果や提案をそのまま受け入れるのではなく、その根拠を検証する姿勢も引き続き重要となる。生成AIには事実と異なる出力を返す可能性が残るためだ。提供時期や対応地域、利用できるプランの範囲など、具体的な展開条件については今後の続報が待たれる。広告エコシステム全体でAIエージェントの導入が進む中、実際の運用現場でどの程度の成果につながるかが、今後の評価の焦点になりそうだ。
a94c0ca7df7462f1.bodyEn:
Google has unveiled Ask Ad Manager, a conversational AI agent built on its Gemini family of models that aims to help digital publishers interrogate their advertising data, understand performance trends and reach decisions more quickly. The announcement, published on Google's Keyword blog, positions the tool as part of a broader effort to embed generative and agentic AI across the company's monetization products, where publishers have historically relied on dashboards, manual reports and specialist knowledge to run complex ad operations.

At its core, Ask Ad Manager appears designed to lower the barrier to insight. Rather than navigating menus or constructing queries inside Google Ad Manager, publishers can pose questions in natural language and receive answers drawn from their own inventory, revenue and performance data. According to Google's description, the agent helps users get deeper insights, understand their performance and make better decisions faster, suggesting an emphasis on summarization, trend detection and explanation rather than simply surfacing raw numbers.

For context, Google Ad Manager is the company's platform for publishers and app developers to sell, schedule and measure advertising across their properties. It combines an ad server with programmatic marketplaces, letting media companies manage both directly sold campaigns and automated, auction-based demand. Operating it effectively can require fluency with metrics such as fill rate, CPMs, viewability and yield across many ad units, which is part of the reason a natural-language layer could be useful for smaller teams that lack dedicated analysts.

Building the agent on Gemini connects it to the same model family Google uses across products including Search, Workspace and the standalone Gemini app. Gemini's reasoning and language capabilities are likely what enable the agent to interpret a question, map it to the relevant data and generate a written explanation. Google has not, in the material summarized here, detailed which specific Gemini variant powers the tool, how customer data is handled for privacy, or the extent to which the agent can take actions versus only providing analysis.

The launch reflects a wider industry shift toward agentic AI, in which assistants are framed not just as chatbots but as systems that can carry out multi-step tasks on a user's behalf. Google has been adding related capabilities elsewhere in its advertising stack, including conversational campaign setup in Google Ads and automated products such as Performance Max. Competitors and independent ad-tech vendors have announced comparable assistants, and the rationale is consistent: advertising data is large, fragmented and time-sensitive, making it a natural fit for tools that can summarize and prioritize.

For publishers, the timing is notable. Many media businesses face pressure on advertising revenue, ongoing changes to web tracking and privacy rules, and uncertainty about how AI-driven search and content experiences will affect referral traffic. A tool that helps teams quickly identify underperforming inventory or revenue opportunities could be valuable, though its real impact will depend on accuracy, the quality of its recommendations and how much it can be trusted without manual verification.

As with other generative AI assistants, potential limitations are worth keeping in mind. Large language models can produce confident but incorrect answers, and outputs tied to financial decisions typically warrant human oversight. The usefulness of Ask Ad Manager will likely hinge on how well it grounds responses in a publisher's actual data and how transparently it explains its reasoning. Availability, pricing, supported languages and regional rollout were not fully specified in the announcement, and such details often determine how widely a feature is adopted.

The introduction of Ask Ad Manager is consistent with Google's stated strategy of integrating Gemini across its product portfolio and with the broader competition to make AI a practical layer over enterprise software. Publishers evaluating the tool will want to watch how it performs against existing reporting workflows, whether its insights hold up against their own analysis, and whether subsequent updates expand it from an analytical assistant toward one capable of executing changes directly within Ad Manager. For now, it is best understood as an early step in bringing conversational AI to publisher monetization rather than a finished replacement for established tools.

c84f81539a16b659.bodyJa:
Pythonでの開発を始める際、最初の関門となるのが環境構築だ。今回紹介する記事は、Windows・Mac・Linuxの主要OSを横断しつつ、Python本体のインストールから仮想環境の作成、そしてVSCodeでの実行までを一連の流れとして解説する入門ガイドである。つまずきやすい初学者にとって、つまずきの起点を減らす実践的な内容といえる。

記事は大きく三つのステップで構成されている。第一にPython本体のインストール、第二に仮想環境（venv）の作成、第三にVSCodeでのコード実行だ。OSによって導入手順が異なるため、それぞれの環境に応じた説明を分けている点が特徴で、特にパスの通し方やコマンド名の違い（WindowsのpythonとmacOS・Linuxのpython3など）でつまずく例は多く、こうした差異を明示する構成は実用的だと見られる。

中でも重要なのが仮想環境（venv）の活用だ。venvはPython標準ライブラリに含まれる機能で、プロジェクトごとに独立したパッケージ環境を作れる。これにより、あるプロジェクトのライブラリ更新が別のプロジェクトに影響を与える事態を避けられる。グローバル環境に直接パッケージをインストールすると、依存関係の衝突やバージョンの不整合が起きやすいため、プロジェクト単位で環境を分離する手法は現在の標準的な作法として広く推奨されている。

エディタにVSCodeを採用している点も、入門記事として理にかなっている。VSCodeはMicrosoftが提供する無償のコードエディタで、Python拡張機能を導入すると、仮想環境の自動検出、コード補完、デバッグ実行といった機能が利用できる。インタプリタの選択をエディタ内で切り替えられるため、venvで作成した環境とVSCodeを連携させる流れは、初学者がつまずきやすい設定を簡略化する効果が期待できる。

なお、Python環境管理にはvenv以外にも選択肢がある。パッケージとプロジェクトを統合的に扱うPoetryや、近年高速さで注目を集めるuv、データサイエンス分野で根強いcondaなど、用途に応じた多様なツールが存在する。本記事はまず標準機能であるvenvから入る構成のため、追加ツールの学習コストを抑えつつ基礎を固めたい読者に向く内容だといえるだろう。環境構築は開発体験を左右する土台であり、最初に正しい手順を押さえておく意義は大きい。
c84f81539a16b659.bodyEn:
Setting up a working Python environment is one of the first hurdles newcomers face, and getting it right early prevents a long tail of confusing errors later. This guide walks through the three core steps that apply across Windows, macOS, and Linux: installing Python itself, creating an isolated virtual environment with venv, and running code from Visual Studio Code. Each step is straightforward on its own, but the way they fit together is what makes a setup reliable and reproducible.

The first step is installing the interpreter. On Windows, the most common approach is downloading the installer from python.org, where it is important to tick the "Add Python to PATH" checkbox during installation so the python and pip commands are available from any terminal. macOS ships with a system Python in some cases, but relying on it is generally discouraged; installing a current version through python.org or a package manager such as Homebrew with a command like brew install python is the preferred route. On Linux, Python is usually present already, and additional versions or the venv module can be added through the distribution's package manager, for example apt install python3 python3-venv on Debian and Ubuntu. After installation, running python --version or python3 --version confirms the interpreter is reachable.

The second step, creating a virtual environment, is where many tutorials add the most value, because it addresses a problem beginners do not yet know they have. A virtual environment is an isolated directory containing its own copy of the interpreter and its own set of installed packages. Without one, every package you install with pip lands in a single global location, and projects with conflicting dependency versions quickly interfere with one another. The venv module is part of the standard library, so no extra installation is required. The typical workflow is to run python -m venv venv inside the project folder, which creates a venv directory. Activation differs by platform: on Windows the command is venv\Scripts\activate, while on macOS and Linux it is source venv/bin/activate. Once activated, the shell prompt usually shows the environment name, and any pip install commands affect only that project. Deactivating is done with the deactivate command.

The third step connects everything to an editor. Visual Studio Code, paired with the official Python extension from Microsoft, has become a widely used combination because it detects virtual environments automatically and offers integrated debugging, linting, and IntelliSense. After opening the project folder, the interpreter selector, reachable through the Command Palette with "Python: Select Interpreter," lets you point VS Code at the venv you created. Once selected, the integrated terminal activates the environment for you, and the Run button or the debugger uses the correct interpreter. This avoids a common source of confusion where code runs against the global Python rather than the intended project environment.

It is worth understanding the surrounding tooling, since the ecosystem offers several alternatives. The Python Launcher for Windows, invoked as py, helps manage multiple installed versions. Beyond the built-in venv, tools such as virtualenv, conda, Poetry, pipenv, and the newer uv from Astral provide more advanced dependency resolution, lock files, or environment management, and some teams standardize on these for reproducibility. A requirements.txt file generated with pip freeze remains the simplest way to record dependencies so collaborators can recreate the same setup. For data science work, the Anaconda distribution bundles Python with scientific packages and its own environment manager, which can be convenient but is heavier than a plain venv approach.

A few practical cautions apply. Mixing the global interpreter with virtual environments, or forgetting to activate the environment before installing packages, accounts for a large share of beginner problems. On macOS and Linux, using python3 and pip3 explicitly avoids ambiguity with any legacy Python 2 references, though Python 2 is now end of life and largely irrelevant. Keeping pip current with python -m pip install --upgrade pip is also good hygiene.

Taken together, these steps form a foundation that scales from a first script to a larger project. The specific commands vary by operating system, but the underlying concepts, an installed interpreter, an isolated environment, and an editor configured to use it, remain consistent and transfer to whatever Python work follows.

de1f765f1faf7fae.bodyJa:
中国のAIスタートアップZ.aiが2026年6月16日に公開したコーディング特化のフラッグシップモデル「GLM-5.2」が、開発者の間で注目を集めている。オープンウェイトとして最高水準のコーディング性能を備えつつ、Claude Opus 4.8やGPT-5.5の数分の一とされる利用コストで運用できる点が最大の特徴で、エディタ「Cursor」と組み合わせることで日々の開発費用を抑えられる手段として紹介されている。

GLM-5.2は、Z.aiが展開してきたGLMシリーズの後継にあたり、コード生成や補完、エージェント的なタスク処理に重点を置いて調整されていると見られる。オープンウェイトで提供されるため、APIを介した従来型の利用だけでなく、条件次第ではセルフホストや独自基盤での運用も視野に入る。プロプライエタリな大規模モデルが性能向上とともに料金も上昇させる傾向にあるなか、性能とコストのバランスを重視する層にとって有力な選択肢となる可能性がある。

Cursorは、VS CodeをベースにしたAI統合型エディタで、コード補完やチャット、エージェント機能を通じて複数のモデルを切り替えて利用できる点が支持されてきた。標準ではAnthropicやOpenAIのモデルが選ばれることが多いが、OpenAI互換のAPIエンドポイントを設定できる仕組みを使うことで、GLM-5.2のような外部モデルを組み込める場合がある。これにより、軽量なタスクは低コストのモデルに任せ、難度の高い処理だけ高性能モデルに振り分けるといった使い分けが現実的になる。

背景には、コーディング支援AIの普及に伴う運用コストの増大がある。エージェント機能が複数回の推論を繰り返す設計では、トークン消費が膨らみ、月間の費用が無視できない規模になりやすい。こうした事情から、安価で実用的なモデルへの需要が高まっており、Z.aiのほかにもMistralやMeta、Alibabaなどがオープンウェイトモデルを相次いで投入し、選択肢は広がっている。

一方で、外部モデルをCursorに接続する際は、性能や応答の安定性、データの取り扱いを自分の用途に照らして検証することが望ましい。ベンチマーク上の数値と実際の開発体験は必ずしも一致せず、コスト削減効果も利用パターンによって左右される。まずは小規模なタスクで試し、既存のワークフローと比較しながら導入を判断するのが堅実な進め方と言えそうだ。
de1f765f1faf7fae.bodyEn:
Z.ai released GLM-5.2 on June 16, 2026, positioning it as a flagship model built specifically for software development, and the immediate draw for many developers is economic. The company describes it as offering top-tier open-weight coding performance while costing a fraction of premium proprietary models such as Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 or OpenAI's GPT-5.5. For anyone who relies heavily on AI assistance inside an editor like Cursor, where token usage accumulates rapidly across autocomplete, chat, and agentic edits, even a modest difference in per-token pricing can translate into a substantial reduction in monthly spend.

GLM-5.2 is the latest entry in the GLM line developed by Z.ai, the company associated with the Zhipu lineage of large language models. The "open-weight" designation matters here: it means the model's parameters are published rather than kept entirely behind a closed API, which allows self-hosting or access through multiple third-party inference providers. That openness tends to create downward pressure on prices, because competing hosts can serve the same weights, and it is one reason a wave of open or semi-open models has narrowed the gap with the most expensive frontier systems over the past two years.

Cursor, the AI-centric editor built on a fork of VS Code, ships with first-party access to models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and others. Crucially, it also lets users point the editor at custom endpoints that follow the OpenAI-compatible API format. This is the mechanism that makes a GLM-5.2 integration possible without waiting for official first-party support. In practice, the workflow generally involves obtaining an API key from Z.ai's developer platform, opening Cursor's model settings, adding the GLM-5.2 model identifier, and overriding the base URL so requests are routed to Z.ai's endpoint rather than the default providers. Once configured, the model can be selected for chat and editing tasks much like any built-in option.

There are caveats worth understanding before switching. Not every Cursor feature is guaranteed to work with a custom model. Tab autocompletion and some of the deeper agentic capabilities are often tuned for specific providers, so behavior with an external endpoint may differ or be unavailable. Latency and reliability also depend on the chosen host and its region, which can affect how responsive the editor feels during rapid back-and-forth coding. Teams handling sensitive code should additionally weigh data-handling and privacy implications, since enabling a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint typically requires loosening Cursor's privacy mode, and source context is then sent to a third-party service. Reviewing the provider's data-retention terms is a sensible prerequisite.

The broader context is a competitive market in which cost-per-token has become a primary battleground. Models such as DeepSeek, Alibaba's Qwen, and various Mistral releases have pushed the open-weight frontier, repeatedly demonstrating that strong coding ability no longer requires the highest-priced tier. Cursor's own pricing model, which combines a subscription with usage-based charges for premium model requests, gives developers a direct incentive to seek cheaper alternatives for routine work while reserving the most capable models for the hardest problems. Routing inexpensive bulk tasks to a model like GLM-5.2 and saving Claude or GPT for complex reasoning is a pattern that appears increasingly common.

It is also worth treating performance claims with appropriate caution. Vendor-reported benchmarks and "best-in-class" framing reflect the company's own positioning, and real-world results vary by language, codebase, and prompt style. The most reliable approach is to test GLM-5.2 on representative tasks from an actual project, comparing its output quality, speed, and total cost against whatever model a developer currently uses, rather than relying on headline numbers alone.

For cost-conscious individuals and small teams, the combination of an open-weight model and Cursor's flexible endpoint configuration is an attractive option that is likely to grow more popular as additional providers host GLM-5.2. The setup is straightforward, reversible, and easy to benchmark, which makes it a low-risk experiment for anyone looking to trim AI tooling costs without abandoning the editor workflow they already know.

8ddd91b3a165e4ed.bodyJa:
TypeScript教育で知られるMatt Pocock氏が、Claude Code向けのスキルセットを「v1.0.0」として正式公開した。注目されているのはスキルそのものの機能よりも、スキルの書き方を体系化した点にある。AIに作業を委ねる際の指示を、再現性の高い「マニュアル」として設計する方法論を示したものだ。

ここでいうスキルとは、Anthropicが提唱するAgent Skillsの枠組みに沿ったもので、SKILL.mdのようなテキストファイルに作業手順や前提、禁止事項を記述し、Claudeが必要に応じて読み込んで振る舞いを変える仕組みを指す。プロンプトを毎回手入力するのではなく、専門知識やコーディング規約をパッケージとして再利用できる点が特徴で、CursorのルールファイルやGitHub Copilotのカスタム指示など、各社が競って整備している領域でもある。

Pocock氏の問題提起は、こうした指示文がしばしば曖昧で、AIの出力が安定しないという実務上の課題に向けられている。同氏は陥りやすい設計上の落とし穴を整理し、指示が抽象的すぎる、前提を書かずに結論だけを求める、判断の余地を残しすぎるといった典型例を避けることで、出力を「予測可能」にできると説く。要は、AIを優秀な新人と見立て、誰が読んでも同じ作業を再現できる手順書を書くという発想だ。

背景には、生成AIの活用が単発の質問から継続的な開発ワークフローへ移りつつある状況がある。プロンプトエンジニアリングからコンテキストエンジニアリングへと関心が広がるなか、AIへの指示を属人的なコツではなく、共有・レビュー可能な資産として管理する流れが強まっている。

公開リポジトリは多くの支持を集めていると伝えられ、こうした実践知の標準化はチーム開発での再現性向上に寄与する可能性がある。一方で、スキルの効果はモデルの世代や対象タスクに左右されるため、提示された原則がどこまで普遍的に通用するかは、今後の検証を待つ部分も残る。
8ddd91b3a165e4ed.bodyEn:
Matt Pocock, the developer and educator best known for Total TypeScript, has formally released a curated set of skills for Anthropic's Claude Code, tagging it version 1.0.0. The release is notable less for the individual skills it bundles than for the documentation that accompanies them, which sets out to systematize how developers should write skills in the first place. In effect, it tries to turn what is often ad hoc prompt tinkering into a repeatable discipline for producing what its author calls "predictable" AI instructions.

Some background helps explain why this is interesting. Claude Code is Anthropic's command-line coding agent, and skills—sometimes referred to as Agent Skills—are one mechanism it uses to extend and steer the model's behavior. A skill is, at its core, a structured Markdown file that supplies reusable instructions for a specific task: how to scaffold a component, how to run a project's tests, or how to follow a team's coding conventions. Unlike a one-off prompt typed into a chat, a skill is meant to be invoked repeatedly and to behave consistently each time. That promise of consistency is precisely what the release focuses on.

The project's central argument is organized around a handful of recurring pitfalls in skill design—six mistakes, as the title frames it, that tend to make AI instructions unpredictable.
