fb50800c5013584e.bodyEn:
Running large language models locally has become an increasingly practical option for developers, and Visual Studio Code now makes it easier to wire a self-hosted model into its AI chat experience. By connecting VS Code to Ollama, a popular runtime for local models, you can perform AI-assisted coding without sending every prompt to a cloud service. This matters for teams concerned about privacy, organizations with strict data-handling rules, and individuals who want to experiment without per-token billing.

The core idea is straightforward. VS Code's chat interface, surfaced through GitHub Copilot Chat and the Chat view, has gained the ability to let you choose a model provider rather than defaulting solely to cloud-hosted options. When Ollama is installed and running on your machine, the models you have pulled locally can appear in the model picker. From there, you select a local model and interact with it the same way you would with a remote one, asking it to explain code, draft functions, or suggest refactors directly inside the editor.

Setting this up generally begins with installing Ollama, which is available for macOS, Windows, and Linux. After installation, you download a model with a command such as pulling a coding-oriented model, then confirm the local server is listening, typically on its default port. Inside VS Code, you open the chat view, locate the model selection control, and point it at your local Ollama instance. Once the connection is recognized, the locally available models become selectable. The exact menu labels and steps can shift between releases, so it is worth checking the current documentation, since this area of VS Code and the surrounding Copilot features has been changing quickly.

Model choice has a large impact on the experience. Lightweight models run comfortably on modest hardware but may produce weaker code suggestions, while larger models tend to reason better at the cost of memory and speed. Several open-weight families are commonly used for coding tasks, and Ollama supports many of them through its model library. Because everything runs on local resources, performance depends heavily on available RAM, CPU, and especially GPU acceleration. Developers on laptops without dedicated graphics should expect slower responses than they would get from a cloud endpoint, and very large models may simply not fit in memory.

The practical sweet spot appears to be using local models for tasks where privacy or offline access outweighs raw capability. Generating boilerplate, writing unit tests, explaining unfamiliar code, and drafting documentation are reasonable fits. For complex, multi-step reasoning or large-context problems, cloud models are still likely to perform better, so a hybrid workflow, switching between local and remote models depending on the task, is a sensible pattern. The ability to swap providers within the same chat interface makes that kind of switching low-friction.

It helps to understand the broader ecosystem. Ollama is one of several tools aimed at simplifying local model deployment; LM Studio and llama.cpp serve similar purposes, with llama.cpp providing the underlying inference engine that many of these tools build upon. On the editor side, extensions such as Continue and Cline have offered local-model integration for some time, giving developers alternative ways to bring open-weight models into their workflow. VS Code's growing native support reflects a wider industry trend in which AI coding assistants are becoming more model-agnostic rather than locked to a single provider.

A few prerequisites and caveats are worth keeping in mind. You need enough disk space for model files, which can range from a few gigabytes to tens of gigabytes. Some Copilot features may still require a GitHub account or subscription even when the underlying chat model is local, so the local model does not necessarily replace every cloud dependency. Security and licensing terms vary by model, and teams should verify that a given open-weight model's license fits their intended use.

Overall, the combination of VS Code and Ollama lowers the barrier to private, offline AI coding. It will not match the strongest hosted models in every scenario, but it gives developers a flexible, cost-controlled option and a way to keep sensitive code on their own machines while still benefiting from in-editor AI assistance.

d5435ec7103bd3c1.bodyJa:
開発支援ツールの進化が、ターミナルからランタイムの内部まで広がっている。2026年6月中旬の技術トレンドでは、GitHub Copilot CLIのカスタムエージェント、GitHubのシークレットスキャン強化、そしてGo 1.26で進むスタック最適化が話題を集めた。いずれも派手さよりも、日々の開発体験を地道に底上げする性格の改良といえる。

まず注目されたのが、GitHub Copilot CLIのカスタムエージェントだ。Copilotはエディタ上の補完から始まり、近年はチャットやコマンドライン、さらに自律的にタスクを進めるエージェントへと適用範囲を広げてきた。CLIのカスタムエージェントは、特定の役割や手順をあらかじめ定義し、ターミナルからその振る舞いを呼び出せるようにする仕組みと見られる。プロジェクト固有のルールやツール連携を組み込めば、定型作業の自動化や、文脈を踏まえた提案がしやすくなる可能性がある。

GitHubのシークレットスキャン改善も、地味ながら影響が大きいテーマだ。APIキーやトークンがリポジトリに誤って混入する事故は後を絶たず、漏洩は重大なセキュリティリスクにつながる。検出精度の向上や対応の自動化が進めば、開発者が安心してコードを公開・共有できる土台が強まる。GitLabなど他社のプラットフォームでも同種の機能が提供されており、サプライチェーンセキュリティ全体への関心の高まりを反映した流れといえそうだ。

言語側の動きとして取り上げられたのがGo 1.26のスタック最適化である。Goはゴルーチンごとに軽量なスタックを割り当てる設計で知られ、その効率はメモリ消費や実行性能に直結する。スタックの拡張や割り当てに関する最適化が入れば、多数の並行処理を扱うサーバー用途などで恩恵が期待できる。言語ランタイムの細かな改善は普段あまり意識されないが、大規模なワークロードでは積み重ねが効いてくる領域だ。

これらに共通するのは、開発者が意識せずとも効いてくる「足回り」の改善だという点だろう。最新機能を試す際は、自分のワークフローにどう組み込めるかを小さく検証してみるのが現実的なアプローチといえる。
d5435ec7103bd3c1.bodyEn:
There is a particular kind of momentum that comes from following technology trends week to week: at some point reading turns into the urge to actually run the code. This roundup gathers several threads from mid-June 2026 that prompted exactly that reaction, centered on GitHub Copilot CLI custom agents, improvements to GitHub's secret scanning, and a stack optimization arriving in Go 1.26. Each touches a different layer of the development workflow, but together they reflect a broader push toward putting AI assistance, security tooling, and runtime efficiency closer to where engineers already work.

The most prominent item is the custom agent capability in GitHub Copilot CLI. The command-line interface brings Copilot's conversational and task-execution features into the terminal, and the custom agent concept appears designed to let teams define specialized assistants with their own instructions, allowed tools, and scope. In practice this means a developer could configure an agent narrowly focused on, say, writing tests, reviewing diffs, or scaffolding infrastructure, rather than relying on a single general-purpose assistant. The approach mirrors a wider industry pattern in which agentic tooling is moving from monolithic chat interfaces toward composable, role-specific configurations. It also overlaps conceptually with custom instructions and prompt files that GitHub has been promoting elsewhere in the Copilot ecosystem, as well as with the Model Context Protocol, which standardizes how assistants connect to external tools and data sources. The value proposition is repeatability: codifying an agent's behavior so a team gets consistent results rather than ad hoc prompting.

Running these agents in the CLI rather than only inside an editor matters because the terminal is where a great deal of real work happens, from running builds and migrations to inspecting logs. Bringing an assistant into that environment lowers the friction of delegating multi-step tasks, though it also raises familiar questions about permissions and what an agent is allowed to execute autonomously. Sensible defaults and explicit approval steps are likely to remain important, particularly as agents gain the ability to run shell commands.

That security angle connects naturally to the second trend, GitHub's continued work on secret scanning. Secret scanning detects credentials such as API keys, tokens, and connection strings that have been committed to repositories, and push protection can block them before they ever land in history. The recent improvements appear aimed at reducing false positives and expanding coverage, which addresses one of the persistent complaints about such tools: noisy alerts that teams learn to ignore. Better precision, combined with validity checks that confirm whether a leaked credential is still active, helps prioritize the findings that genuinely need rotation. For organizations, this kind of refinement is less glamorous than new AI features but arguably more consequential, since leaked secrets remain a common entry point for breaches. It also fits the larger "shift left" philosophy of catching problems during development rather than after deployment.

The third item moves down the stack to the language runtime. Go 1.26 is reported to include a stack optimization, and while the precise details depend on the final release notes, work in this area typically targets how goroutine stacks are allocated, grown, or copied. Go's runtime manages many lightweight goroutines, each starting with a small stack that expands as needed, so even modest reductions in allocation overhead or copying cost can compound across highly concurrent workloads. Optimizations of this nature usually deliver incremental performance and memory gains rather than dramatic leaps, but for services running at scale they are welcome precisely because they require no code changes. This continues Go's long-standing pattern of using point releases to tune the runtime and garbage collector quietly beneath stable application code.

Taken together, these trends illustrate how progress in modern software development is distributed across the stack rather than concentrated in any single breakthrough. AI agents are reshaping how developers interact with their tools, security scanning is becoming more precise and less intrusive, and language runtimes keep extracting efficiency from mature codebases. None of these individually transforms a workflow overnight, and readers should treat early descriptions as provisional until features ship in stable form. Still, the practical lesson is consistent: the fastest way to understand any of them is to install the tooling, configure a small experiment, and see how it behaves against a real project.

9539faa1b205b50c.bodyJa:
GoogleおよびAlphabetのCEOであるSundar Pichai氏が、米Stanford大学の2026年卒業式で記念スピーチ（commencement address）を行い、その全文がGoogleの公式ブログ「The Keyword」で公開された。AIとテクノロジーが急速に社会を変えつつある時代に、次世代を担う卒業生へ向けたメッセージとして注目を集めている。

Stanford大学はPichai氏にとって縁の深い場所だ。インドのIIT Kharagpurを卒業後、同氏はStanfordで材料科学・半導体分野の修士課程に学んだ経歴を持つ。シリコンバレーの中心に位置する同大学は、Googleの共同創業者であるLarry Page氏とSergey Brin氏が在学中に検索エンジンの原型を生み出した場所としても知られ、テクノロジー業界との結びつきが強い。

公開された内容によれば、スピーチではAIをはじめとする技術の進歩が今後の社会や働き方をどう変えていくか、そしてその変化に卒業生がどう向き合うべきかが語られたとみられる。Googleは近年、対話型AI「Gemini」や研究部門Google DeepMindを軸に生成AI分野へ大規模な投資を続けており、OpenAIやAnthropic、Microsoftなどとの競争も激化している。こうした背景は、スピーチの語り口に少なからず反映されている可能性がある。

米国の卒業式における著名人のスピーチは、社会への問いかけや人生訓を伝える場として長く重視されてきた。過去にはAppleのSteve Jobs氏が2005年に同じStanfordで行った「Stay hungry, stay foolish」の演説が広く知られている。AIをめぐる議論が高まる中でテック企業の経営者が壇上に立つことは、産業界と教育機関の距離の近さを象徴しているとも言える。

AIが雇用や学びのあり方に与える影響への関心が高まるなか、業界を代表する経営者が若い世代に直接語りかける内容は、今後の技術と社会の関係を考えるうえで一つの視点を提供するものとなりそうだ。全文が公開されたことで、当日会場にいなかった人もその内容を確認できるようになっている。
9539faa1b205b50c.bodyEn:
Google has published the full text of a commencement address delivered by its chief executive, Sundar Pichai, to the 2026 graduating class at Stanford University, posting the transcript on the company's official Keyword blog. The release matters because it offers an extended, on-the-record view of how the leader of one of the world's most influential technology companies frames artificial intelligence and the pace of technological change for an audience about to enter the workforce and, in many cases, the industry itself.

According to the published summary, Pichai used the speech to share reflections on technology, the trajectory of AI, and what he describes as the path forward for the next generation. Commencement addresses occupy a particular niche in corporate communications. They are ceremonial by design, blending personal anecdote with broad advice, and they tend to avoid product announcements or financial detail. As a result, the value of such a speech lies less in news and more in tone: how a chief executive chooses to characterize the moment, the risks, and the opportunities for graduates who will spend their careers working alongside increasingly capable software systems.

The setting carries a degree of personal resonance. Pichai earned a master's degree from Stanford earlier in his career before moving into the technology sector, and the university sits at the heart of Silicon Valley, having produced founders and early employees of numerous major firms, including Google itself. Speaking to graduates there positions the address within a long tradition of technology leaders returning to influential campuses to reflect on their own paths and offer guidance.

The choice to publish the complete transcript, rather than a brief excerpt or summary, appears consistent with Google's broader communications approach, in which the Keyword blog frequently hosts long-form posts, executive essays, and policy statements. Making the full text available allows the company to control the framing of Pichai's remarks and gives readers, journalists, and students direct access to his wording rather than secondhand paraphrase.

The emphasis on AI reflects the dominant theme in the technology industry over the past several years. Google has invested heavily in the field through its Google DeepMind division and its Gemini family of models, which power features across Search, Workspace, Android, and the company's cloud offerings. That work unfolds against intense competition from OpenAI, whose ChatGPT helped accelerate mainstream interest in generative systems, as well as from Microsoft, Anthropic, Meta, and a growing roster of well-funded startups. For graduates entering this environment, the practical questions are immediate: which skills remain durable, how to work effectively with tools that automate parts of knowledge work, and how to weigh the benefits of these systems against concerns about reliability, bias, and labor displacement.

Pichai has addressed these tensions in other venues, often describing AI as among the most significant developments he expects to see in his lifetime while acknowledging the need for responsible deployment and regulatory engagement. Commencement speeches generally favor optimism, and it is likely that the Stanford address strikes a similar balance, encouraging graduates to embrace the technology while remaining mindful of its limitations and societal effects. Readers seeking the precise arguments and any specific commitments would need to consult the published transcript directly, since the themes can be summarized but the nuance resides in the full text.

For context, the publication continues a familiar pattern in which executives from major technology firms use academic ceremonies to articulate a worldview to younger audiences and, indirectly, to the public. Such speeches are frequently shared widely on social platforms and video channels, extending their reach far beyond the graduating class. Whether Pichai's remarks introduce notably new framing or restate established positions is best judged from the document itself. What is clear is that Google has chosen to give the address a durable home online, signaling that it views the message as worth preserving and circulating well beyond the single afternoon it was delivered at Stanford.

e9393736cbf6aa53.bodyJa:
複数のAIコーディング支援ツールを併用する開発現場が増えるなか、ツールごとに異なる「指示ファイル」の二重管理が新たな課題になっている。GitHub Copilot の Skill と、AWS が手がける AI 統合開発環境「Kiro」の Steering を自動同期する取り組みが、Qiita のブログ記事で紹介された。

背景には、両ツールが似た目的を持ちながら互換性を欠くという事情がある。Copilot の Skill も、Kiro の Steering も、プロジェクト固有のコーディング規約や設計方針、技術スタックの前提などをマークダウン形式で AI に伝えるための仕組みだ。AI が生成するコードの一貫性や精度を高める役割を担う点では共通している。

しかし、ファイルの配置場所やフォーマットはツールごとに異なる。Copilot は .github 配下などに、Kiro は .kiro/steering 配下に専用ファイルを置く構成を採るとされ、片方向けに書いた内容をもう一方へそのまま流用できない。両ツールを並行利用するプロジェクトでは、同じ内容を二か所で書き直し、更新のたびに手作業で両者を揃える必要が生じてしまう。

記事が示す解決策は、Copilot 用に整備した Skill を「単一の情報源」とし、その内容を Kiro の Steering へ自動的に変換・反映させるというものだ。手動同期に伴う記述漏れや内容のずれを防ぎ、どちらのツールから見ても一貫した指示を維持できる狙いがあると見られる。

こうした「指示ファイルの分断」は、Copilot と Kiro に限った話ではない。Cursor の Rules、Claude Code の CLAUDE.md、各種エージェントの設定ファイルなど、ツールごとに独自フォーマットが乱立しているのが現状だ。業界では設定方法の標準化を模索する動きもあるが、当面は今回のような変換・同期の工夫が現実的な選択肢となりそうだ。複数ツールを使い分けるチームにとって、運用負荷を下げる一つの実装パターンとして参考になるだろう。
e9393736cbf6aa53.bodyEn:
Teams that adopt more than one AI coding assistant quickly run into a quiet maintenance problem: each tool wants its own configuration files, written in its own format and stored in its own location. A blog post on Qiita illustrates this friction with a concrete case, describing a project that uses both GitHub Copilot and Kiro, and proposing a way to automatically synchronize the guidance written for one tool into the format the other expects.

The core issue is that Copilot's "Skill" and Kiro's "Steering" serve a similar purpose but are not interchangeable. Both mechanisms let developers give the assistant persistent, project-specific instructions—coding conventions, architectural notes, preferred libraries, or domain rules—so that the model produces more consistent output without the user repeating the same context in every prompt. However, Copilot and Kiro look for these instructions in different places and expect slightly different file structures, so a Skill authored for Copilot is not read by Kiro, and vice versa.

GitHub Copilot has expanded its customization options over time, moving from simple chat completion toward agent-style workflows that can read repository-level instruction files. Kiro, an AI-centric development environment, leans heavily on its steering files, which typically live under a dedicated project directory and can carry metadata controlling when each file is applied—always, only when certain file patterns are touched, or on demand. Because the two ecosystems evolved separately, there is no shared standard that guarantees a single source of truth.

The approach described is to treat the Copilot Skill as the canonical source and generate the Kiro Steering automatically from it. In practice this appears to involve a script or small automation that reads the Skill files, transforms them into the structure Kiro expects—adjusting front matter, directory layout, or naming as needed—and writes the result into Kiro's steering directory. Running this on save, as a pre-commit hook, or through a watch process keeps both tools aligned without forcing the developer to edit two copies by hand.

The benefit is straightforward: a single edit propagates to every assistant, reducing drift between configurations and the subtle problems that arise when one tool follows outdated guidance. For teams, it also lowers the cost of experimenting with a second assistant, since onboarding no longer means rewriting all existing instructions from scratch.

This pattern reflects a broader industry trend. As AI assistants proliferate—Copilot, Kiro, Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf, and others—each has introduced its own flavor of persistent context files, from Cursor's rules to repository-level instruction files and the emerging "AGENTS.md" convention that several tools have begun to recognize. The absence of a universal format means developers increasingly maintain parallel configurations, and lightweight sync utilities or converters have appeared to bridge them. Some efforts aim to standardize on a common file, while others, like the one in this post, accept the fragmentation and automate the translation between formats instead.

There are caveats worth noting. Automatic conversion is only as reliable as the mapping between the two formats, and features unique to one tool—conditional inclusion rules, tool-specific directives, or richer metadata—may not translate cleanly. The sync as described is one-directional, so edits made directly in Kiro's steering files could be overwritten on the next run. Anyone adopting the technique would likely want to document which file is authoritative and clearly mark the generated files as machine-produced, so that contributors do not unknowingly edit the wrong copy.

For developers juggling multiple assistants, the takeaway is practical rather than novel: until a shared standard settles, small automations that convert one tool's configuration into another's can meaningfully reduce maintenance overhead. The Qiita post offers a concrete starting point for anyone running Copilot and Kiro side by side, and the same idea generalizes to other combinations of AI coding tools, where the underlying challenge—keeping one set of intentions consistent across several agents—remains the same.

7ca16e56505762c6.bodyJa:
クラウド型の生成AIサービスが突然停止する事態を受け、手元のノートPCだけでどこまでローカルLLMを動かせるのかを検証した個人の観察記録が公開された。GPUを搭載しないメモリ16GBのノートという、ごく一般的な環境を舞台に、小型モデルの実用度を探る内容となっている。

きっかけは、話題を集めていた「Fable 5」が公開からわずか数日で提供停止となったことだという。生成AIに公私で深く依存する生活を送るなか、特定のクラウドサービスに頼り切ることのリスクを実感し、ローカル環境という代替手段を試す動機につながったと見られる。

検証の中心となったのは、Googleが提供する小型オープンモデル「Gemma」系の量子化版だ。記事ではQAT（Quantization Aware Training、量子化を見据えた学習）を適用したモデルなどが取り上げられている。QATは、モデルの重みを低ビットに圧縮しても精度の劣化を抑えやすくする手法で、メモリやストレージが限られる環境で大規模モデルを動かす際の現実的な選択肢として注目されている。

実際に複数の小型モデルを動かしたところ、応答速度や回答品質はモデルごとに差が出たという。なかでも印象的だったのが、推論過程を長く展開するタイプのモデルが「考えすぎ」て処理が破綻したケースだ。思考を冗長に重ねるうちに結論にたどり着けず、実用に耐えない結果になった可能性がある。推論特化型モデルは複雑な問題で力を発揮する一方、こうした暴走的な挙動が課題として指摘されることもある。

ローカルLLMをめぐっては、推論を効率化するllama.cppやOllama、LM Studioといったツールの普及により、専門知識がなくても手元のPCでモデルを試しやすくなっている。MetaのLlama系やMistral、Microsoftのphiなど、軽量で高性能を狙ったオープンモデルの選択肢も広がりを見せている。

本記事はあくまで個人環境での観察であり、性能評価やベンチマークを目的としたものではないと断っている。とはいえ、クラウドサービスの不安定さが意識されるなか、手元で動く小型モデルがどこまで使えるのかという視点は、多くの利用者にとって参考になりそうだ。
7ca16e56505762c6.bodyEn:
Running large language models locally — without a dedicated GPU and within the memory limits of a typical laptop — is becoming a practical question for anyone who has grown dependent on cloud-based generative AI. A recent personal write-up published on Zenn explores exactly that, documenting one developer's attempt to see how far small open models can go on a GPU-less notebook with 16GB of RAM. The author is careful to frame the piece as an observation log rather than a benchmark, but the experiment touches on a concern many users now share: what happens when the cloud service you rely on disappears.

The trigger was the abrupt withdrawal of a much-discussed cloud offering referred to as Fable 5, which the author says was pulled only a few days after its release. For someone who leans on generative AI heavily in both work and daily life, that kind of sudden discontinuation is a reminder that hosted services can vanish, change pricing, or restrict access with little warning. Keeping a local fallback that runs entirely on your own machine is one way to reduce that exposure, even if the local option is slower and less capable.

The technical setup matters here. Without a discrete GPU, models run on the CPU and lean on system RAM rather than dedicated video memory. On a 16GB machine, the operating system and other applications already consume part of that budget, so only a few gigabytes may remain for the model itself. This is why the experiment focuses on small models, typically those in the low single-digit billions of parameters, and on quantization, the process of compressing model weights to lower numerical precision so they fit in less memory and run faster.

One of the models tested was Gemma 4 in a QAT variant. QAT stands for quantization-aware training, an approach in which the model is trained or fine-tuned with quantization effects simulated during the process, so that the final low-precision version loses less quality than it would from naive post-training quantization. Google's Gemma line has previously shipped QAT builds aimed specifically at consumer hardware, and the appeal is straightforward: better output quality at a given memory footprint, which is precisely the constraint that matters on a 16GB laptop.

The article's headline detail is that one of the small models "thought too much" and effectively ran out of steam. This appears to describe a reasoning-oriented model that entered a long internal chain of thought and either failed to converge, exhausted its context window, or simply became too slow to be useful on CPU-only hardware. Reasoning models, which deliberately generate extended intermediate steps before answering, can be especially demanding in this setting, because every additional token of "thinking" costs time the CPU may not be able to spare. It is a useful illustration that more elaborate model behavior does not always translate into better results on constrained machines.

For readers wanting to try something similar, the surrounding ecosystem has matured considerably. Tools such as Ollama, LM Studio, and the underlying llama.cpp project make it relatively easy to download quantized models in formats like GGUF and run them locally, often with a few commands or a graphical interface. Open model families from Google, Meta, Alibaba's Qwen, Microsoft's Phi, and Mistral now routinely release smaller variants in the one-to-eight-billion-parameter range that are explicitly intended for laptops and edge devices.

The broader context is an industry shift toward smaller, more efficient open models that can run on-device, driven partly by privacy considerations and partly by the kind of service unpredictability the author experienced firsthand. The takeaway from this hands-on report is measured rather than triumphant: a GPU-less 16GB laptop can run small local LLMs for light tasks, but performance, speed, and reliability vary widely by model, and reasoning-heavy models in particular may struggle. As a personal record rather than a formal evaluation, it offers a realistic snapshot of what is achievable today, and where the limits still lie.

7ad913684da3e008.bodyJa:
Power Platform を中心に活動する地域ユーザーコミュニティ「PLUG（Power Platform Local User Group）」が、2026年5月31日（日）に「PLUG MeetUp Vol.2」を開催した。今回のテーマは「GitHub Copilot × Power Platform」で、生成AIをローコード／ノーコード開発の現場にどう取り入れるかを、登壇者と参加者が語り合う一日になったと見られる。

Power Platform は、Microsoft が提供する業務アプリ開発基盤だ。アプリ作成の Power Apps、業務自動化の Power Automate、データ分析の Power BI、対話ボット構築の Copilot Studio などで構成され、プログラミング経験が浅い「市民開発者」でも業務システムを組み立てられる点が特徴とされる。近年は企業のDX推進を支える存在として浸透してきた。

一方の GitHub Copilot は、GitHub と OpenAI、Microsoft が関わるAIコーディング支援サービスで、コードの補完や生成、説明などを自然言語ベースで行える。もともとはプロの開発者向けのツールだが、Power Platform 側でも各機能への Copilot 統合が進んでおり、ローコード開発と本格的なコード開発の境界が曖昧になりつつある。両者を組み合わせる発想は、こうした流れを背景にしたものと言える。

イベントでは、AIアシスタントを実際の開発フローに組み込んだ事例や、数式・ロジックを記述する Power Fx の作成を効率化する手法などが共有されたと考えられる。Microsoft は近年、Copilot ブランドを Windows や Microsoft 365、Azure など製品横断で展開しており、Power Platform もその一環に位置づけられる。AIによる開発支援は他社でも活発で、ローコード領域全体が大きな転換点を迎えている可能性がある。

コミュニティ主導の勉強会は、公式ドキュメントだけでは得にくい現場の知見を交換する場として機能している。生成AIの進化は速く、機能追加や仕様変更も頻繁なため、実際に手を動かすユーザー同士の情報共有の価値は一段と高まっているとみられる。PLUG のような地域コミュニティの継続的な活動は、AIとローコードが融合していく今後の開発スタイルを占ううえでも注目される。
7ad913684da3e008.bodyEn:
On Sunday, May 31, 2026, the Power Platform Local User Group, known as PLUG, held its second community gathering, PLUG MeetUp Vol.2. The session was built around the theme of pairing GitHub Copilot with Microsoft's Power Platform, framed as a day to discuss what a future of building alongside AI might look like. The event matters because it sits at the intersection of two fast-moving trends: the spread of AI coding assistants and the maturation of low-code development, and it reflects how practitioner communities are working through that convergence in practice rather than in marketing slides.

PLUG is a Japan-based, community-run user group focused on Microsoft Power Platform, the family of business application tools that includes Power Apps for building custom apps, Power Automate for workflow automation, Power BI for analytics, Power Pages for external-facing sites, and Copilot Studio for creating conversational agents. Local user groups like this typically operate independently of the vendor, organizing talks, demonstrations, and networking sessions where members share real-world lessons. A "Vol.2" meetup signals an early-stage but growing community effort, and the event report format suggests the day combined presentations with hands-on discussion among attendees.

The headline pairing—GitHub Copilot and Power Platform—is worth unpacking because the two products come from different ends of the development spectrum. GitHub Copilot is an AI pair-programming assistant that suggests code, completes functions, and answers questions inside editors such as Visual Studio Code, drawing on large language models. Power Platform, by contrast, is designed to let people build solutions with minimal hand-written code, using visual designers and expression languages like Power Fx. Bringing them together points toward what the industry often calls fusion development, where professional developers and so-called citizen developers collaborate, and where AI assistance lowers the barrier between low-code and pro-code work.

In practice, that combination can take several forms. Developers extending Power Platform solutions frequently write custom components, connectors, or plug-ins in languages such as TypeScript, JavaScript, or C#, and GitHub Copilot can assist with that conventional code. Power Platform also supports more advanced scenarios through tools like the Power Platform CLI, Azure functions, and the Dataverse data layer, all of which involve traditional coding that an assistant can speed up. An event organized around this theme likely explored how Copilot fits into these professional workflows, as well as how it complements the AI features Microsoft has been embedding directly into Power Platform itself.

That last point provides important context. Microsoft has been weaving its Copilot branding across nearly all of its products, and Power Platform now includes native generative AI capabilities, such as describing an app or a flow in natural language and having a draft generated automatically. Copilot Studio, formerly Power Virtual Agents, lets organizations build their own copilots and agents. So a discussion of "GitHub Copilot × Power Platform" appears to address a broader question many teams are facing: how to coordinate multiple AI assistants—some aimed at writing code, others at generating apps and automations—into a coherent way of working. Community events are a natural venue for surfacing the practical friction and the genuine wins that this raises.

For readers outside Japan, the meetup is also a useful snapshot of how Microsoft's developer and maker communities are responding to AI tooling on the ground. User groups have long been a channel through which platform knowledge spreads, and they tend to be candid about limitations as well as benefits. The emphasis on talking about the future "together with AI" suggests an exploratory, optimistic tone, while the event's grounding in a specific toolchain keeps the conversation concrete.

Anyone interested in following this space can look to adjacent resources, including Microsoft's official Power Platform and GitHub Copilot documentation, the Power Platform Community forums, and the growing body of guidance on responsible and effective use of AI coding assistants. As organizations weigh how to govern AI-generated code and apps, including questions of security, licensing, and data handling, community reports like this one offer an early read on what is working for practitioners. The PLUG MeetUp Vol.2 recap, in that sense, is less a product announcement than a window into how a regional community is experimenting with the tools that are reshaping both software development and business application building.

28a7a53907bf6beb.bodyJa:
省電力性を特長とする1ビット級の大規模言語モデル「BitNet」について、その省エネ効果を自宅PCのハードウェア計測機能で確かめる試みが公開された。クラウドに頼らずローカルでLLMを動かす関心が高まるなか、消費電力は実運用の現実的な指標として注目されている。

BitNetは、モデルの重みを一般的な16ビットや8ビットではなく、-1・0・+1の三値（約1.58ビット相当）で表現する点に特徴がある。重みが三値であれば乗算の多くを加算・減算へ置き換えられ、計算負荷とメモリ使用量を抑えられるとされる。Microsoftは「BitNet b1.58-2B」がQwen2.5系の同規模モデルと比べて約12倍エネルギー効率が高いと示したが、この数字は技術レポートに「Estimated（推定値）」と明記された計算上の値であり、実機の消費電力を直接測定したものではない。

筆者が用いたのはIntel CPUのRAPL（Running Average Power Limit）だ。RAPLはCPUパッケージやメモリが消費したエネルギーをカウンタとして読み出せる機能で、外部の電力計を用意しなくてもソフトウェアから取得できる。これを使い、BitNet向けの推論ランタイム「bitnet.cpp」などを動かした際の実測値を、公表されている推定値と突き合わせる狙いがある。

ローカルLLMの分野では、llama.cppに代表される軽量推論基盤や、4ビット前後への量子化技術が普及し、限られたメモリのCPUやGPUでも実用的な速度を引き出せるようになってきた。BitNetはさらに踏み込み、学習段階から低ビット化を前提とする設計を採る点で、学習後に圧縮する一般的な量子化とは異なるアプローチと位置づけられる。

ただし、RAPLが捉えるのはCPUとメモリ周辺が中心で、GPUや電源効率、システム全体の消費電力までは反映しにくい。測定環境やモデル、入力長によって結果が変わる可能性もあり、公称値との差をそのまま優劣の結論とするのは早計だと見られる。それでも、メーカー公表の推定値を個人が再現・検証する取り組みは、ローカルLLMの省エネ性能を見極めるうえで有益な視点を提供すると言えそうだ。
28a7a53907bf6beb.bodyEn:
A developer has published an experiment that puts one of Microsoft's headline claims about BitNet to a practical test, measuring the model's actual power draw on a consumer desktop using Intel's RAPL interface rather than relying on the vendor's published numbers. The exercise matters because energy efficiency is increasingly a selling point for low-bit language models, and the gap between estimated and measured figures has real implications for anyone planning to run inference locally.

BitNet is Microsoft's line of extremely low-precision language models. The widely discussed BitNet b1.58 variant uses ternary weights, meaning each parameter is constrained to one of three values: -1, 0, or 1. This roughly 1.58-bit representation is the headline feature, because it allows much of the costly floating-point multiplication in a transformer to be replaced by simpler additions and sign operations. In principle, that reduces both memory bandwidth and arithmetic energy, which is why BitNet has attracted attention from the local-LLM community looking to run capable models on modest hardware. Microsoft also maintains bitnet.cpp, an inference framework optimized for these ternary models on CPUs.

The specific figure under scrutiny is the claim that BitNet b1.58-2B is roughly 12 times more energy efficient than a comparable Qwen2.5 model. As the author points out, this number appears in Microsoft's technical report explicitly labeled as "Estimated." In other words, it is a calculated projection derived from operation counts and energy-per-operation models, not a wall-socket measurement of a running system. That distinction is important. Estimated energy figures typically isolate the arithmetic cost of matrix multiplications and assume idealized hardware behavior, whereas a real workload includes memory traffic, framework overhead, operating-system activity, and the simple fact that a CPU continues to consume baseline power regardless of how efficient the math is.

To get an empirical reading, the author turned to RAPL, which stands for Running Average Power Limit. RAPL is a feature built into modern Intel processors (and supported in a similar form on recent AMD chips) that exposes on-die energy counters for domains such as the whole CPU package, the cores, and in some cases the DRAM. On Linux these counters are readable through the powercap sysfs interface, commonly found under /sys/class/powercap/intel-rapl, and tools like perf or turbostat can sample them as well. By reading the counter before and after an inference run and dividing by the elapsed time, one can estimate average power and total energy consumed. RAPL is convenient because it requires no external meter, though it is worth noting that it reports modeled energy for specific silicon domains rather than the full system draw at the wall, so it tends to undercount components like the power supply, storage, and peripherals.

Running this kind of comparison on a home desktop, in this case a Core-class machine, introduces caveats that the article is careful to acknowledge. A real measurement folds in idle power, thread scheduling, memory access patterns, and the maturity of the inference kernels for each model. Because a ternary model still has to load activations, manage the key-value cache, and run non-linear layers in higher precision, the end-to-end efficiency gain measured in practice is generally expected to be smaller than the arithmetic-only estimate. This is a familiar pattern across hardware benchmarking: theoretical peak advantages rarely translate one-to-one into measured results once the full system is accounted for.

The broader context is a wave of interest in quantization and low-bit inference as a way to make large models cheaper to run. Techniques such as GPTQ, AWQ, and the GGUF quantization formats used by llama.cpp have made 4-bit and even lower-precision inference mainstream, and BitNet pushes that frontier toward the extreme of ternary weights. Efficiency claims in this space are frequently expressed as estimates because measuring energy rigorously is hard and hardware-dependent, which is precisely what makes independent, reproducible measurements valuable.

The takeaway is not that Microsoft's number is wrong, but that an "Estimated" label deserves to be read literally. Hands-on measurement with a tool like RAPL offers a useful sanity check, grounding marketing-friendly multipliers in the messier reality of a running machine. Readers interested in reproducing the work should pay attention to the exact CPU, the inference framework version, and which RAPL domains are being sampled, since all three can meaningfully shift the result.

8278c44bd096343f.bodyJa:
STMicroelectronicsのマイコン「STM32」の開発を、専用IDEではなくVSCode上で行う手法が注目を集めている。使い慣れた編集環境やGitHub Copilotを活用できる点が魅力だが、ツール周りの情報が錯綜しており、導入時に戸惑う場面も少なくない。

STM32の開発では、従来Eclipseベースの「STM32CubeIDE」や、Keil MDK、IAR Embedded Workbenchといった統合開発環境が広く使われてきた。これらはコンパイラやデバッガ、コード生成ツールが一体化しており導入は比較的容易な一方、エディタの操作性や拡張性に不満を持つ開発者もいる。

そこでSTMicroelectronicsは公式の「STM32 VS Code Extension」を提供している。これを使うと、ペリフェラル設定を行う「STM32CubeMX」で生成したプロジェクトをVSCodeで開き、ビルドからフラッシュ書き込み、デバッグまでを一通り行える。内部ではCMakeやコンパイラ(arm-none-eabi-gcc)、ST-LINK向けのデバッガといったツールチェーンを呼び出す構成と見られる。

VSCodeを使う最大の利点は、普段の開発で慣れたキーバインドや豊富な拡張機能をそのまま流用できる点にある。とりわけGitHub Copilotによるコード補完を組み込み開発でも使えることは、生産性の面で期待が大きい。

一方で注意点もある。拡張機能やCubeMXのバージョンによって手順や挙動が変わりやすく、ネット上の情報が古かったり断片的だったりするケースが目立つ。環境変数やツールチェーンのパス設定でつまずく可能性があるため、公式ドキュメントを基準に、自分のバージョンに合った情報を確認することが望ましい。

なお、VSCodeでマイコン開発を行う流れはSTM32に限った話ではない。PlatformIOのようにマルチプラットフォーム対応の拡張機能を使う方法もあり、ESP32やArduino互換ボードを含め、エディタ中心の開発スタイルは広がりつつある。用途やチームの状況に応じて、従来のIDEとVSCodeを使い分けるのが現実的だろう。
8278c44bd096343f.bodyEn:
STMicroelectronics' STM32 line of 32-bit microcontrollers has traditionally been developed inside dedicated environments such as STM32CubeIDE, but many engineers would rather stay in Visual Studio Code. With the official STM32 VS Code Extension, it is now possible to create, build, and debug STM32 firmware directly inside VSCode instead of a separate IDE. For developers who already live in VSCode, this matters because it removes the friction of switching tools and brings embedded work into the same editor they use for everything else.

The most cited benefit is environment consistency. Anyone comfortable with VSCode can keep their existing keybindings, themes, and extensions rather than learning the Eclipse-based interface of STM32CubeIDE. Just as importantly, VSCode supports GitHub Copilot, so firmware authors can use the same AI code completion and chat assistance they rely on in other languages. Embedded development involves a lot of repetitive peripheral configuration and register manipulation, so that assistance can be genuinely useful, although how helpful it is for low-level C still depends on the quality of the model's suggestions.

In practice, the extension is a coordinator rather than a single self-contained tool, and that is where much of the confusion around setup comes from. It relies on several separate ST packages working together. STM32CubeMX, the graphical configurator, is typically still used to pick a chip or board, assign pins, set up clock trees, and generate the initialization code. STM32CubeCLT, the Command Line Tools package, supplies the Arm GCC toolchain, the ST-LINK GDB server, and flashing utilities. The VS Code Extension then generates a CMake-based project, wires up the build tasks, and configures debugging.

On the technical side, projects produced this way usually build with CMake and Ninja, compiled by the GNU Arm Embedded toolchain (arm-none-eabi-gcc). Debugging is handled through the Cortex-Debug extension, which connects to the target by way of the ST-LINK GDB server or OpenOCD. Cortex-Debug also provides register and peripheral views when an SVD description file is supplied, giving roughly the same visibility into the hardware that a full IDE would. Flashing and on-chip debugging generally work over an ST-LINK probe, which is built into most STM32 Nucleo and Discovery boards.

Part of the reason the information can feel scattered is that the workflow has changed over time and older guides describe different approaches. For years, developers who wanted VSCode used community solutions instead: PlatformIO offers an integrated, multi-platform path for many STM32 boards, and others assembled their own setups around Makefiles, the Cortex-Debug extension, and manual launch configurations. Some existing CubeMX projects still generate Makefiles rather than CMake, so following one tutorial against a project created a different way can lead to mismatched expectations. Reconciling the versions of CubeMX, CubeCLT, and the extension is often the hardest part of getting started.

It is worth remembering what the alternatives still offer. STM32CubeIDE remains the all-in-one, officially supported option that bundles configuration, build, and debug with less manual assembly, and commercial toolchains such as Keil MDK and IAR Embedded Workbench continue to be common in professional settings, particularly where certified compilers or vendor support are required. The VSCode route trades that turnkey experience for flexibility and a more customizable editor.
