defb6096de13523f.bodyJa:
クラウド型の生成AIが普及する一方で、手元のパソコンだけで大規模言語モデル(LLM)を動かす「ローカルLLM」への関心が高まっている。今回紹介する記事は、デスクトップアプリ「LM Studio」を使い、Mac環境でローカルLLMを構築する手順を紹介したものだ。月額課金やAPI利用料を抑えつつ、手元でモデルを試せる点が魅力とされる。

筆者は前回、コマンドライン中心のツール「Ollama」でローカルLLM環境を構築した経験を踏まえ、今回は別のアプローチとしてLM Studioを取り上げている。Ollamaがターミナル操作を前提とするのに対し、LM StudioはGUI(グラフィカルな操作画面)を備えており、モデルの検索・ダウンロードからチャット形式での対話までを画面上で完結できる点が特徴だ。プログラミングに不慣れな利用者でも導入しやすいと見られる。

ローカルLLMの背景には、データを外部サーバーへ送らずに処理できるというプライバシー面の利点がある。社内文書や個人情報を扱う場面では、クラウドサービスに入力をためらうケースもあり、手元で完結する環境には一定の需要があると考えられる。また、ネットワークに接続せずに動作する点や、利用量に応じた従量課金が発生しない点も、用途によっては利点となり得る。

技術的には、LM StudioはHugging Faceなどで公開されているオープンモデルを、GGUFと呼ばれる軽量化されたファイル形式で扱うのが一般的だ。モデルは「量子化」によってデータ精度を落とし、メモリ消費を抑えた形で配布されることが多く、これによりMacのApple Silicon搭載機のような一般的なハードウェアでも動作させやすくなっている。ただし、モデルの規模やパラメータ数が大きいほど必要なメモリやストレージは増え、応答速度や回答品質はクラウド上の最新モデルに及ばない場合もある点には留意が必要だ。

ローカルLLMをめぐっては、MetaのLlamaシリーズやMistral、Google系のGemmaなど、オープンに公開されるモデルが相次いでおり、それを動かす実行環境の選択肢も広がっている。OllamaやLM Studioのほか、テキスト生成向けのWeb UIなど多様なツールが存在し、用途や好みに応じて使い分けられる状況だ。今回の記事は、こうした選択肢の一つとしてGUI重視のLM Studioを実際に試した記録であり、ローカルLLMに関心を持つ初学者にとって導入の足がかりになりそうだ。
defb6096de13523f.bodyEn:
Running large language models locally has become increasingly practical, and tools that lower the barrier to entry are a meaningful part of that shift. This article walks through setting up a local LLM environment using LM Studio on macOS, following a previous experiment with Ollama. For users who value privacy, want to avoid recurring API costs, or simply enjoy tinkering, comparing different tools that accomplish similar goals helps clarify which workflow fits best.

LM Studio is a desktop application that lets you discover, download, and run open-weight language models on your own machine. Where Ollama leans toward a command-line workflow with a lightweight server model, LM Studio centers on a graphical interface. After installing the application, users are presented with a built-in model browser that searches repositories such as Hugging Face, a chat window for interacting with loaded models, and a settings panel for adjusting parameters. This GUI-first approach appears designed to make local inference approachable for people who would rather not work in a terminal.

Under the hood, LM Studio relies on the same broad ecosystem that powers many local tools. It primarily runs models in the GGUF format, a quantized file format associated with the llama.cpp project, which is the inference engine that made running models on consumer hardware feasible in the first place. Quantization reduces the precision of a model's weights, shrinking memory requirements at some cost to accuracy. LM Studio typically offers multiple quantization levels for a given model, so users can trade quality against the amount of RAM or VRAM available. On Apple Silicon Macs, the application can take advantage of Metal for hardware acceleration, which generally improves throughput compared with CPU-only execution.

A notable feature is the local server mode. LM Studio can expose a running model through an OpenAI-compatible API endpoint, usually on a local port. This means applications written to call the OpenAI API can often be pointed at the local server with minimal changes, swapping the base URL and supplying a placeholder key. For developers prototyping retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, agents, or chat features, this compatibility is convenient because it keeps existing code largely intact while moving inference off external services. Ollama offers a comparable capability, so the choice between the two often comes down to interface preference and model management style rather than fundamental functionality.

Choosing a model is an important step. Smaller models in the range of a few billion parameters tend to run comfortably on machines with modest memory, while larger models demand more resources and may respond slowly or fail to load if memory is insufficient. Popular open-weight families such as Llama, Mistral, Qwen, and Gemma are commonly available through the browser, frequently in several sizes and quantization variants. The practical guidance is to start small, confirm that the environment works end to end, and then scale up only if the hardware allows. Monitoring memory usage during a first run helps avoid the frustration of a model that exhausts available resources.

It is worth placing these tools in a broader context. The local LLM space has grown quickly, partly because open-weight models have improved and partly because the surrounding tooling has matured. Beyond LM Studio and Ollama, projects such as llama.cpp, text-generation-webui, and Jan provide overlapping but distinct experiences, ranging from raw libraries to full-featured interfaces. Hugging Face functions as the central distribution hub for the model files themselves. None of these options entirely replaces the largest hosted models, which still tend to lead on raw capability, but for many tasks a well-chosen local model is sufficient and runs at no marginal cost.

The headline appeal of a local setup is captured by the phrase used in the earlier Ollama piece: an environment that costs nothing per month. Once the model is downloaded, inference happens on hardware you already own, and no data leaves the machine unless you send it elsewhere. The tradeoffs are upfront effort, the limits of consumer hardware, and the need to manage updates yourself. For those willing to accept that, LM Studio offers a polished and beginner-friendly entry point, and trying it alongside Ollama is a reasonable way to understand the strengths of each before committing to one for everyday use.

ca43cfae6dc08095.bodyJa:
ローカルLLMを業務に活かす実践例として、Mac mini を基盤に「AI秘書」として議事録作成を自動化する試みが紹介された。クラウドのAPIに頼らず手元のマシンで大規模言語モデルを常時稼働させ、機密情報を外部に出さずに高品位な議事録を生成できる点が大きな利点とされる。

この取り組みは、筆者が以前検討した「24時間365日稼働する自分用ローカルLLMに最適なMacは何か」という問いの延長線上にある。そこでの結論は、推論性能を左右するのはメモリ帯域だけでなく、入力テキストをまとめて処理するprefill段階の速度、すなわちGPUコア数が重要だというものだった。この知見を踏まえ、稼働基盤としてMac mini M4 Pro（64GB）が選択・導入された。

Apple Silicon はCPUとGPUがメモリを共有するユニファイドメモリ構造を採用しており、64GBという容量があれば数十億から数百億パラメータ規模のモデルも量子化して動かせる。消費電力が比較的小さく、常時稼働させてもコストを抑えやすいことから、個人や小規模チームのローカルLLMサーバーとして現実的な選択肢になりつつある。

実際の議事録自動化では、文字起こししたテキストを複数のLLMに与え、要約や決定事項の抽出、ToDoの整理といった処理を比較している。モデルによって日本語の自然さや構造化の精度、ハルシネーションの傾向に差が出ると見られ、用途に応じた使い分けが品質を左右する可能性がある。Ollama や LM Studio といったローカル実行環境、文字起こしを担う Whisper 系モデルを組み合わせれば、一連のワークフローを手元で完結させやすくなる。

背景には、生成AIの利用で情報漏洩を懸念する声が根強いことがある。会議の音声や議事録には人事や経営に関わる機密が含まれやすく、外部サービスへの送信をためらう組織も少なくない。ローカルLLMはこうした懸念に応える手段として位置づけられ、Meta の Llama や Alibaba の Qwen、Google の Gemma など高性能なオープンモデルの登場が追い風となっている。

一方で、ローカル環境はクラウドの最上位モデルに比べ、推論速度や絶対的な精度で見劣りする場面もある。今回の比較は、どの程度の規模・構成であれば実用に足る議事録が得られるかを見極める実践的な指針として、同様の環境構築を検討する読者の参考になりそうだ。
ca43cfae6dc08095.bodyEn:
A growing number of developers are running large language models entirely on their own hardware, and a recent Zenn post documents one such effort: turning a Mac mini into an always-on "AI secretary" that automatically produces high-quality meeting minutes. The appeal is straightforward. Meeting transcripts frequently contain sensitive business information, so processing them locally rather than sending them to a cloud API can address privacy and compliance concerns while keeping running costs predictable.

The project builds directly on an earlier article by the same author that asked which Mac is best for a personal local LLM intended to run around the clock. Its conclusion was notable because it argued against the common assumption that memory bandwidth is the decisive factor. Instead, the author recommended selecting hardware based on prefill performance, which is largely governed by GPU core count and compute throughput. Following that reasoning, the author settled on a Mac mini M4 Pro with 64GB of unified memory as the operating platform for this round of experiments.

The distinction between prefill and decode is central to understanding the choice. Prefill is the phase in which the model ingests and processes the input prompt, and its speed scales primarily with available compute. Decode, the token-by-token generation of the response, tends to be more sensitive to memory bandwidth. For a meeting-minutes workload this balance matters: the input is a long transcript that may run to thousands of tokens, while the output, a structured summary, is comparatively short. Because so much of the work is reading and digesting the transcript, prefill throughput appears to be the more relevant metric, which is consistent with the earlier recommendation.

The central experiment compares several LLMs running on the same machine to see which best handles Japanese-language minutes. Evaluating models side by side on identical hardware isolates model quality from infrastructure differences, allowing a clearer view of how each handles summarization, formatting, faithfulness to the source, and the tendency to hallucinate details that were not actually said. For minutes specifically, the qualities that matter include accurate attribution of statements, correct capture of decisions and action items, and a consistent, readable structure, all of which can vary noticeably between models even when their general benchmark scores are similar.

It helps to situate this within the broader local-LLM toolchain. On Apple Silicon, runtimes such as Ollama, LM Studio, and llama.cpp make it relatively easy to download and serve open-weight models, while Apple's MLX framework is increasingly used to take advantage of the unified memory architecture, in which CPU and GPU share the same pool of RAM. That shared memory is what allows a 64GB Mac mini to load models that would otherwise require a discrete GPU with substantial dedicated VRAM. A complete minutes pipeline typically pairs such a model with a speech-to-text stage, commonly Whisper or its optimized variant whisper.cpp, so that recorded audio is first transcribed and then passed to the LLM for structuring and summarization.

The choice of open-weight models is itself part of a wider industry shift. Families such as Qwen, Llama, Gemma, and Mistral have made locally runnable models considerably more capable, and several offer strong Japanese performance, which is essential for this use case. Quantization techniques, which compress model weights to lower precision, further reduce memory requirements and make larger models practical on consumer hardware, usually at some cost to accuracy. The trade-off between model size, quantization level, and output quality is one of the recurring tensions in projects like this.

The reported approach reflects a pragmatic philosophy that is becoming more common: rather than chasing the largest possible model, match the hardware and model to the specific task and run it continuously as a personal service. An always-on Mac mini consumes relatively little power compared with a workstation-class GPU, which strengthens the case for it as a 24/365 appliance. Readers should note that results from a single-author comparison are inherently workload-specific, and the best model for one organization's meetings may differ from another's. Even so, the post offers a useful, reproducible template for anyone weighing whether locally hosted LLMs can deliver dependable meeting minutes without relying on external cloud services.

ed0fea9a5cfe6dde.bodyJa:
ローカル環境で動かせる小型の大規模言語モデル（LLM）を使い、社内文書などを検索して回答を生成するRAG（検索拡張生成）が広がるなか、日本語タスクでのモデル選定が改めて注目されている。あるブログ記事は、複数のモデルファミリーを対象に8B（80億パラメータ）級モデルを比較し、欧米系モデルが日本語RAGで振るわない理由として「日本語ファインチューンの有無」が決定的だったと報告した。

RAGは、ユーザーの質問に関連する文書を外部から検索し、その内容をプロンプトに添えてLLMに回答させる仕組みだ。モデル自身がすべての知識を記憶していなくても、最新情報や社内固有の情報に基づいた回答を生成できるため、ローカルLLMの実用的な活用先として人気が高い。一方で、検索した日本語文書を正確に読み取り、自然な日本語で要約・回答する能力は、モデルの言語性能に強く依存する。

記事によると、MetaのLlamaやMistralといった欧米発の8Bモデルは、英語中心の学習データで訓練されているため、日本語の文章理解や生成で取りこぼしが生じやすいと見られる。同じパラメータ規模でも、日本語コーパスで追加学習（ファインチューン）されたモデルや、多言語データを厚く含むモデルのほうが、日本語RAGで安定した出力を示したという。英語版の記事では、中国製の8Bモデルが欧米モデルを上回ったとも言及されている。

背景には、トークナイザの設計やトークン効率の問題もある。日本語は英語に比べて1文字あたりのトークン消費が多くなりがちで、欧米モデルでは日本語処理が非効率になる場合がある。日本語に最適化されたモデルは、こうした面でも有利に働く可能性がある。

国内ではELYZAやrinna、サイバーエージェントなどが日本語特化モデルを公開しており、多言語に強いQwenなども選択肢に入る。今回の記録は限られた条件下のベンチマーク結果であり、評価方法やタスク次第で結論は変わりうる点には注意が必要だ。ただ、小さなパラメータ規模で日本語RAGを構築する際には、モデルの言語特性とファインチューンの有無を見極めることが重要だと示唆している。
ed0fea9a5cfe6dde.bodyEn:
Running large language models locally has become increasingly practical, and for Japanese-language applications the choice of base model can determine whether a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline returns usable answers or unreliable noise. A recent benchmark write-up on Zenn extends an earlier local-model selection experiment to several additional model families and arrives at a pointed conclusion: among models in the roughly 8-billion-parameter class, Western-developed models tend to underperform on Japanese RAG, and explicit Japanese fine-tuning appears to be the decisive factor separating the strong performers from the weak ones.

The headline observation, echoed in the author's English-language version of the post, is that a Chinese-developed 8B model outperformed comparable Western models on the same Japanese tasks. That outcome is less surprising than it might first seem. Parameter count is only one dimension of model quality, and at the 8B scale a model has limited capacity to absorb every language equally well. How that capacity is allocated during pretraining and fine-tuning matters enormously, and a model trained on a data mix with substantial Japanese or other CJK content can hold an advantage that raw size does not capture.

In a RAG setup, the model is not asked to recall facts from memory. Instead, relevant passages are retrieved from a document store and inserted into the prompt, and the model must read that context, reason over it, and produce a grounded answer. This shifts the burden toward reading comprehension and instruction following in the target language rather than toward world knowledge. A model that struggles to parse Japanese context, follow Japanese instructions, or stay faithful to the supplied text will produce hedged, off-topic, or hallucinated responses even when the retrieval step works correctly. The author's results suggest that Western 8B models often falter at exactly this stage.

Tokenization is a likely contributing factor. Many Western base models use tokenizers optimized for English and other Latin-script languages, which can fragment Japanese text into a larger number of tokens per character. Inefficient tokenization both inflates the effective context length consumed by retrieved passages and can degrade the model's representation of the input. Japanese-focused models and continued-pretraining efforts frequently extend or rebuild the vocabulary to handle kanji, hiragana, and katakana more compactly, which tends to improve both efficiency and downstream quality.

The broader context is a fairly active ecosystem of Japanese-adapted open models. Projects such as ELYZA's Llama-based releases, the Swallow series of continued-pretrained models, and various instruction-tuned derivatives have demonstrated that taking a capable English-centric base and applying Japanese continued pretraining plus instruction tuning can meaningfully close the gap. Meanwhile, model families like Qwen, developed with strong multilingual and CJK coverage from the outset, often perform competitively in Japanese without additional adaptation. The benchmark's finding aligns with this pattern: the deciding variable is exposure to high-quality Japanese data, whether that comes from a multilingual base or from targeted fine-tuning.

For practitioners assembling a local stack, these results carry practical weight. Tools such as Ollama, llama.cpp, and the GGUF quantization format have made it straightforward to run 8B-class models on consumer hardware, and quantization to 4-bit or similar precision is common to fit memory budgets. But choosing a model by size or popularity alone risks disappointing results on Japanese workloads. The author's approach of benchmarking across multiple model families on representative RAG tasks is a reasonable methodology, though readers should note that single-author benchmarks can be sensitive to prompt design, the specific retrieval setup, evaluation criteria, and quantization level, so the rankings are best treated as directional rather than definitive.

The takeaway is a useful reminder that language coverage is a first-class selection criterion, not an afterthought. As more organizations build internal knowledge assistants and document-search systems on local infrastructure for privacy or cost reasons, the relative strength of Japanese-tuned and CJK-strong models at small scales is likely to remain a recurring theme. Anyone planning a Japanese RAG deployment would do well to evaluate candidate models on their own data, paying particular attention to instruction adherence and faithfulness to retrieved context rather than relying on general-purpose leaderboards.

f9bdca7a863ad63e.bodyJa:
Anthropicの「Claude Code」において、複数のAIエージェントを協調させて動かすための仕組みが、大きく3つの系統として語られ始めている。具体的には「Dynamic Workflows」「Agent View」「Managed Agents」で、いずれもチームや企業規模での開発・運用を念頭に置いた機能群と見られる。対象はClaude Code v2.1.139以降とされ、Pro・Max・Team・Enterprise・APIの各プランで段階的に利用できる構成が想定されている。

マルチエージェントとは、単一のモデルにすべてを任せるのではなく、役割を分けた複数のエージェントが分担・連携してタスクを進める設計思想を指す。コード生成、レビュー、テスト、調査といった工程を別々のエージェントに割り当てることで、長時間にわたる複雑な作業でも文脈を保ちやすくなる利点がある。

3系統のうち「Dynamic Workflows」は、状況に応じてエージェントの処理手順を動的に組み替える仕組みを担うと考えられる。あらかじめ固定したフローではなく、入力やタスクの内容に合わせて実行経路を変える点が特徴とされる。「Agent View」は、複数エージェントの稼働状況や処理の流れを可視化する役割を持つ可能性が高い。エージェントが並行して動くと全体像の把握が難しくなるため、観測性（オブザーバビリティ）を高める層として位置づけられると見られる。「Managed Agents」は、組織側が権限や実行範囲を管理しながらエージェントを運用するための仕組みを指すとみられ、Enterprise用途との親和性が高い。

背景には、AIエージェントを単発の補助ツールから継続的な業務基盤へと押し上げようとする業界全体の流れがある。OpenAIやGoogle、Microsoftなども同様にエージェント連携やワークフロー自動化の枠組みを整備しており、Anthropicの動きもこの競争の一環といえる。一方で、複数エージェントを企業で運用する際には、権限管理・コスト・監査ログといった統制面の課題も伴う。今回の3系統は、こうした実運用の要請に応えるための整理と位置づけられる可能性がある。

なお現時点では機能の詳細やステータスが流動的な部分もあり、正式な仕様は公式ドキュメントやリリースノートで確認することが望ましい。
f9bdca7a863ad63e.bodyEn:
Anthropic appears to be consolidating its agent tooling for Claude Code into three distinct but related tracks: Dynamic Workflows, Agent View, and Managed Agents. For teams that have been stitching together their own orchestration scripts, this matters because it signals a move from ad hoc multi-agent experiments toward a more structured, supported framework. According to the source material, the documentation targets Claude Code v2.1.139 and later and spans the Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise, and API tiers, with a last update noted around the end of May 2026.

Dynamic Workflows is positioned as the mechanism for coordinating multiple agents whose execution path is not fixed in advance. Rather than running a predetermined sequence of steps, a dynamic workflow appears to let the system decide at runtime which subtasks to spawn, in what order, and how to recombine their results. This is the pattern often described elsewhere as an orchestrator-worker model, where a lead agent decomposes a request into smaller pieces, delegates them, and then synthesizes the outputs. The practical appeal is handling tasks whose shape is unknown until the work begins, such as multi-file refactors, broad codebase searches, or research questions that branch unpredictably. The trade-off, as with any agentic system, is that more autonomy tends to increase token consumption and makes runs harder to reproduce exactly.

Agent View is described as the observability layer. As agent systems fan out into parallel subtasks, understanding what each agent is doing, what it decided, and where it spent time becomes genuinely difficult. A dedicated view that surfaces the active agents, their delegation tree, intermediate state, and tool calls would address a recurring complaint about black-box behavior in multi-agent setups. It is reasonable to expect this to function as both a debugging aid and a cost-monitoring tool, since visibility into which branches consume the most resources is a prerequisite for tuning them. The summary indicates that Dynamic Workflows and Agent View share a status designation, which suggests the two are being rolled out or maturing together, likely because orchestration and observability are most useful as a pair.

Managed Agents reads as the enterprise-oriented track. Where the first two features concern how agents run and how you watch them, managed agents appear to focus on defining, provisioning, and governing reusable agents at the organization level. In practice this typically means centrally configured agents with set permissions, tool access, and scope, so that an administrator can publish an approved agent for a whole team rather than having each developer assemble one locally. That framing aligns with the enterprise tag on the post and with the broader industry pattern of adding role-based controls, audit trails, and policy enforcement once a capability moves from individual use into regulated organizations.

It is worth placing these three tracks in context. Claude Code already supports subagents and custom agent definitions, along with hooks and the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, which standardizes how models connect to external tools and data sources. The new tracks appear to build on that foundation rather than replace it, layering coordination, visibility, and governance on top of existing primitives. Anthropic has previously written about its own internal multi-agent research system, and the concepts here echo that work: a coordinator that delegates, parallel workers, and careful attention to the cost and reliability of orchestration.

The competitive backdrop is also relevant. OpenAI, Google, and a range of open-source frameworks such as LangGraph, AutoGen, and CrewAI have all pushed multi-agent orchestration, so a first-party, integrated offering inside Claude Code is a logical step to keep developers within the platform. The distinction Anthropic seems to be drawing is between the runtime engine, the inspection surface, and the management plane, which is a cleaner separation than many homegrown setups achieve.

Readers should treat specific behaviors as provisional until confirmed against official documentation, since features at this stage of rollout can change names, availability, or tier gating. The version requirement alone means older installations will not see these capabilities, and tier differences likely affect how much of Managed Agents is exposed. Still, the overall direction is clear enough: Claude's multi-agent story is being organized into orchestration, observation, and administration, and that structure is likely to make it easier to reason about, debug, and deploy agentic work at scale.

4d30a0793b29ab54.bodyJa:
複数の制作物を並行して進める個人クリエイターにとって、非公開の作業メモと公開用の実績一覧が別々のツールに散らばる問題は悩みの種になりやすい。Zennで公開された本稿は、この二重管理を解消する仕組みとして「my-atelier-vault」（Obsidian Wiki）と「Gallery」（Gitベース）を組み合わせた運用法を提案している。

筆者が指摘する課題は明快だ。趣味の制作を続けていると、進行中のアイデアや試行錯誤を書き留める私的なメモと、完成品を世に見せるポートフォリオが別ツールに分かれ、同じURLや公開日を二度入力する手間が生じる。情報の出典が分散すれば、更新漏れや表記揺れも起こりやすくなる。

提案されたアプローチは、作業の母艦となる知識ベースをObsidianで一元管理し、そこから公開用のGalleryへ必要な情報を流す構成と見られる。Obsidianはローカルのマークダウンファイルを相互リンクで結ぶ知識管理ツールで、データをプレーンテキストとして手元に保持できる点が特徴だ。一方のGalleryをGitで管理すれば、変更履歴を追いやすく、静的サイトとして公開する流れにもつなげやすい。

この発想が「AIエージェント全盛時代」と結びつくのは、GitHub CopilotやCursorといったAIコーディング支援ツールの普及が背景にある。タグにもcopilotとcursorが挙げられており、メモから公開用データへの変換や定型作業の補助をAIエージェントに委ねることで、二重入力の負担をさらに軽くできる可能性がある。プレーンテキストとGitを基盤に据える設計は、こうしたツールが内容を解析し編集しやすい形式でもある。

同種の課題に対しては、NotionやLogseq、あるいはJekyllやHugoといった静的サイトジェネレーターを使う方法も広く知られている。今回の構成はそれらと競合するというより、ローカル優先の知識管理とバージョン管理を組み合わせ、AIエージェントとの親和性を高めた一例として位置づけられそうだ。個人の制作活動を継続的に記録し公開する基盤づくりに関心がある読者にとって、参考になる視点を提供していると言えるだろう。
4d30a0793b29ab54.bodyEn:
Creators who juggle several side projects at once tend to hit the same friction point: the private notes that track works in progress live in one tool, while the polished list of finished pieces shown to the public lives in another. Because the two are disconnected, the same URL, release date, or project title often has to be typed twice and then kept in sync by hand. A recently published pair of tools, my-atelier-vault and Gallery, sets out to close that gap by treating personal work logs and a public portfolio as two views of the same underlying material.

The problem is worth taking seriously because the space between "working memory" and "published record" is a reliable source of stale or contradictory information. When a draft note says one thing and a portfolio entry says another, the public version is usually the one that quietly drifts out of date. Consolidating both around a single source of truth is a familiar pattern in software engineering, and the project appears to apply that same discipline to hobby and creative output.

The setup combines two well-established building blocks. my-atelier-vault is built on Obsidian, the Markdown-based note-taking application that stores everything as plain text files inside a local folder commonly called a vault. Obsidian is popular for personal knowledge management because its wiki-style internal links and graph view make it easy to connect related notes, and because the underlying files remain portable and tool-independent. Keeping private working notes in this format means the raw data is structured, searchable, and not locked into a proprietary database.

Gallery, the second component, is described as a Git-based portfolio. Storing the public-facing record in a Git repository brings version history, the ability to review changes before they go live, and a natural deployment path through services that build and host static sites directly from a repository. The likely intent is that information entered once on the private side can be transformed or exported into the public Gallery without manual re-entry, so a single edit propagates to both the personal log and the published portfolio.

This is where the framing around AI agents becomes relevant. The article is tagged with GitHub Copilot and Cursor, two AI coding assistants that have moved from autocomplete toward more agent-like behavior, where the tool can read across multiple files, follow instructions, and propose multi-step edits. For a setup that depends on Markdown notes feeding into a Git-managed site, such assistants can plausibly help with the repetitive glue work: reformatting a note into a portfolio entry, generating metadata, or scripting the conversion between the two formats. The piece appears to argue that this kind of automation is what makes maintaining parallel systems practical rather than tedious.

It helps to place this in the broader tooling landscape. The combination of Markdown files, Git, and a static site generator is a long-running pattern for personal sites and documentation, predating the current wave of AI agents. Tools such as Hugo, Astro, and Eleventy, along with platforms like GitHub Pages and Netlify, have made it routine to publish a website straight from text files. What is changing is less the file formats and more the labor of moving content between them, which AI assistants are increasingly able to absorb. Obsidian itself has a large plugin ecosystem, including publishing and Git-sync extensions, so the broad goal of bridging private notes and public output is not new; the contribution here is a specific, opinionated configuration.

For readers considering a similar workflow, a few prerequisites are worth noting. Comfort with Git basics, an understanding of how Markdown front matter carries structured fields like dates and tags, and some willingness to script or delegate the transformation step all make the model more viable. The benefits, reduced duplicate entry and a consistent public record, are concrete, but they come with the maintenance cost of keeping a custom pipeline working. As with any personal system, the optimal balance is likely to depend on how many projects someone runs in parallel and how much they value owning their data as plain, portable text.

13192bb44c5ed4f7.bodyJa:
ローカルでLLMや音声合成(TTS)を動かす環境として、AMDの「Ryzen AI Max+ 395」は魅力的な選択肢に見える。96GBにおよぶ大容量メモリをGPUと共有できるため、本来なら高価なグラフィックスカードを複数枚そろえなければ載らないような大きなモデルも、一台のマシンで扱える可能性があるからだ。本記事は、その環境で実際にLLMを動かそうとした筆者が直面した「地獄」を率直に記録したものである。

筆者は以前、「秘書AI」にTTSで声を与える記事のなかで、処理時間の計測を手元のRyzen AI Max+ 395(96GB)で行ったと触れていた。しかしそのときは「NVIDIAではないので動かすだけで本当に苦労した」とだけ書き、詳細は別記事に回していた。今回はその後日談にあたる。

苦労の根底には、AI・機械学習のソフトウェア資産がNVIDIAのCUDAに強く依存している現状がある。多くのライブラリやサンプルコードはCUDAを前提に書かれており、AMD環境では基本的にROCmと呼ばれる対応スタックを使うことになる。ただしROCmは対応GPUやOSの組み合わせが限られ、Ryzen AI Max+ 395が内蔵するような比較的新しいGPUでは、導入や認識の段階でつまずきやすいと見られる。

回避策として、CUDAにもROCmにも依存しないVulkanバックエンドを備えるllama.cppや、それを利用するOllama、LM Studioといったツールが挙げられる。これらはAMDのGPUでも比較的動かしやすい一方、CUDA向けに最適化された実装と比べると、性能や対応機能で差が出る場合がある。どの経路を選ぶかで、得られる速度も導入の難易度も大きく変わってくる。

このRyzen AI Max+ 395は「Strix Halo」と呼ばれる設計に基づくとされ、統合GPUとNPUを備える点で、ローカルAI向けの製品として注目を集めてきた。AMDもROCmの対応範囲拡大を進めており、状況は今後改善に向かう可能性がある。とはいえ現時点では、NVIDIA以外の環境で大規模モデルを快適に動かすには相応の試行錯誤が避けられない、という現実を本記事は浮き彫りにしている。同じハードウェアの購入を検討している人にとっては、性能の数字だけでなく、こうしたソフトウェア面の手間も判断材料になりそうだ。
13192bb44c5ed4f7.bodyEn:
Running large language models locally on AMD's Ryzen AI Max+ 395 promises a lot on paper, but the practical experience of getting that hardware to behave can be far from smooth. A recent blog post recounts the author's struggle to use a 96GB Ryzen AI Max+ 395 machine for local inference and text-to-speech (TTS) benchmarking, summarizing the journey with a phrase that translates roughly to "seeing the hell of local LLMs." The account matters because the chip is one of the more interesting options for memory-hungry models, yet it sits outside the well-worn NVIDIA and CUDA path that most tutorials assume.

The Ryzen AI Max+ 395, part of AMD's "Strix Halo" family, pairs a Zen 5 CPU with a large integrated Radeon GPU and, crucially, a unified memory architecture that can address well over 64GB. That large, shared memory pool is the main draw for local LLM work: models that would not fit on a typical consumer graphics card's 8GB to 24GB of dedicated VRAM can in principle be loaded into the APU's memory. For anyone wanting to run mid-sized or quantized large models, or to keep an LLM resident alongside a TTS pipeline, that capacity is appealing and comparatively affordable next to multi-GPU NVIDIA rigs.

The difficulty, as the post makes clear, is software. AMD's accelerated compute stack, ROCm, has historically lagged behind NVIDIA's CUDA in breadth of support, packaged tooling, and out-of-the-box compatibility with consumer and APU-class hardware. New architectures often arrive before ROCm officially lists them as supported, leaving users to wrestle with environment variables, version mismatches, kernel and driver requirements, and the precise allocation of system memory to the GPU. The result is that "just getting it to run," in the author's words, can consume far more time than the actual measurement or application work that motivated the purchase.

That experience is consistent with the broader state of the AMD local-AI ecosystem. Many practitioners reach for llama.cpp, which offers multiple backends including ROCm/HIP and a more portable Vulkan path; the Vulkan route sometimes works when ROCm does not, at the cost of some performance. Higher-level wrappers such as Ollama and LM Studio have improved AMD support over time, but coverage for the newest integrated GPUs can lag, and behavior may depend on whether the runtime correctly detects the device and the amount of memory it is allowed to use. On Linux, configuring how much of the unified memory is exposed to the GPU, and ensuring the right ROCm and kernel versions are installed, are common friction points.

The wider context helps explain why people persist despite the pain. Unified-memory designs have become a recognizable strategy for local inference: Apple's M-series chips popularized the idea that a large shared memory pool can run sizable models without discrete GPUs, and NVIDIA has pushed its own compact AI systems aimed at developers. AMD's Strix Halo is its answer in that space, and a number of mini-PCs and compact workstations built around the part now ship with large memory configurations specifically marketed for AI workloads. The hardware capability is real; the question is how quickly the supporting software matures to match it.

For prospective buyers, the takeaway appears to be that the Ryzen AI Max+ 395 can be a capable local-LLM platform, but it is likely best suited to users comfortable troubleshooting drivers, build flags, and runtime configuration rather than those expecting a turnkey setup. Checking current ROCm support status, recent llama.cpp and Ollama release notes, and community reports for the specific GPU and operating system before committing is a sensible precaution. The situation is also a moving target: ROCm and downstream tools are updated frequently, so issues that block a model today may be resolved in a later release.

The blog's framing, halfway between a cautionary tale and a how-it-went diary, reflects a common stage in any maturing hardware ecosystem, where the silicon arrives ahead of the polished software. For now, the gap between the chip's promise and its day-to-day usability is exactly the story worth telling.

f7d6c7d24557bfa3.bodyJa:
AIコーディングエージェントの利用が広がるなか、Microsoftが「Agent Package Manager(APM)」と呼ばれるツールを公開し、開発者コミュニティの注目を集めている。エージェントに与える指示やコンテキストを、npmのようにパッケージとして扱う発想が特徴で、「npm for agent context」と紹介されている。

背景にあるのは、AIコーディング支援ツールの乱立による設定ファイルの分断だ。Claude Codeでは「CLAUDE.md」、GitHub Copilotでは「.github/copilot-instructions.md」、Cursorでは独自のルールファイルと、ツールごとに異なる形式でプロジェクトの前提や規約を記述する必要がある。複数のエージェントを併用する開発者にとっては、同じ内容を各ファイルに重複して書く手間や、内容のずれが生じやすい点が課題となっていた。

APMはこうしたコンテキストを共通のパッケージとして定義し、各ツール向けの設定へ展開する仕組みを目指していると見られる。npmがJavaScriptの依存関係を扱うように、再利用可能な指示セットを配布・共有できるようになれば、チーム内でのコーディング規約の統一や、プロジェクト横断でのノウハウ流用が容易になる可能性がある。エージェントへの指示が増えるほど、その管理コストは無視できなくなるため、こうしたパッケージ的なアプローチには一定の需要があると考えられる。

この領域では標準化の動きも進んでいる。エージェントへの指示を記述する「AGENTS.md」のような共通フォーマットを採用するツールが増えつつあり、各社が独自仕様から相互運用可能な形へ歩み寄る兆しが見える。APMもこうした潮流の一つに位置づけられるだろう。

一方で、APMは比較的新しい取り組みであり、対応ツールの範囲や実運用での安定性については、今後の検証が必要だ。今回の記事では筆者が実際に導入を試しており、複数エージェント環境での設定管理を効率化する選択肢として、その動向は引き続き注目に値する。
f7d6c7d24557bfa3.bodyEn:
Anyone who has worked with more than one AI coding assistant has probably run into the same friction: every tool insists on its own configuration file. Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md, GitHub Copilot looks for .github/copilot-instructions.md, and Cursor relies on its own rules files. Microsoft's Agent Package Manager, abbreviated APM and described as "npm for agent context," is an attempt to bring order to this fragmentation. It matters because the instructions, conventions, and project knowledge that steer an agent are quickly becoming as important as the code itself, yet today they are scattered across incompatible files.

The core problem APM targets is duplication and drift. A team that wants its coding standards, architectural notes, or review checklists respected by every agent currently has to maintain near-identical content in several places. When one file is updated, the others fall out of sync, and onboarding a new tool means recreating the same context by hand. The "npm for agent context" framing suggests the proposed answer: treat reusable instruction sets as packages that can be installed, shared, and versioned, rather than as one-off Markdown files copied between repositories.

In practice, APM appears to act as a layer that defines context in a single canonical form and then distributes it to the tool-specific locations each agent expects. The npm analogy is instructive here. Just as npm lets developers declare dependencies in a manifest, pull them from a registry, and pin versions for reproducibility, a package manager for agent context would let a project declare which instruction modules it depends on and generate the appropriate CLAUDE.md, copilot-instructions.md, or equivalent outputs. This would, in principle, allow common guidance to be authored once and reused across projects and across competing assistants.

It helps to place APM against the broader move toward standardization. The industry has been converging on AGENTS.md, an emerging convention for a single, tool-agnostic instructions file that several agents have agreed to read. APM and AGENTS.md are not necessarily competitors; a format standard defines where context lives, while a package manager addresses how that context is composed, distributed, and maintained over time. The two could complement each other, with APM producing standardized files as one of its outputs.

Another relevant piece of context is the Model Context Protocol, or MCP, which Anthropic introduced and which Microsoft and others have adopted. MCP standardizes how agents connect to external tools and data sources at runtime. APM, by contrast, focuses on the static instructional layer, the prose and rules that shape an agent's behavior before any tool call happens. Seen together, they reflect a wider effort to turn ad hoc agent setups into something more like conventional software infrastructure, with protocols for connectivity and package management for configuration.

Microsoft's involvement is notable given its position across the ecosystem. The company owns GitHub and ships GitHub Copilot, operates npm itself, and has invested heavily in agentic developer tooling through Visual Studio Code and Azure. A package manager that smooths over differences between rival assistants, including those it does not control, is consistent with a strategy of making its platforms the connective tissue of agent-based development. Whether APM gains traction will likely depend on how many tools honor its output and whether a meaningful registry of shareable context packages emerges, much as npm's value came from its catalog rather than the command-line client alone.

For now, APM should be understood as an early-stage project rather than a settled standard. Hands-on reports, including the one this article draws on, describe experimenting with installing and generating context files rather than deploying it in production. The concept is promising because the underlying pain is real and growing as teams adopt multiple agents simultaneously. The open questions are practical: how conflicts between overlapping instruction packages are resolved, how versioning interacts with fast-changing agent behavior, and how much adoption competing vendors are willing to grant. Developers evaluating it would be wise to treat it as a useful experiment in a space that is still forming, and to watch whether the npm analogy holds up beyond the initial framing.

9d88ee612b481c72.bodyJa:
マイクロソフトが自社のオウンドメディア「Microsoft Source」で、AIが経済の基盤となる時代に企業がどう変わるべきかを論じた考察記事を公開した。記事は、人材が持つ「ヒューマンキャピタル(人的資本)」と、AIが処理する「トークンキャピタル(トークン資本)」を循環させ、複利的に強化し続けることが、あらゆる企業の競争力を左右すると主張している。

ここでいうトークンとは、大規模言語モデル(LLM)が文章を処理する際の最小単位を指す。生成AIの利用量は入力と出力で消費されるトークン数で計測され、その総量はクラウド上の計算資源への投資規模を反映する。記事は、このトークン消費を単なるコストではなく、企業が蓄積していく「資本」と捉え直す視点を提示している。

主張の核心は、人とAIを対立的に扱うのではなく、両者の間にフィードバックループを築く点にある。人材がAIを使いこなして成果を生み、その経験や知見がAIの活用方法をさらに洗練させ、結果としてより多くの価値あるトークン消費へとつながる。この循環が複利のように回り続けることで、企業全体の生産性が時間とともに加速する可能性があると論じている。

背景には、生成AIの普及で企業の業務プロセスが急速に変わりつつある現状がある。マイクロソフトは「Copilot」シリーズをはじめ、業務アプリやクラウド「Azure」にAIを深く統合する戦略を進めており、今回の記事もそうした方向性を補強する内容と見られる。同様にグーグルやアマゾン、OpenAIなども企業向けAIの導入支援に注力しており、AIをいかに組織の能力として定着させるかが各社共通の課題となっている。

ただし、こうした考察はマイクロソフト自身がAI事業を推進する立場からの提言である点には留意が必要だ。トークン消費の拡大がそのまま価値創出に直結するとは限らず、人材の再教育や業務設計、データ基盤の整備といった前提が伴わなければ、複利的な効果は得にくいとの指摘もある。AIを競争力に変えられるかは、ツールの導入以上に、組織が学習を続ける仕組みをどう作るかにかかっていると言えそうだ。
9d88ee612b481c72.bodyEn:
Microsoft's Source blog has published an opinion piece arguing that the defining competitive question for companies in an AI-driven economy is no longer whether to adopt artificial intelligence, but how to compound two distinct forms of capital together: human capital and what the author calls token capital. The framing matters because it reframes AI spending from a one-off technology purchase into an ongoing asset that, like financial capital, can either sit idle or be reinvested to generate returns over time.

Token capital refers to the capacity an organization holds to run AI models, measured in the tokens that large language models consume and produce. A token is the basic unit of text—roughly a few characters or part of a word—that models read as input and generate as output, and the volume of tokens processed is closely tied to both the cost and the practical throughput of generative AI systems. As enterprises deploy assistants and autonomous agents, their token consumption becomes a rough proxy for how much cognitive work they are offloading to machines. Treating that consumption as capital, rather than as a utility bill, is the conceptual move at the heart of the article.

Human capital, by contrast, is the familiar stock of skills, judgment, institutional knowledge, and relationships held by employees. The piece's central claim is that these two stocks are complements rather than substitutes, and that the returns from each depend on the other. People who know how to direct, verify, and refine AI output generate more value per token, while richer AI capacity frees people to focus on higher-judgment work, which in turn produces better data and better prompts that improve subsequent AI use. The author describes this as a feedback loop that, if managed deliberately, can compound—each cycle raising the productivity ceiling of the next.

The argument sits within a broader industry shift toward what vendors call agentic AI, in which models do not simply answer questions but plan and execute multi-step tasks using tools and data. Microsoft has been positioning its Copilot assistants, the Copilot Studio and Azure AI Foundry development environments, and a growing catalog of agents as the infrastructure for this transition. Competitors including OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have made similar moves, and the economics of inference—the cost of running a model to produce output—have become a focal point as token prices fall and usage scales. The piece appears designed in part to give enterprise leaders a vocabulary for budgeting and governing that usage.

Several practical implications follow from the thesis, though the article presents them as direction rather than prescription. Organizations are encouraged to measure AI not only by cost but by the output it enables, to invest in training so employees can extract more value from each interaction, and to build the data pipelines and guardrails that let agents operate safely. The compounding metaphor implies that early, disciplined investment is likely to widen gaps between firms over time, much as reinvested earnings separate companies financially. That conclusion is plausible but unproven, and it depends on assumptions about how reliably AI systems perform in production and how quickly workforces adapt.

Readers should keep the source in mind. As a Microsoft blog post, the piece reflects a vendor that benefits commercially when enterprises expand their AI consumption, and the token-capital framing aligns neatly with a consumption-based cloud business. The underlying observation—that the value of AI depends heavily on the people and processes around it—is widely shared among researchers and practitioners, and echoes long-standing findings that technology gains accrue mainly to organizations that also change how they work. Whether token capital becomes a durable management concept or remains a useful metaphor is unclear, but the article's core point, that human and machine capacity should be cultivated together rather than traded off, is consistent with much current thinking on enterprise AI adoption.

4fa898c2d4c824d4.bodyJa:
「Cursorが話題だが、ZedやVS Codeはどうなのか、乗り換えるべきか」という相談は増えている。本記事のソースは、用途に応じてエディタを選ぶ視点として「速度」「AI深度」「エコシステム」の3軸を提示しており、唯一の正解を押し付けない整理が参考になる。

前提として、3者の出自は異なる。VS CodeはMicrosoftが開発するElectron（Web技術）ベースの定番エディタで、拡張機能の数と普及度で他を圧倒する。CursorはそのVS Codeをフォークして作られたAIファーストのエディタで、UIや拡張資産の多くを引き継ぎつつ、AI機能を中核に据えている。ZedはAtomやTree-sitterに関わった開発者らが手がけるRust製の新興エディタで、性能と軽快さを前面に押し出している。

速度の軸では、ネイティブかつGPU描画を活用するZedが、起動やスクロール、大きなファイルの扱いで優位とされる。VS CodeはElectronゆえに相対的に重いと指摘されることがあるが、日常用途では十分という評価も多い。CursorはVS Code由来のため、基盤の重さを引き継ぐ可能性がある。

AI深度の軸では、Cursorが先行している。コードベース全体を参照した編集や、複数ファイルにまたがる変更を指示できるエージェント的な機能が強みだ。VS CodeはGitHub Copilotを中心に、近年はエージェント機能も拡充している。Zedも各種モデルとの連携を進めているが、AI体験の作り込みでは発展途上と見られる。

エコシステムの軸では、VS Codeが圧倒的だ。膨大な拡張機能やテーマ、企業内での採用実績が蓄積されている。CursorはこのVS Code拡張資産をある程度活用できる点が大きい。ただし公式Marketplaceの利用条件など、フォーク勢には制約が生じる場面もあるとされる。

総じて、安定性と資産を重視するならVS Code、AIを軸に開発フローを再構築したいならCursor、速度と将来性に賭けるならZed、という整理ができる。いずれも更新が速く機能差は流動的なため、最終的には自分のワークフローで短期間試して判断する価値があるだろう。
4fa898c2d4c824d4.bodyEn:
The question of which code editor to adopt has become unusually active over the past year, as AI-assisted development moves from a novelty to a daily workflow. Developers who once defaulted to a single tool are now weighing Zed, Cursor, and Visual Studio Code against one another, and a useful way to frame that decision is along three axes: raw speed, the depth of AI integration, and the maturity of the surrounding ecosystem. Each editor leans toward a different corner of that triangle, which makes the choice less about which is best and more about which trade-offs fit a given team or project.

Speed is where Zed makes its strongest case. Built from the ground up in Rust by several of the people behind Atom, Zed is engineered for low-latency editing, fast startup, and efficient handling of large files. Its rendering and input pipeline are designed to keep keystroke-to-screen latency minimal, and it has built-in collaboration features for real-time pairing. By comparison, VS Code and Cursor are both built on Electron, which carries a heavier memory and startup footprint. For developers who value a snappy, native-feeling experience and work primarily in text without heavy reliance on a large extension catalog, Zed appears to be the most responsive of the three. Its AI capabilities have grown, including assistant panels and agentic editing, though the surrounding tooling is still younger.

AI depth is the dimension where Cursor has built its reputation. Cursor is a fork of VS Code developed by Anysphere, which means it inherits much of the familiar interface and editor behavior while layering its own AI workflows on top. Its features include inline code generation, a chat interface aware of the codebase, multi-file editing through what it calls Composer, and agent-style modes that can plan and apply changes across a project. Because Cursor controls the editor itself rather than operating as an extension, it can integrate model interactions more tightly into the editing surface than a plugin typically can. The trade-off is that staying current with upstream VS Code updates and extension compatibility depends on Anysphere's own release cadence, and the most capable features are tied to a paid subscription and the underlying model providers.

VS Code remains the strongest on ecosystem, and that advantage is hard to overstate. As Microsoft's flagship editor, it sits at the center of an enormous marketplace of extensions, themes, debuggers, and language servers, and it benefits from deep integration with GitHub, the Language Server Protocol, the Debug Adapter Protocol, and remote development through containers, SSH, and the Web. On the AI side, GitHub Copilot and Copilot Chat are integrated directly, and Microsoft has been expanding agentic features as well. For many developers, this means VS Code can approach much of what Cursor offers while retaining the broadest tooling support and the most predictable long-term maintenance. The cost is that it is not as fast as Zed and that its AI experience, delivered largely through extensions, can feel less seamlessly woven into the editor than Cursor's native approach.

It is worth noting how interconnected these tools are. Cursor's VS Code lineage means muscle memory, keybindings, and many extensions carry over, lowering the switching cost. The Language Server Protocol, which VS Code popularized, is now a shared standard that benefits all three editors. And the AI layer itself increasingly depends on external model providers such as those from OpenAI and Anthropic, so the practical quality of suggestions can shift as those models update, somewhat independently of the editor.

In practice, the three axes rarely point in the same direction, so a realistic recommendation is to match the tool to the priority. Zed suits those who want performance and a lean editing experience; Cursor suits those who want AI woven tightly into multi-file work and are comfortable with a fork; and VS Code suits those who prioritize stability, extension breadth, and a vendor with long-term backing. Running more than one in parallel is also reasonable, since the configuration overlap is significant. Given how quickly this space is evolving, any assessment is likely to need revisiting as each project ships new releases.

aa9a45451ea7bcb5.bodyJa:
GitHub Copilot の自作カスタムエージェントを呼び出した途端、AI が具体的な作業の手を止めて「何を進めますか？」と問い返すだけの状態に陥った——。そんな現象を、システムプロンプトを約9割削減することで改善したという体験談が、VS Code 関連のブログで公開された。

筆者であるアーキテクトのやまぱん！氏は、Copilot に独自の指示を与えるカスタムエージェント（カスタムチャットモード）を構築していたところ、エージェントを呼び出した瞬間に挙動が変わり、自律的に手を動かさず確認ばかりを返す状態になったと報告している。

GitHub Copilot は VS Code 上で、ユーザーが定義した指示ファイル（instructions）やカスタムモードを通じて振る舞いを調整できる。こうした指示は内部的にシステムプロンプトとして AI に渡され、回答の方針やツールの使い方を方向づける。便利な一方で、指示が長大になったり相互に矛盾したりすると、モデルが本来の能力を発揮しづらくなる可能性がある。

筆者が取った対応は、肥大化したシステムプロンプトを約90%削減するというものだった。詳細な手順を細かく書き込むより、要点を絞った簡潔な指示の方が、エージェントが自律的に作業を進めやすくなったと見られる。これは大規模言語モデル一般で指摘される傾向とも整合的で、過剰な制約や冗長な文脈はかえって出力品質を下げる場合がある。

背景として、近年は Copilot に限らず、Cursor や Cline といったエージェント型ツールでもプロンプト設計（プロンプトエンジニアリング）の重要性が高まっている。指示を盛り込みすぎるとトークン消費が増え、文脈の希薄化も招きやすい。「足し算」より「引き算」の発想で指示を整理する手法は、他のツールにも応用できる知見と言えそうだ。

タイトルの「なにもしてないのにこわれた」は、設定やバージョンの小さな変化で挙動が崩れる開発現場の「あるある」を表す表現でもある。AI コーディング支援が日常化するなか、システムプロンプトをいかに保守し、シンプルに保つかは、多くの開発者に共通する課題となりつつある。
aa9a45451ea7bcb5.bodyEn:
GitHub Copilot's support for custom agents gives developers a way to tailor the assistant's behavior by supplying their own system prompts, but a recent Japanese-language blog post illustrates how that flexibility can quietly work against you. Writing under the handle "Yamapan," an architect recounts how a custom agent they had built abruptly stopped acting on its own and instead turned into what they describe as a "What shall we proceed with?" machine, asking for direction over and over rather than completing tasks. Their reported fix was blunt: trim the system prompt by roughly 90 percent.

The post's title, loosely "GitHub Copilot broke even though I did nothing, part 2," plays on a well-worn developer joke about software that appears to break on its own. In practice, behavior like this is rarely truly spontaneous. Agent platforms evolve, underlying models are updated, and prompt-handling logic changes, so an instruction set that worked one week can produce different results the next. That makes the experience worth examining beyond the humor.

A custom agent, sometimes called a custom chat mode, is essentially a configuration layer on top of Copilot. The developer writes a system prompt that defines the agent's role, tone, constraints, and the steps it should follow. In VS Code, this is increasingly tied to agent mode, where Copilot can read files, run tools, and make multi-step changes across a project. The system prompt sits in front of the user's request and the model's other context, shaping every response.

The trouble, as the post suggests, is that longer prompts are not automatically better. When a system prompt grows to include many rules, caveats, and "always ask before doing X" clauses, those instructions compete for the model's attention and consume part of a finite context window. Heavy emphasis on caution and confirmation appears to be a common culprit behind passivity: if a prompt repeatedly tells the agent to verify intent, seek approval, or avoid assumptions, the model may comply by doing little except asking questions. Reducing the prompt removes that conflicting pressure and lets the agent fall back on more capable default behavior.

This aligns with guidance that major model providers have offered. Both OpenAI and Anthropic have published prompt-engineering advice emphasizing clear, concise, non-contradictory instructions, and noting that piling on directives can dilute the ones that matter. The phenomenon is sometimes discussed as instruction conflict or "lost in the middle," where content buried in a long prompt receives less weight than material at the beginning or end. Cutting a prompt by 90 percent, while dramatic, is consistent with the broader lesson that prompt quality tends to matter more than prompt quantity.

There is also a maintenance dimension. As models become more capable, much of the scaffolding that early prompts contained, such as detailed formatting rules, exhaustive edge-case handling, and defensive reminders, can become redundant or even counterproductive. A prompt written against one model generation may need pruning when the platform upgrades the model beneath it. This is plausibly part of why the author felt the agent "broke" without any change on their end.

For developers building their own Copilot agents, the practical takeaways are straightforward. Start small and add instructions only when a concrete failure justifies them. Watch for directives that encourage hesitation, since excessive confirmation language can produce exactly the indecisive behavior described. Test agents after platform or model updates rather than assuming stable behavior, and keep prompts under version control so regressions can be traced. Treating the system prompt as a living artifact, rather than a one-time setup, fits the current pace of change in AI tooling.

1680595eccc9b2c7.bodyJa:
GitHub Copilotが2026年6月より従量課金（クレジット）制へ移行したことを受け、定額かつ低コストで使い続けたい個人開発者の間で、OpenCode GoをVS CodeのCopilot Chatのカスタムプロバイダとして利用する手法が話題になっている。

GitHub Copilotは個人向けに月額固定で利用できる点が支持を集めてきたが、今回の変更では利用量に応じてクレジットを消費する形になったとされる。生成AIの推論コストは、利用するモデルの高度化やエージェント的な処理の増加とともに膨らみやすく、提供側がコストを実態に合わせて回収する狙いがあると見られる。一方で、日常的に多用する個人にとっては月々の支出が読みにくくなり、定額制への回帰を望む声も少なくない。

そこで選択肢として挙がるのがOpenCode系のツールだ。OpenCodeはターミナル上で動作するオープンソースのコーディングエージェントとして知られ、Go実装版はそのバリエーションと位置づけられる。複数のモデルやAPIを切り替えて使える柔軟さが特徴で、定額系のサブスクリプションや比較的安価なAPIと組み合わせることでコストを抑えやすいとされる。

今回紹介されている手法の要点は、OpenCode GoをローカルでOpenAI互換のエンドポイントとして動かし、それをCopilot Chat側のカスタムプロバイダ（カスタムモデル）として登録する点にある。Copilot Chatは近年、独自のモデルやエンドポイントを指定できる仕組みを拡充しており、こうした外部プロバイダの差し込みが現実的になっている。これにより、使い慣れたエディタのチャットUIやワークフローを保ったまま、応答を生成するバックエンドのモデルだけを差し替えられる可能性がある。

同種の発想はCursorやCline、Continue.dev、Aiderといったツールでも見られ、OpenAI互換APIを介して任意のモデルを接続する流れは広がっている。ただし、Copilot本来のコンテキスト連携や補完精度をそのまま再現できるとは限らず、各サービスの利用規約や認証の扱いにも注意したい。コスト最適化と機能性のバランスをどう取るかが、移行を検討する際の判断材料になりそうだ。
1680595eccc9b2c7.bodyEn:
GitHub Copilot's billing model is changing, and for individual developers the shift has practical consequences. According to reports circulating in the developer community, from June 2026 Copilot moves toward a credit-based, pay-as-you-go structure rather than the flat monthly subscription that many users had grown accustomed to. From a business standpoint the change is defensible, since serving large language models at scale is expensive, but developers who prefer predictable costs are now looking for alternatives. One approach gaining attention is to keep using the familiar Copilot Chat interface in the editor while routing requests through OpenCode Go configured as a custom provider.

The motivation is straightforward. Under a usage-based model, heavy users who previously paid one fixed fee may see variable bills that rise with the number of premium requests or credits consumed. Casual users may pay less, but anyone who leans on AI assistance throughout the day faces uncertainty. OpenCode Go has become well known among developers who want a flat-rate, low-cost setup, and the idea here is to combine its cost profile with the editor integration that makes Copilot Chat convenient.

OpenCode Go is an open-source, terminal-oriented AI coding agent written in Go. VS CodeのGitHub Copilotで、選択したコードの意味を素早く尋ねたい場面は多い。本稿が扱うのは、その操作をキーボードショートカット一発で呼び出せるようにする設定方法だ。地味ながら、日々のコードリーディングの効率を確実に高める工夫といえる。

代替策として有効なのが、keybindings.jsonに独自のショートカットを登録する方法だ。VS Codeのコマンドパレットから「基本設定: キーボードショートカットを開く(JSON)」を選び、説明用のチャットコマンドに任意のキーを割り当てる。コマンドには引数としてプロンプトを渡せるため、選択範囲を対象に「このコードを説明して」といった依頼を自動で送る形にしておけば、毎回入力する手間が省ける。割り当てるキーは既存のショートカットと衝突しないものを選ぶとよい。

この仕組みの背景には、Copilot Chatがインラインチャット、サイドのチャットビュー、エディタ内チャットなど複数の入り口を持つことがある。/explainのほかにも、テストを生成する/tests、修正案を求める/fixといったコマンドが用意されており、用途に応じて使い分けられる。

同種の機能は他社のAI支援ツールでも一般化しつつある。CursorやJetBrains系IDEのAIアシスタント、Amazon Q Developerなども選択コードの説明や修正提案に対応しており、説明機能自体はコーディング支援の標準装備になりつつあるといえる。

ショートカット化は、こうした機能を「使いたい瞬間に最短で呼び出す」ための小さな最適化だ。コマンドIDや設定項目は今後のアップデートで変わる可能性があるため、動作しなくなった際は公式ドキュメントやコマンドパレットで最新の名称を確認するとよいだろう。
2206d16a3f56d2f1.bodyEn:
GitHub Copilot's chat features in Visual Studio Code have become a routine way for developers to understand unfamiliar code, and a common workflow is to select a block and ask the assistant to explain what it does. This piece looks at how to bind that action to a dedicated keyboard shortcut, a small piece of customization that matters because the path to triggering an explanation has shifted as Copilot's interface has evolved.

The starting point is VS Code's inline chat, opened by default with Ctrl+I (Cmd+I on macOS). Inline chat places a small prompt box directly in the editor next to the cursor or selection, letting you ask questions without leaving your code or switching to the side panel. For a long time, the quickest way to get an explanation was to select the relevant lines, open inline chat, and type the /explain slash command. Copilot would then return a description of the selected code in place.

According to the original post, that /explain command appears to no longer be available within inline chat. Slash commands in Copilot have been reorganized more than once, and some that were previously offered in the inline context were moved, renamed, or surfaced only in the dedicated Chat view. The /explain command still exists in the main Copilot Chat panel, but relying on the side panel adds steps compared with an in-editor prompt, which is the friction the author is trying to remove.

The workaround is to define a custom keybinding that invokes Copilot's explain action directly. VS Code exposes its commands through keybindings.json, which you can open with the "Preferences: Open Keyboard Shortcuts (JSON)" command from the command palette. Copilot registers commands such as github.copilot.chat.explain, and a keybinding entry can map a key combination to that command. A typical entry specifies a "key" value, a "command" value, and optionally a "when" clause to limit when the binding is active, for example only when text is selected or the editor has focus.

Some Copilot chat commands also accept arguments, which means a binding can pass a fixed prompt rather than relying on a built-in command name. In that pattern, the keybinding calls a command such as workbench.action.chat.open or an inline chat equivalent and supplies an "args" object containing the query text, such as an instruction to explain the current selection. This approach is useful when a named command has been removed but the underlying chat interface can still receive a prompt, and it gives you control over the exact wording sent to the model.

For readers setting this up, the prerequisites are an active GitHub Copilot subscription, the Copilot and Copilot Chat extensions installed, and a reasonably current version of VS Code, since command identifiers and available arguments change between releases. It is worth confirming the exact command name in your installation, because the identifiers Copilot registers can differ over time. The Keyboard Shortcuts UI lets you search existing Copilot commands to verify what is available before committing a binding to a JSON file.

This kind of customization fits a broader pattern in how AI coding assistants are being integrated into editors. Beyond Copilot, tools such as Cursor, Continue, and the assistants bundled with JetBrains IDEs offer similar explain, refactor, and document actions, and many let users tailor prompts or shortcuts. VS Code itself has been steadily expanding its chat surface, including agent-style modes and participant extensions, so the precise commands and their behavior are likely to keep changing.

Binding a stable shortcut to a frequently used action is one way to insulate a personal workflow from those interface shifts. The same technique can be reused for other recurring prompts, such as generating tests, writing documentation comments, or summarizing a diff, by changing the command or the prompt text passed in the arguments. For developers who lean on Copilot many times a day, the few minutes spent editing keybindings.json can pay back as a consistent, low-friction way to reach an explanation regardless of how the menus and slash commands are arranged in a given release.

37b4894f06cc0a3b.bodyJa:
ローカルで動かす大規模言語モデル(LLM)を、.NET製のクロスプラットフォームフレームワークであるMAUIから呼び出す実装例が公開された。クラウドのAPIに頼らずにアプリへ生成AI機能を組み込む手法として、コストやプライバシーの面で関心を集めそうだ。

きっかけは、AIを使ったアプリ開発を試みた際に、ChatGPTのSDKを利用するとクレジット(有料の利用枠)が必要になる点だったという。そこで、無料かつ手元の環境で完結するローカルLLMで代替できないかと考え、Ollamaを採用した。今回の実装では、MAUIアプリ側からプロンプトを送信し、レスポンスを受け取る一連の流れを構築している。

Ollamaは、LlamaやMistral、Gemmaといったオープンなモデルを手軽にダウンロードして動かせるツールで、ローカルでHTTPサーバーとして起動する点が特徴だ。標準でREST APIを備えており、特定のエンドポイントにプロンプトを送ればモデルからの応答がJSONで返ってくる。このためMAUI側では、HttpClientを使ってリクエストを送るだけで連携でき、SDKに依存しない構成が組みやすい。

MAUIはマイクロソフトが提供するUIフレームワークで、単一のコードベースからWindows、macOS、iOS、Androidのアプリを開発できる。デスクトップ向けであれば、同じ端末上でOllamaを動かしてローカル通信させる構成が現実的とみられる。一方、モバイル端末では本体のリソースが限られるため、別途サーバーを用意するなどの工夫が必要になる可能性がある。

ローカルLLMをめぐっては、Ollama以外にもLM Studioやllama.cppなど実行環境の選択肢が増えており、個人開発者が生成AIを手軽に試せる土壌が整いつつある。クラウドAPIと異なり通信費や従量課金が発生しない点は大きな利点だが、応答速度や精度は実行するマシンの性能とモデルサイズに左右される。用途に応じて、ローカルとクラウドを使い分ける判断が求められそうだ。
37b4894f06cc0a3b.bodyEn:
A developer's recent write-up documents a practical experiment: invoking a locally hosted large language model through Ollama from a .NET MAUI application. The motivation matters because it reflects a growing pattern among hobbyists and professional developers alike. Rather than paying for cloud API credits, such as those required by commercial SDKs tied to ChatGPT, the author chose to run a model on local hardware and call it from a cross-platform app. The result is a self-contained AI feature that incurs no per-request billing and keeps data on the user's own machine.

The two core technologies in this setup are Ollama and .NET MAUI. Ollama is an open-source tool that simplifies downloading, managing, and running open-weight language models on a personal computer. It packages models into a single command-line workflow and, importantly, exposes a local HTTP server, typically reachable at a localhost address on port 11434. This server provides REST endpoints, most commonly for generating completions and for chat-style conversations, which means any application capable of making HTTP requests can communicate with the model. Ollama supports a range of open models, including Meta's Llama family, Google's Gemma, Microsoft's Phi, Mistral, and Qwen, among others, allowing developers to choose a model that fits their hardware and quality needs.

.NET MAUI, or Multi-platform App UI, is Microsoft's framework for building native applications that run on Android, iOS, macOS, and Windows from a single C# codebase. Because the article's experiment combines MAUI with a local model, the integration essentially comes down to standard networking code. The app constructs a prompt, sends it as a JSON payload via an HttpClient to the Ollama endpoint, and parses the returned text to display in the user interface. This is the same general approach one would use to consume any web API, which is part of what makes the local model appealing: there is little new client-side concept to learn beyond the request format.

One technical detail worth noting is how responses are delivered. Ollama can stream output token by token, or return a complete response in one block when streaming is disabled. Streaming generally improves perceived responsiveness, since the user sees text appear progressively rather than waiting for the full answer, but it adds complexity to the client code that must read the response incrementally. For a first experiment, sending a single prompt and waiting for the full reply, as the author appears to have done, is the simpler path.

There are practical considerations that accompany this convenience. Running a capable model locally demands sufficient memory and, ideally, a GPU, although smaller quantized models can run on modest hardware with reduced quality or speed. Latency depends heavily on the machine, and a laptop without dedicated graphics may respond noticeably slower than a cloud service. When the model runs on a desktop while the MAUI app runs on a mobile device, the developer must also account for networking: the app would need to reach the host machine's IP address rather than localhost, and firewall or binding settings may require adjustment.

The broader context helps explain why this approach is gaining traction. The local LLM ecosystem has expanded quickly, with tools such as LM Studio, llama.cpp, GPT4All, and Jan offering similar capabilities through different interfaces. The shared appeal is cost control, offline operation, and data privacy, since prompts never leave the device. These benefits are particularly relevant for prototyping, internal tools, or applications handling sensitive information. The trade-off is that open models running on consumer hardware may not match the reasoning quality or speed of the largest commercial systems.

For developers working in the Microsoft stack, this pairing is a logical fit. Microsoft has also been promoting Semantic Kernel and the Microsoft.Extensions.AI abstractions, which can target multiple providers, including Ollama, potentially offering a more structured alternative to hand-written HTTP calls as a project matures. The experiment described here remains a straightforward proof of concept rather than a production architecture, but it illustrates an accessible entry point. By treating a local model as just another HTTP endpoint, a MAUI app can gain conversational AI features without external dependencies or recurring fees, lowering the barrier for those who want to explore on-device intelligence before committing to a paid cloud service.

8174023bb71168f2.bodyJa:
AIコーディングツールを複数併用しながら個人開発を進めるスタイルが、エンジニアの間で定着しつつある。今回取り上げるブログ記事は、Amazon が手がける「Kiro」と、Anysphere が開発する「Cursor」を用途ごとに使い分け、その方針と実際にかかったコストを実体験ベースで整理したものだ。両者は同じAI支援系ツールでありながら設計思想が異なるため、併用する意義があると筆者は説明している。

Cursor は、VS Code をベースにしたAI統合型のコードエディタとして知られる。チャットやインライン補完、コードベース全体を参照した編集などを通じて、既存コードの修正や反復的な実装作業をテンポよく進められる点が特徴とされる。普段使いのエディタとしてそのまま開発に組み込めるため、手を動かしながら細かく指示を出す作業との相性がよいと見られる。

一方の Kiro は、Amazon が公開したエージェント型の開発環境で、仕様(スペック)を起点に設計・実装を進める「スペック駆動開発」を打ち出している点が話題になった。要件をドキュメント化し、それをもとにタスクへ落とし込んでいく流れは、ゼロから機能を立ち上げる場面や、設計を固めながら進めたいケースで効果を発揮しやすいと考えられる。記事でも、両ツールはこうした得意分野の違いから自然と役割分担が生まれると述べられている。

コスト面については、いずれもサブスクリプション型の料金体系を採るのが一般的で、利用量やモデルの選択によって実質的な負担が変わってくる。個人開発では予算が限られるため、常時使うツールと、特定の局面だけ投入するツールを切り分ける発想が、無駄な支出を抑えるうえで現実的だという見方を筆者は示している。具体的な金額感は契約形態や時期によって変動するため、最新の公式情報を確認したうえで判断するのが望ましい。

8174023bb71168f2.bodyEn:
Using two AI coding assistants side by side has become a practical strategy for individual developers, and a recent hands-on report compares Amazon Kiro and Cursor specifically through the lens of personal projects and running costs. The premise is straightforward: rather than betting on a single tool, the author runs both, assigning each to the tasks it handles best and weighing what that division of labor costs over time.

The two tools come from different starting points, which is why they tend to complement rather than replace one another. Kiro is an agentic development environment that Amazon introduced in 2025, built on the open-source base that also underpins Visual Studio Code. Its distinguishing idea is what is often called spec-driven development: before generating code, Kiro guides the work through requirements, a design document, and a structured task list. The intent is to make larger or longer-lived features more deliberate, leaving behind artifacts that explain why the code was written a certain way. This appears well suited to greenfield work, scaffolding a new module, or any situation where having a written specification reduces the risk of an agent drifting off course.

Cursor, developed by Anysphere, is also a fork of VS Code, but it has grown up around fast, in-editor assistance. It is widely used for inline autocomplete, conversational edits across a codebase, and an agent mode that can plan and apply multi-file changes. In day-to-day practice, Cursor tends to shine when a developer already knows roughly what they want and needs to move quickly: small fixes, refactors, exploratory edits, and tight feedback loops. Because both editors share the VS Code lineage, switching between them carries little friction in terms of keybindings, extensions, and overall layout, which is part of what makes running both at once feasible.

The cost dimension is where individual developers feel the difference most directly. Cursor uses a tiered subscription model, with a free option and paid plans that expand request limits and model access; heavier use of premium models can push consumption higher. Kiro's pricing has been positioned around usage tiers as well, and because it draws on capable underlying models for its agentic and spec-generation steps, the expense scales with how much of that automated planning and code generation a developer actually invokes. The practical takeaway from this kind of comparison is that the two are not simply cheaper or more expensive than each other in the abstract; the real cost depends on workload. Reserving Kiro's more deliberate, spec-heavy workflow for substantial features while leaning on Cursor for rapid iteration is one way to keep the combined monthly bill predictable.

It helps to place this within the broader market. The category of AI-assisted coding has expanded rapidly, with GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Windsurf, Claude Code, and now cloud-vendor entrants such as Kiro all competing for developer attention. A clear trend is the move from autocomplete toward agentic workflows, where the tool can reason about a task, plan steps, and execute changes across multiple files with some autonomy. Spec-driven approaches like Kiro's represent one response to a known weakness of these agents: without structure, they can produce plausible but misaligned output. Writing the specification first is an attempt to keep the human in control of intent while delegating implementation.

For readers evaluating a similar setup, a few prerequisites are worth understanding. Both tools rely on large language models accessed over the network, so output quality and latency depend on the chosen model and connection. Privacy and code-sharing settings deserve attention, particularly for proprietary work. And because pricing and feature sets in this space change frequently, any cost comparison reflects a snapshot rather than a fixed conclusion. The reported approach, in essence, is less about declaring a winner than about matching each tool to the work it does well: Kiro for structured, specification-led building, Cursor for speed and in-the-moment edits. For a solo developer mindful of both productivity and spend, that pragmatic split is likely the most durable lesson, even as the specific numbers continue to shift.

bd3926d6e3f28604.bodyJa:
GitHub Copilot の利用に不満を感じた開発者が、Claude Code、Google AI Studio、そして OpenAI の Codex を順に試した体験を綴ったブログ記事が公開された。AI コーディング支援ツールが乱立するなか、実際の使用感を比較した記録として参考になる内容だ。

記事の発端は、GitHub Copilot Pro の挙動が安定しないと感じた点にあるという。GitHub Copilot は VS Code などのエディタに統合され、コード補完やチャットによる対話的な開発を支援するツールとして広く普及しているが、近年は各社が同種のサービスを次々と投入しており、選択肢が大きく広がっている。

筆者がまず試したのが Anthropic の Claude Code だ。これはターミナル上で動作するエージェント型のツールで、コードベース全体を把握しながらタスクを遂行できる点が特徴とされる。次に検証した Google AI Studio は、Gemini モデルを手軽に試せる開発者向けの環境で、プロンプトの調整やマルチモーダル入力に対応している。

最終的に筆者が、VS Code と Copilot による「セミバイブコーディング」に近い使用感として挙げたのが、ChatGPT Plus で利用できる Codex だったという。バイブコーディングとは、AI に大まかな指示を与えながら対話的にコードを生成していく開発スタイルを指す言葉で、近年広まりつつある。

この記事はあくまで個人の使用環境に基づく感想であり、料金プランやモデルの性能は時期によって変動する可能性がある。各ツールの優劣は用途や好みによって異なるため、一概にどれが最適とは言い切れない。ただ、応答速度やエディタとの統合度合いなどを実際に比較した記録は、同様の悩みを抱える開発者にとって判断材料になり得るだろう。

AI コーディング支援の分野は、GitHub、OpenAI、Anthropic、Google といった主要各社が競合しており、機能や価格の更新も頻繁だ。一つのツールに固定せず、複数を試しながら自分のワークフローに合うものを探す姿勢が、当面は現実的な選択肢となりそうだ。

The post documents a hands-on tour through several alternatives after the author judged GitHub Copilot Pro to be increasingly unreliable, before settling on OpenAI's Codex, accessed through a ChatGPT Plus subscription, as the option that best reproduced the working style they had grown accustomed to.

The reference point throughout is the combination of Visual Studio Code and GitHub Copilot, which the author characterizes as enabling a "semi-vibe coding" experience. The term "vibe coding," popularized by Andrej Karpathy earlier in the AI-assistant boom, describes a loose style of programming in which the developer expresses intent in natural language and leans on the model to produce working code, reviewing the results rather than writing every line by hand. A "semi" version implies a middle ground, where the human stays more closely involved in editing and steering than in fully hands-off generation.

The first stop after Copilot is Claude Code, Anthropic's command-line agent. Unlike an editor plug-in, Claude Code runs in the terminal and can read a repository, plan multi-step changes, run commands, and edit files directly, making it well suited to larger refactors and agentic tasks. Its strengths are widely credited to Anthropic's Claude models, which have earned a strong reputation for code generation, though the tool's usage-based costs and terminal-centric interaction differ noticeably from the inline suggestions that Copilot users expect inside an editor.

The author also tries Google AI Studio, the web-based environment for prompting Google's Gemini models. AI Studio is attractive partly because it offers generous access to capable models and a straightforward interface for experimentation, but it is primarily a prompting and prototyping surface rather than a tool tightly integrated into an editing workflow. That distinction appears to matter for day-to-day coding, where switching between a browser and an editor introduces friction that an in-editor assistant avoids.

The journey ends with Codex. OpenAI revived the Codex name in 2025 for a new generation of coding tools, including a cloud-based software-engineering agent and a command-line interface, and made access available to ChatGPT subscribers.
